A price floor

Above equilibrium price

A surplus

q.q: Which policy would most likely create a shortage?

A binding price floor

q.q: A legal maximum rent of $1,000 is shown on the apartment-market graph. How should this policy be classified?
options: Binding ceiling: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Nonbinding ceiling: $1,000 is below equilibrium.

Nonbinding floor: $1,000 is above equilibrium.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: The posted price is held below equilibrium, but buyers wait in long lines. What policy most likely caused this?
options: A binding price ceiling
A binding price floor
A tax on sellers
An outward PPF shift

labels: LO6.1

The ceiling creates a shortage
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling shifts supply right

options: Landlords have less incentive to maintain units when price cannot rise
Tenants always demand less housing at lower prices
Quantity supplied rises above quantity demanded
The ceiling is above equilibrium

q.q: A binding price ceiling and a tax both reduce market efficiency, but they do so differently. Which statement is correct?
options: A ceiling holds price below equilibrium, while a tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
A ceiling always creates a surplus, while a tax always raises quantity
A tax eliminates scarcity, while a ceiling eliminates opportunity cost
Both policies are the same as a demand increase
q.feedback: A price ceiling directly limits price, while a tax creates a gap between what buyers pay and sellers receive.

labels: LO6.1

Surpluses and unsold apartments
A rightward supply shift caused by lower rent

q.feedback: A binding rent ceiling creates shortages, so apartments may be rationed through waiting, search costs, or other nonprice methods.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. Officials lower a price ceiling from $50 to $40 and predict that the market price will fall by $10. With demand and supply unchanged, which assessment is correct?
options: Price falls from $50 to $40 because the ceiling sets the transaction price.
Price stays $30 because both legal maxima permit the equilibrium price.
Price rises from $30 to $40 because sellers charge the highest legal price.
Price falls from $30 to $20 because the legal maximum fell by $10.
q.feedback: The intersection is $30 and 200 units. Both ceilings are above $30, so both are nonbinding. Lowering a nonbinding ceiling while it remains above equilibrium changes the legal limit, not the competitive market outcome.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. A policy holds the price at $20. What is the full market result?
options: A binding price ceiling with a shortage of 100 units
A nonbinding price ceiling with no effect
A binding price floor with a surplus of 100 units
A nonbinding price floor with no effect
q.feedback: $20 is below the $30 equilibrium, so it is a binding ceiling. At $20, Qd is 250 and Qs is 150, so the shortage is 100.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. At $10, what are quantity demanded and quantity supplied?
options: Quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100
Quantity demanded is 100 and quantity supplied is 300
Quantity demanded is 150 and quantity supplied is 250
Quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150
q.feedback: At a low price of $10, buyers demand 300 units while sellers supply 100 units.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the graph. Relative to the competitive equilibrium, how do quantity demanded and quantity supplied change at the $1,000 ceiling?
options: Quantity demanded -100; quantity supplied +100.
Quantity demanded +200; quantity supplied unchanged.
Quantity demanded unchanged; quantity supplied -200.
Quantity demanded +100; quantity supplied -100.
q.feedback: At equilibrium both quantities are 150. At $1,000, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 50. Demand therefore rises by 100 while supply falls by 100, opening a 200-unit shortage.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. A price ceiling of $50 is imposed. Which answer is best?
options: The ceiling is nonbinding because it is above the $30 equilibrium price
The ceiling is binding because it is above the $30 equilibrium price
The ceiling creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
The ceiling creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
q.feedback: A ceiling above equilibrium does not restrict the market price, so it is nonbinding.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. A $20 price ceiling is imposed. Beyond the lower posted price, what additional market effect should occur?
options: Nonmoney rationing rises because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Nonmoney rationing falls because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Producer competition rises because sellers have excess unsold units
The market clears because the legal price is below equilibrium
q.feedback: A binding ceiling creates shortage, so rationing shifts into waiting, search costs, quality loss, and favoritism.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A city caps rent below equilibrium. The advertised rent falls, but apartment searches become longer, maintenance falls, and landlords screen tenants harder. What is the best economic diagnosis?
options: The ceiling lowers the posted price but creates shortage and nonmoney rationing
The ceiling lowers the posted price and therefore eliminates scarcity
The ceiling raises quantity supplied and creates seller competition
The ceiling is nonbinding because landlords still choose tenant quality
q.feedback: The posted money price is only part of the cost. Binding ceilings create shortage and hidden rationing costs.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A legal maximum price is set above equilibrium. A student predicts a shortage. What is wrong?
options: A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a shortage
Any price ceiling always creates a shortage
A ceiling above equilibrium creates a surplus
A ceiling above equilibrium is actually a price floor
q.feedback: A price ceiling binds only when it is below equilibrium.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A binding price ceiling on gasoline leads stations to sell out early. Some stations favor regular customers. What is the best interpretation?
options: The shortage creates nonprice rationing
The market clears because the legal price is low
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling increases supply
q.feedback: When price cannot ration the good, other methods like waiting, favoritism, and side payments can take over.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A rent ceiling causes landlords to convert apartments into short-term rentals outside the regulated market. What does this show?
options: The ceiling reduced regulated rental supply by changing landlord incentives.
A ceiling always increases quantity supplied
A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes
q.feedback: A binding ceiling lowers returns in the regulated market and can push suppliers to adjust around the policy.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the binding $1,000 rent ceiling, what is the maximum number of apartments that can actually be rented?
options: 200 thousand apartments
300 thousand apartments
400 thousand apartments
100 thousand apartments
q.imageAlt: The apartment market has monthly price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at 200 thousand apartments and 1,500 dollars. A ceiling at 1,000 dollars intersects supply at 100 thousand and demand at 300 thousand.
q.feedback: Transactions are limited by the short side, quantity supplied.
q.graphDescription: The apartment market has monthly price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at 200 thousand apartments and 1,500 dollars. A ceiling at 1,000 dollars intersects supply at 100 thousand and demand at 300 thousand.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A city caps rent below equilibrium to help renters. In the short run, some renters pay less, but many cannot find apartments and landlords reduce maintenance. Which answer best explains the full economic result?
options: The legal price falls, but shortage, rationing, and quality decline create hidden costs
The policy eliminates scarcity because rent is lower
The policy creates a surplus because quantity supplied rises
The market reaches equilibrium because demand and supply adjust immediately
q.feedback: A binding rent ceiling lowers the legal price but creates a shortage, rationing, search costs, and weaker maintenance incentives.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A city creates a low legal parking fee below equilibrium. Drivers spend extra time circling for spaces, miss class, and compete for limited spots. What is the best economic interpretation?
options: The ceiling lowers the money price but raises nonmoney costs through shortage and rationing
The ceiling creates a surplus of parking spaces
The ceiling is nonbinding because drivers still pay with time
The ceiling shifts demand left
q.feedback: A binding price ceiling can lower the posted price while raising search and waiting costs.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A binding rent ceiling lowers the rent paid by tenants who retain apartments by $300. At that rent, 28,000 more households want apartments than landlords offer. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: Continuing tenants save on rent, but the shortage does not identify how many former tenants lost housing
All 28,000 unmatched households must previously have rented apartments
Every household is better off because the legal rent is lower
The rent saving proves aggregate consumer surplus increased
q.feedback: The shortage compares current quantities demanded and supplied; it is not a count of displaced former tenants. Continuing tenants save on rent, but the net effects on all households also depend on lost access, allocation and any search costs.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A city subsidizes apartment construction while also imposing a binding rent ceiling. Which combined result is most likely?
options: More supply can ease—but not necessarily end—rationing under a binding ceiling.
The subsidy makes the ceiling irrelevant in all cases
The ceiling shifts demand left and eliminates scarcity
The policy must create a surplus because supply increases
q.feedback: A supply subsidy can ease shortage pressure, but a binding ceiling can still hold price below equilibrium and cause rationing.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the apartment graph. Under the displayed ceiling, what is the maximum number of rentals and the excess demand, assuming landlords offer the quantity on S0?
options: At most 50 rentals and excess demand of 200 apartments
At most 250 rentals and excess demand of 200 apartments
At most 150 rentals and excess demand of 100 apartments
At most 50 rentals and excess supply of 200 apartments
q.feedback: The ceiling is below the $2,000 equilibrium rent. At $1,000, supply is 50 and demand is 250. Supply limits possible rentals to 50, while excess demand is 250 − 50 = 200. Actual matching could be lower; the graph alone establishes a maximum.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compare a $20 ceiling with a $40 ceiling, assuming efficient matching and no other restrictions. Which policy comparison is correct?
options: $20 permits 150 trades and creates a 100-unit shortage; $40 allows the 200-unit equilibrium
$20 permits 250 trades and creates a 100-unit shortage; $40 allows the 200-unit equilibrium
$20 permits 150 trades; $40 forces 250 trades and a 100-unit surplus
Both ceilings leave the market at 200 trades because both are legal maximum prices
q.feedback: Equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. The $20 maximum binds: Qs = 150 and Qd = 250, so the shortage is 100 and at most 150 units trade. The $40 maximum allows the equilibrium price below it; it does not force the market to charge $40.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A binding ceiling reduces the number of apartments rented. Under which allocation would it create an additional loss beyond the gains from the missing rentals?
options: Some available apartments go to lower-value applicants while higher-value applicants go without
The remaining apartments all go to the highest-value applicants
The lower rent transfers money from landlords to continuing tenants
Landlords supply exactly the number of apartments willing buyers rent
q.feedback: A quantity reduction loses gains from missing beneficial trades. A further allocation loss arises if a lower-value recipient displaces a higher-value applicant. A ceiling does not by itself prove that this misallocation occurs.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: At a binding rent ceiling, 4,000 households demand apartments and landlords offer 2,700. A construction program adds 500 apartments at that rent, while new arrivals raise quantity demanded by 200. Assuming all offered apartments are rented, what changes?
options: Rentals rise by 500 and the shortage falls by 300
Rentals rise by 500 and the shortage falls by 500
Rentals rise by 200 and the shortage falls by 700
Rentals rise by 700 and the shortage stays unchanged
q.feedback: Initially the shortage is 4,000 − 2,700 = 1,300. Afterward demand is 4,200 and supply is 3,200, so rentals rise by 500 and the shortage is 1,000, down 300. Additional demand partly offsets the construction program.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the apartment graph. One tenant keeps the same apartment after the displayed ceiling is imposed but now spends time searching and queuing valued at $1,100 per month. With apartment quality unchanged, which evaluation is correct?
options: The tenant gains $1,000 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments
The tenant loses $100 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments
The tenant loses $100 net, and all 200 unmatched applicants must be former tenants
The tenant gains $100 net, and the market has excess supply of 200 apartments
q.feedback: The graph shows rent falling from $2,000 to $1,000, a $1,000 saving. Subtract the stated $1,100 time cost: the continuing tenant loses $100 net. At the ceiling, Qd = 250 and Qs = 50, giving excess demand of 200. The time cost is specified for this tenant, not asserted for every ceiling.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the graph. A student says a $2,000 rent ceiling binds and creates a 200-thousand-apartment shortage. Which diagnosis corrects both errors and identifies the policy that could sustain the gap at $2,000?
options: Binding ceiling: $2,000 and 100 thousand; Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding floor.
Nonbinding ceiling: $1,500 and 200 thousand; at $2,000, Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding ceiling.
Nonbinding ceiling: $1,500 and 200 thousand; at $2,000, Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding floor.
Binding ceiling: $2,000 and 300 thousand; Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding ceiling.
q.imageAlt: The apartment market has monthly price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at 200 thousand apartments and 1,500 dollars. A ceiling at 2,000 dollars intersects demand at 100 thousand and supply at 300 thousand.
q.feedback: Equilibrium is $1,500 and 200 thousand. A maximum of $2,000 permits that equilibrium and does not force price up. At $2,000, Qs=300 thousand and Qd=100 thousand: the hypothetical gap is a 200-thousand surplus. A floor at $2,000, not the stated ceiling, could hold price above equilibrium.
q.graphDescription: The apartment market has monthly price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at 200 thousand apartments and 1,500 dollars. A ceiling at 2,000 dollars intersects demand at 100 thousand and supply at 300 thousand.

labels: LO6.1

options: 25 units
45 units

115 units

labels: LO6.1

options: 350 apartments

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A price ceiling is set at $18 when equilibrium price is $25. At $18, Qd = 900 and Qs = 600. Which statement is correct?
options: The ceiling is binding and creates a shortage of 300
The ceiling is nonbinding and creates no shortage
The ceiling is binding and creates a surplus of 300
The ceiling is a price floor because it is below equilibrium
q.feedback: A ceiling below equilibrium is binding. Shortage is 900 - 600 = 300.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. If a price ceiling is set at $10, what shortage results?
options: 200 units
100 units
300 units
400 units
q.feedback: At $10, quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100. The shortage is 300 - 100 = 200 units.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A rent ceiling is set below equilibrium. Quantity demanded is 900 apartments and quantity supplied is 600. What occurs?
options: A shortage of 300 apartments
A surplus of 300 apartments
A shortage of 1,500 apartments
No effect because ceilings are minimum prices
q.feedback: The shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: 900 - 600 = 300.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $20, what shortage results?
options: 100 units
50 units
150 units
400 units
q.feedback: At $20, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150. The shortage is 250 - 150 = 100 units.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A city sets a price ceiling below equilibrium to make apartments affordable. The legal rent falls, but renters wait longer, landlords reduce maintenance, and some units are rented off-book. What is the strongest economic conclusion?
options: The posted price falls, but shortage shifts part of the cost into waiting, quality loss, and rationing
The posted price falls, so the policy removes the main cost renters face in the market
The posted price falls, but the shortage means sellers now compete harder for renters
The posted price falls, so the market clears through a lower equilibrium rent
q.feedback: A binding ceiling can lower the posted price while creating shortage, search costs, lower quality, rationing, and misallocation.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph and treat the plotted curves as straight lines. An enforced ceiling rises from $20 to $25. All units sellers offer are purchased, and there are no side payments or other changes. What happens to the shortage and quantity actually traded?
options: Shortage falls by 25 units; quantity traded rises by 50 units.
Shortage rises by 50 units; quantity traded falls by 25 units.
Shortage falls by 50 units; quantity traded falls by 25 units.
Shortage falls by 50 units; quantity traded rises by 25 units.
q.feedback: At $20, Qd=250 and Qs=150: shortage is 100 and trades are 150. Halfway to the $30 equilibrium, at $25, Qd=225 and Qs=175: shortage is 50 and trades are 175. The smaller gap reflects both lower quantity demanded and higher quantity supplied; trades are limited by the latter.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: Initially Qd=140-2P and Qs=2P, with a price ceiling of $40. Later demand becomes Qd=200-2P while supply stays fixed. What happens to the ceiling’s effect?
options: Initially nonbinding at equilibrium $35; later binding at $40, with Qd=120, Qs=80 and a shortage of 40.
Initially binding at $40 with a shortage of 20; later nonbinding because demand growth raises equilibrium above the ceiling.
Initially nonbinding at $35; later nonbinding at $50 because a ceiling never changes when only demand shifts.
Initially nonbinding at $35; later binding at $40, with a surplus of 40 because sellers supply more than buyers demand.
q.feedback: Initially 140-2P=2P gives P=35. Later 200-2P=2P gives P=50, above the ceiling. At P=40, demand is 120 and supply 80, so the previously nonbinding maximum becomes binding and creates a 40-unit shortage.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A binding price ceiling reduces the legal price from $100 to $70. At $70, buyers want 500 units and sellers offer 300 units. Which outcome is most likely?
options: A shortage of 200 units and rationing by waiting, favoritism, or side payments
A surplus of 200 units and falling inventories
No shortage because the legal price is lower
A demand decrease because buyers dislike lower prices
q.feedback: At the ceiling, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by 200 units. Because price cannot rise, the good must be rationed some other way.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A policy lowers the legal price, creates a shortage, reduces product quality, and causes buyers to spend time searching. Which policy best matches this pattern?
options: A binding price ceiling
A binding price floor
A nonbinding price floor
A seller tax with perfectly elastic demand
q.feedback: Lower legal price plus shortage and search costs points to a binding price ceiling.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A binding rent ceiling creates a 200-unit shortage. The city allocates apartments to whoever waits in line longest. Which conclusion best completes the analysis?
options: The money price is lower, but time costs rise and apartments may not go to those who value them most
The lower money price eliminates the economic cost of housing
Waiting lines prove that quantity supplied now exceeds quantity demanded
The allocation is efficient because every renter faces the same legal price
q.feedback: A binding ceiling lowers the posted price but can replace money costs with waiting, search, quality loss, and inefficient rationing.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: At a binding rent ceiling, Qd=8,000 and Qs=5,600. Of the supplied units, 400 are assigned by waiting list; they are not additional apartments. Later, 300 landlords withdraw units while Qd at the ceiling is unchanged. An official subtracts the 400 waiting-list allocations from the later shortage. What is the correct diagnosis?
options: Shortage rises from 2,000 to 2,300; waiting-list allocation reduces excess demand independently of the supplied apartments.
Shortage rises from 2,400 to 2,700; waiting lists allocate existing supply and do not add units or reduce the underlying gap.
Shortage falls from 2,400 to 2,100; withdrawals remove potential renters as well as the landlords’ supplied units.
Shortage stays 2,400; nonprice allocation prevents a change in the shortage when legal rent is unchanged.
q.feedback: Initial excess demand is 8000-5600=2400. Supply then falls to 5300, giving 8000-5300=2700. The 400 apartments are already counted in supply, so subtracting them again double counts an allocation as new capacity.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A rental market has Qd=10,000-2P and Qs=1,000+P. A $2,000 ceiling is introduced. Over time, 500 units are converted out of the regulated market at every rent, while demand is unchanged. Which sequence follows, and what can be inferred about tenants?
options: Equilibrium was $3,000; surplus is initially 3,000 and later 3,500 units, so all tenants necessarily gain from easier apartment access.
Equilibrium was $3,000; shortage is initially 3,000 and later 3,500 units, while search and quality costs can offset some tenants’ posted-rent savings.
Equilibrium was $2,000; the ceiling is nonbinding initially, and conversion creates a 500-unit shortage only because demand shifts right.
Equilibrium was $3,000; shortage falls from 3,000 to 2,500 units, and lower legal rent guarantees every prospective tenant is better off.
q.feedback: Set 10000-2P=1000+P to get P=3000 and Q=4000. At P=2000, Qd=6000 and Qs=3000, a shortage of 3000. Conversion lowers supply to 2500 and raises shortage to 3500. Lower posted rent does not ensure access or exclude search and quality costs.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A maximum legal price is binding only when it is set:
options: Below equilibrium price
Above equilibrium price

labels: LO6.2

q.q: At a binding minimum price for milk, farms offer 700 cartons and households want 455. There are no government purchases, and households buy all 455. A clerk calls the 455 sold cartons "the surplus." Which correction is accurate?
options: 245 cartons are unsold; 455 cartons are purchased.
455 cartons are unsold; 245 cartons are purchased.
245 cartons are unmet demand; 455 cartons are purchased.
1,155 cartons are unsold; 455 cartons are purchased.
q.feedback: Purchases are 455 cartons. The surplus is the amount offered but not purchased: 700 - 455 = 245 cartons. Supply exceeds demand, so the gap is unsold output, not unmet demand.

labels: LO6.2

q.q: A competitive market has:
options: Many buyers and sellers, none with much price control
One seller who controls the price
Only government buyers
No price signals
q.feedback: A competitive market has many buyers and sellers, each with little control over price.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A price taker is a buyer or seller who:
options: Accepts the market price as given
Sets the market price alone
Creates a legal maximum price
Always avoids trade
q.feedback: A price taker accepts the market price because no single buyer or seller controls it.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A price-taking seller is one that:
options: Sets any price without losing customers.
Controls the total market supply.
Cannot noticeably affect the market price by changing its own output.
Faces no competitors.
q.feedback: A price taker is too small relative to the market to influence the market price.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: Which feature most supports a competitive market?
options: One dominant seller.
Legal barriers blocking entry.
A unique product with no substitutes.
Many buyers and sellers with no single participant controlling price.
q.commonError: Using the everyday meaning of rivalry instead of the market structure.
q.feedback: Competitive markets disperse market power among many participants.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A wheat farmer sells at the posted market price because charging more would cause buyers to switch. This illustrates:
options: Price-taking behavior.
Monopoly pricing.
A binding price floor.
Perfect price discrimination.
q.commonError: Treating any chosen price as market power.
q.feedback: The farmer accepts the market price because close substitutes are readily available.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: If one small seller exits a highly competitive market, the market price usually changes little because:
options: Demand becomes perfectly vertical.
The seller represents a tiny share of total market supply.
The seller owns a patent.
All remaining sellers coordinate prices.
q.commonError: Overstating the influence of one small firm.
q.feedback: A small participant has little effect on total market supply.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: Which change would make a market less competitive?
options: More firms entering.
Lower switching costs for buyers.
A merger that leaves one firm with substantial control over output.
Better price information.
q.feedback: Concentration can give firms greater ability to influence price.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: Why does easy entry matter in a competitive market?
options: Economic profits attract new sellers, reducing market supply as existing firms divide sales among more rivals.
Economic profits attract new sellers, lowering each entrant’s costs until all firms share the same cost curve.
Economic profits attract new sellers, raising market demand as buyers redistribute purchases among rivals.
Economic profits attract new sellers, increasing competition and making those profits harder to sustain.
q.commonError: Ignoring how entry responds to profit opportunities.
q.feedback: Profit opportunities attract entrants when entry is easy. Their additional supply puts downward pressure on price and economic profits. Redistributing sales does not itself increase market demand, and entry does not make firms’ production costs identical.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A new technology lowers switching costs to nearly zero. Holding other factors constant, what competitive effect is most likely?
options: Sellers face more elastic demand and less pricing discretion.
Sellers gain more market power.
Entry becomes legally impossible.
Market demand becomes perfectly inelastic.
q.commonError: Reversing the effect of easier switching.
q.feedback: When customers can switch easily, a price increase causes a larger loss of buyers.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: Which observation most strongly contradicts the strict competitive-market model?
options: A firm can raise price persistently without losing many customers.
A firm earns accounting profit in one month.
Market demand changes over time.
Some firms have different bookkeeping methods.
q.commonError: Using temporary profit as conclusive evidence of market power.
q.feedback: Persistent price discretion indicates a downward-sloping firm demand curve rather than price taking.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A restaurant market has many sellers, but each offers a differentiated experience. Which statement is best?
options: The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.
The large number of restaurants makes each a price taker despite customers’ preferences for particular experiences.
Differentiation gives each restaurant the pricing freedom of a sole supplier because other dining experiences are distinct.
Competition should be assessed only through price differences, since differences in service quality do not affect buyer choice.
q.commonError: Treating market structures as all-or-nothing labels.
q.feedback: Many restaurants can compete for customers even when differentiated experiences give individual sellers some price discretion. Differentiation means the strict identical-product price-taking benchmark need not hold, but competing restaurants can still constrain each other’s prices.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A firm in a competitive market raises price above the market price while rivals do not. The likely result is:
options: Higher sales because price signals quality.
A sharp loss of customers to close substitutes.
No change because buyers cannot switch.
Automatic market-wide inflation.
q.commonError: Assuming a small firm can raise price without losing demand.
q.feedback: Buyers can switch to other sellers offering the same or similar product.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A licensing rule sharply limits new sellers. What is the most direct competitive effect?
options: The rule guarantees lower prices.
The rule creates perfect information.
Reduced entry can increase the market power of existing sellers.
The rule makes every firm a price taker.
q.commonError: Ignoring how entry barriers protect incumbents.
q.feedback: Barriers can weaken competitive pressure and preserve market power.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A market has many sellers, but buyers face high search costs and cannot compare prices. Why might price-taking be weakened?
options: Many sellers always eliminate market power.
High search costs strengthen competition by making buyers compare prices more carefully.
Price comparison is unrelated to competition.
Information frictions can give individual sellers some pricing discretion.
q.commonError: Assuming seller count alone determines competitiveness.
q.feedback: Competition also depends on buyer information and ability to switch.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A market appears fragmented by seller count, but four firms own most capacity through subsidiaries. What should an analyst examine?
options: Only the number of storefronts.
Whether prices are written in dollars.
Whether consumers enjoy variety.
Control of effective output rather than the number of brand names.
q.commonError: Counting labels instead of economic control.
q.feedback: Competitive pressure depends on independent control of capacity and decisions.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A market has free entry but strong network effects favor the largest platform. What is the best conclusion?
options: Legal freedom to enter makes the incumbent face perfectly elastic demand despite its user network.
Formal entry may be easy while effective competition remains weak.
Network effects remove the incumbent’s advantage because every entrant can start with an equally valuable user network.
The incumbent’s user advantage implies formal entry is restricted, so the premise of free entry cannot hold.
q.commonError: Equating legal permission to enter with practical competitive viability.
q.feedback: Permission to enter does not ensure that a new platform can attract enough users to compete effectively. When a platform becomes more valuable as its user base grows, the incumbent’s network can be an entry obstacle even without legal restrictions. That advantage does not establish perfectly elastic demand or equal starting networks.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: Two exchanges each list hundreds of sellers of standardized grain. On X, buyers can immediately compare prices and switch suppliers. On Y, contracts impose large switching charges. Which claim best separates seller count from effective competition?
options: An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on Y because switching charges protect buyer choice.
The same seller count ensures equal pricing discretion even when switching costs differ.
An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on X because buyers can readily use competing offers.
Standardization gives each seller a unique product, preventing price taking on either exchange.
q.commonError: Listing many traders without explaining why individual price control is limited.
q.feedback: Many sellers support competition when buyers can substitute among their offers. Price transparency and low switching costs on X make an individual price increase harder to sustain. Seller count alone does not establish equal competitive pressure.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A town has many independent sellers of identical notebooks. Customers can compare prices and switch stores at negligible cost. One store raises its price while others do not. Which outcome is most consistent with a competitive market?
options: It loses many customers because comparable alternatives limit its pricing discretion.
It keeps most customers because many sellers guarantee each store a loyal share.
It raises the market price because one seller’s posted price defines equilibrium.
It forces rival prices down because customers cannot compare standardized products.
q.commonError: Assuming a small firm can raise price without losing demand.
q.feedback: Independent rivals, a standardized good and easy comparison make close alternatives available. An individual store has little ability to sustain an above-market price.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: An economist points to a wheat farmer selling at the going market price. Why is the farmer a price taker?
options: The farmer's individual output is too small to control the market price
The farmer legally sets the national wheat price
The farmer faces no competitors
The farmer can ignore supply and demand
q.feedback: A price taker accepts the market price because no single seller has enough influence to set it.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A market has many buyers but only one seller, and that seller has control over price. Is this a competitive market?
options: No, because one seller has market power
Yes, because many buyers are enough
Yes, because all markets are competitive
No, because buyers never matter
q.feedback: A competitive market requires many buyers and sellers, with no single participant controlling price.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: Which seller is most clearly a price taker?
options: A patented-drug producer.
A small grain farmer selling a standardized crop at a market quotation.
A sole local utility.
A platform with locked-in users.
q.commonError: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.
q.feedback: A small grain farmer supplies a tiny share of a standardized market. Buyers can turn to other farmers, so this farmer generally accepts the quoted market price.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: What makes sustained economic profit difficult in a competitive market?
options: A single seller restricts output.
Buyers face high switching costs.
Entry by new firms expands supply.
Products become more unique.
q.commonError: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.
q.feedback: Entry adds market supply when existing firms earn economic profit. The resulting competitive pressure makes that profit harder to sustain.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A market has many buyers and sellers and standardized products. What does this imply about an individual seller’s ability to set price?
options: Each seller controls market demand.
Each seller can raise price without losing sales.
Buyers cannot compare offers.
An individual seller faces strong pressure to accept the market price.
q.commonError: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.
q.feedback: With many sellers offering standardized products, buyers can switch to competing offers. An individual seller therefore has little scope to charge above the market price.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A price taker is a seller that:
options: Accepts the market price because its own output is too small to move it.
Sets the market price for all firms.
Has no production costs.
Faces no buyers.
q.feedback: Price takers choose output but cannot materially influence the market price.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A market becomes more competitive when:
options: One seller acquires rivals.
Entry and switching become easier.
Products lose all substitutes.
Buyers receive less price information.
q.commonError: Reversing the effects of entry and switching costs.
q.feedback: Easier entry and switching strengthen competitive pressure.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: A price-taking firm is one that:
options: Cannot individually influence the market price
Sets any price it wants
Faces no competitors
Always earns zero profit
q.feedback: In a competitive market, an individual firm is too small to affect the market price.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: An online marketplace makes prices easy to compare and lets buyers switch with one click. This tends to:
options: Create a monopoly automatically.
Make demand for every seller inelastic.
Reduce each seller’s ability to charge above rivals.
Eliminate all production costs.
q.commonError: Failing to apply competition logic to digital markets.
q.feedback: Transparent prices and low switching costs constrain seller pricing power.

labels: LO4.1

q.q: Which statement defines willingness to pay?
options: The maximum amount a buyer would voluntarily pay
The amount every buyer actually pays
The minimum amount a seller will accept
The seller’s total revenue
q.feedback: Willingness to pay is the buyer’s maximum acceptable payment.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Which statement defines willingness to accept?
options: The price every seller actually receives
The minimum amount a seller would voluntarily accept
The maximum amount a buyer will pay
The seller’s total fixed cost
q.feedback: Willingness to accept is the seller’s minimum acceptable payment.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Consumer surplus is calculated as:
options: Price paid minus willingness to pay
Price paid plus willingness to pay
Willingness to pay minus the price paid
Seller revenue minus buyer value
q.feedback: Consumer surplus is buyer value minus price.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Producer surplus is calculated as:
options: Willingness to accept minus price received
Price received plus willingness to accept
Buyer value minus seller revenue
Price received minus willingness to accept
q.feedback: Producer surplus is price minus minimum acceptable amount.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Total surplus in a market equals:
options: Consumer surplus plus producer surplus
Consumer surplus minus producer surplus
Market revenue plus total cost
The price times every possible unit
q.feedback: Total surplus adds buyer and seller gains.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Ava is willing to pay at most $18 for a concert ticket. The market price is $12. What is the outcome?
options: $12 of consumer surplus
$6 of consumer surplus
$18 of consumer surplus
$30 of consumer surplus
q.feedback: Ava values the concert ticket at $18 and pays $12, so consumer surplus is $6.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Ben is willing to pay at most $25 for a used textbook. The market price is $17. What is the outcome?
options: $17 of consumer surplus
$25 of consumer surplus
$8 of consumer surplus
$42 of consumer surplus
q.feedback: Ben values the used textbook at $25 and pays $17, so consumer surplus is $8.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Cam is willing to pay at most $14 for a farmers-market basket. The market price is $14. What is the outcome?
options: $14 of consumer surplus
$28 of consumer surplus
$7 of consumer surplus
$0 of consumer surplus
q.feedback: Cam values the farmers-market basket at $14 and pays $14, so consumer surplus is $0.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Dina is willing to pay at most $11 for a bike tune-up. The market price is $15. What is the outcome?
options: No purchase; the price exceeds willingness to pay
A purchase with $4 of consumer surplus
A purchase with $15 of consumer surplus
A purchase with $11 of consumer surplus
q.feedback: The price exceeds Dina’s willingness to pay, so the purchase does not occur.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Alba will provide one museum pass only for at least $7. The market price is $12. What is the outcome?
options: $12 of producer surplus
$5 of producer surplus
$7 of producer surplus
$19 of producer surplus
q.feedback: Alba receives $12 and requires at least $7, so producer surplus is $5.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Brock will provide one meal-kit box only for at least $15. The market price is $21. What is the outcome?
options: $21 of producer surplus
$15 of producer surplus
$6 of producer surplus
$36 of producer surplus
q.feedback: Brock receives $21 and requires at least $15, so producer surplus is $6.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Cora will provide one tutoring session only for at least $10. The market price is $10. What is the outcome?
options: $10 of producer surplus
$20 of producer surplus
$5 of producer surplus
$0 of producer surplus
q.feedback: Cora receives $10 and requires at least $10, so producer surplus is $0.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Dev will provide one theater seat only for at least $16. The market price is $13. What is the outcome?
options: No sale; the price is below willingness to accept
A sale with $3 of producer surplus
A sale with $13 of producer surplus
A sale with $16 of producer surplus
q.feedback: The market price is below Dev’s minimum acceptable amount, so the sale does not occur.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: A buyer values a museum pass at $30 and pays $22. Which number is the buyer’s willingness to pay?
q.feedback: The buyer’s maximum value is $30.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: A seller would provide a meal-kit box for no less than $9 and receives $14. Which number is willingness to accept?
q.feedback: The minimum acceptable amount is $9.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: At the market price, the marginal buyer is the buyer who:
options: Has the highest willingness to pay
Receives the largest consumer surplus
Would buy every unit
Is just willing to purchase the last unit traded
q.feedback: The marginal buyer is at the trading cutoff.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: At the market price, the marginal seller is the seller who:
options: Is just willing to provide the last unit traded
Has the lowest cost
Receives the largest producer surplus
Would supply every unit
q.feedback: The marginal seller is at the trading cutoff.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: A voluntary exchange creates gains when:
options: Seller cost exceeds buyer value
The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least the seller’s willingness to accept
Price exceeds both value and cost
Buyer and seller surplus are equal
q.feedback: Value must cover cost.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: Why does a buyer with willingness to pay below price normally not purchase?
options: The buyer would receive producer surplus
The seller would have zero revenue
The exchange would give the buyer negative consumer surplus
The market would lower price automatically
q.feedback: Paying above value creates negative buyer surplus.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: Why does a seller with willingness to accept above price normally not sell?
options: The buyer would receive zero surplus
The seller would earn the largest surplus
The market would raise price automatically
The exchange would give the seller negative producer surplus
q.feedback: Receiving below cost creates negative seller surplus.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: On a standard graph, consumer surplus lies:
options: Below demand and above price through the quantity traded
Above demand and above price
Below supply and below price
Beyond the quantity traded
q.feedback: Consumer surplus is the value-price gap on traded units.

labels: Calculate consumer, producer, and total surplus from schedules, tables, and graphs.

q.q: On a standard graph, producer surplus lies:
options: Below supply and below price
Above supply and below price through the quantity traded
Above demand and above price
Beyond the quantity traded
q.feedback: Producer surplus is the price-cost gap on traded units.

labels: Calculate consumer, producer, and total surplus from schedules, tables, and graphs.

q.q: In the standard competitive model, the efficient quantity is reached where:
options: Every buyer receives zero surplus
Every seller receives equal surplus
Marginal willingness to pay equals marginal willingness to accept
The price is judged fair
q.feedback: Efficiency stops where marginal value equals marginal cost.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes efficiency from equity?
options: Both require equal surplus
Efficiency concerns only price
Equity always maximizes total surplus
Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution
q.feedback: Efficiency and equity answer different questions.

labels: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.

q.q: A market can maximize total surplus and still be criticized because:
options: The gains may be distributed very unevenly
Every efficient market has zero consumer surplus
Efficiency requires identical incomes
Producer surplus must exceed consumer surplus
q.feedback: Efficiency does not settle fairness.

labels: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.

q.q: Why is demand used to measure consumer surplus?
options: It records seller revenue
It represents marginal willingness to pay for successive units
It measures fixed costs
It counts firms
q.feedback: Demand height represents marginal buyer value.

labels: Calculate consumer, producer, and total surplus from schedules, tables, and graphs.

q.q: Why is supply used to measure producer surplus?
options: It records buyer income
It shows consumer surplus directly
It represents marginal willingness to accept or marginal cost
It measures maximum buyer value
q.feedback: Supply height represents marginal seller cost.

labels: Calculate consumer, producer, and total surplus from schedules, tables, and graphs.

q.q: If willingness to pay exactly equals price, the buyer receives:
options: Maximum consumer surplus
Negative producer surplus
Surplus equal to price
Zero consumer surplus
q.feedback: The difference is zero.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: If willingness to accept exactly equals price, the seller receives:
options: Zero producer surplus
Maximum producer surplus
Negative consumer surplus
Surplus equal to revenue
q.feedback: The difference is zero.

labels: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.

q.q: When two identical units are available, which buyer allocation maximizes measured surplus?
options: Give them to the two buyers with the lowest willingness to pay
Give them to the two buyers with the highest willingness to pay
Assign them randomly regardless of value
Give both to the marginal seller
q.feedback: Higher buyer values create greater total surplus when costs are unchanged.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: Total surplus measures the combined gains received by:
options: Sellers only
Government only
Buyers and sellers
Buyers only
q.feedback: Total surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: A market creates $40 of gains for buyers and $35 of gains for sellers. Which welfare measure combines both sets of gains?
options: Total revenue
Total surplus
Consumer surplus
Producer surplus
q.feedback: Total surplus combines the gains received by buyers and sellers.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: A trade creates $12 of consumer surplus and $9 of producer surplus. The gain from that trade is:
q.feedback: The total gain from exchange is the sum of the buyer’s and seller’s surplus.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: A voluntary trade is mutually beneficial when:
options: The seller’s willingness to accept exceeds the buyer’s willingness to pay
The market price is zero
Consumer surplus must equal producer surplus
The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least as high as the seller’s willingness to accept
q.feedback: A trade can create gains when the buyer values the unit at least as much as the seller’s opportunity cost.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: If a transaction creates no consumer surplus but $6 of producer surplus, total surplus from that transaction is:
options: Cannot be positive unless both sides receive surplus
q.feedback: Total surplus adds the gains of both sides; one side may receive all of the measured surplus.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: Which statement about total surplus is correct?
options: It ignores all gains from voluntary exchange
It can rise even if one side receives a smaller share of the gains
It rises only when consumer and producer surplus rise by identical amounts
It is the same thing as total revenue
q.feedback: Efficiency concerns the size of total gains, not whether those gains are split evenly.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: If a mutually beneficial trade is prevented, the unrealized gain is best described as:
options: Lost total surplus
A transfer from buyer to seller
Higher total revenue
Producer surplus that still exists
q.feedback: Preventing a beneficial trade destroys the buyer-seller gain that would otherwise be created.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: Consumer surplus falls by $8 while producer surplus rises by $8 and no trades are lost. Total surplus:
options: Falls by $16
Rises by $16
Must become zero
Does not change
q.feedback: An equal transfer between buyers and sellers changes distribution but not the combined surplus.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: In an efficient allocation, a unit should be produced when:
options: The market price is below zero
Consumer and producer surplus must be equal
The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least the seller’s willingness to accept
The seller’s willingness to accept exceeds every buyer’s willingness to pay
q.feedback: Production creates a nonnegative gain when value to the buyer covers the seller’s opportunity cost.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: Efficiency requires goods to go to buyers who:
options: Always pay the highest possible price
Value them most highly as measured by willingness to pay
Have the lowest willingness to pay
Arrive first regardless of value
q.feedback: Allocating units to higher-value buyers maximizes measured gains from consumption.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: Efficiency requires production by sellers who:
options: Can supply at the lowest opportunity cost
Have the highest willingness to accept
Charge the highest price
Receive the largest fixed subsidy
q.feedback: Using lower-cost sellers preserves more surplus from each unit produced.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: Once the next seller’s willingness to accept exceeds the next buyer’s willingness to pay, producing one more unit would:
options: Increase total surplus
Leave total surplus unchanged by definition
Create consumer surplus with no cost
Reduce total surplus
q.feedback: The next unit costs more to produce than the buyer values it, so it destroys surplus.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: The efficient quantity is the quantity that:
options: Maximizes consumer surplus only
Guarantees equal incomes
Maximizes total surplus
Maximizes producer surplus only
q.feedback: Efficiency in this model is defined by maximizing the combined gains from exchange.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: If the next unit has willingness to pay of $26 and willingness to accept of $20, producing that unit would:
options: Have no effect on total surplus
Add $6 to total surplus
Reduce total surplus by $6
Transfer $46 from buyer to seller
q.feedback: The gain from the unit is $26 - $20 = $6.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: If a policy merely transfers $10 of surplus from buyers to sellers and no trades change, total surplus:
options: Must equal zero
Is unchanged
Falls by $10
Rises by $10
q.feedback: A pure transfer changes who receives surplus, not the combined amount.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: If a policy prevents mutually beneficial trades, total surplus generally:
options: Falls
Rises
Is guaranteed to stay constant
Becomes equal to government revenue
q.feedback: Prevented beneficial exchanges eliminate gains that would otherwise exist.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: When market price rises and the same units continue to trade, consumer surplus generally:
options: Rises
Must stay constant
Becomes producer surplus one-for-one in every case
Falls
q.feedback: Buyers pay more for the same units, reducing their value-minus-price gains.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: When market price rises and the same units continue to trade, producer surplus generally:
options: Must stay constant
Becomes consumer surplus
Rises
Falls
q.feedback: Sellers receive a higher price relative to their willingness to accept.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: A policy causes some trades with positive gains to disappear. The value of those lost gains is:
options: Guaranteed government revenue
A loss in total surplus
A pure transfer between buyers and sellers
Additional consumer surplus
q.feedback: Lost mutually beneficial trades reduce the combined gains available in the market.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: A market outcome can maximize total surplus but still raise concerns about:
options: Whether buyers have preferences
Equity or distribution
Whether any exchange occurred
Whether prices exist
q.feedback: Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.

labels: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.

q.q: Why can willingness to pay understate the importance of a good to a low-income consumer?
options: Ability to pay can constrain the amount the consumer can bid
Willingness to pay never reflects preferences
Low-income consumers always have zero consumer surplus
Market prices automatically correct income differences
q.feedback: Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power.

labels: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.

q.q: Surplus analysis by itself does not determine whether an outcome is:
options: Efficient in the total-surplus sense
Based on voluntary exchange
Associated with gains from trade
Fair
q.feedback: Total surplus is an efficiency measure, not a complete theory of fairness.

Market prices eliminate all distributional concerns.
Willingness to pay measures need independently of income.
Willingness to pay can reflect ability to pay as well as preferences, so measured efficiency does not by itself settle fairness.
q.feedback: Willingness to pay is measured in dollars and can be constrained by purchasing power. A surplus-maximizing allocation can therefore be efficient without resolving questions of need or fairness.

labels: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.

q.q: Market A has consumer surplus of $80 and producer surplus of $70, but production creates $40 of external damage. Market B has consumer surplus of $75 and producer surplus of $65 with no external damage. Which statement is strongest?
options: B is necessarily unfair because producer surplus is lower
External damage should be ignored because it is outside buyer and seller surplus
Private surplus favors A, but including the stated external damage gives B higher social surplus
A is necessarily socially efficient because its private surplus is larger
q.feedback: A has $150 private surplus but $110 after the external cost; B has $140 and no stated external cost.

labels: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.

q.q: Two allocations produce the same total surplus. Allocation X gives almost all gains to one household; Allocation Y distributes gains across many households. Which conclusion is economically defensible from surplus data alone?
options: The allocations cannot have equal total surplus if distributions differ
They are tied on measured efficiency, while choosing between distributions requires an equity judgment
X is more efficient because concentrated gains are larger per person
Y is more efficient because more people receive gains
q.feedback: Total surplus measures the size of the pie; distribution of the pie is a separate criterion.

labels: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.

q.q: A price rises by $5. Ten existing buyers continue, and two buyers leave. Why can the consumer-surplus loss exceed $50?
options: Continuing buyers lose $50, and departing buyers lose their former surplus too
Multiply $5 by every potential buyer
Producer surplus is subtracted twice
Total surplus always falls by $5
q.feedback: The loss includes the rectangle on continuing units plus lost surplus of exiting buyers.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: A price falls by $4. Eight sellers continue, and two high-cost sellers exit. Why can the producer-surplus loss exceed $32?
options: Multiply $4 by all firms
Continuing sellers lose $32, and exiting sellers lose their former surplus too
Consumer surplus is counted as a seller loss
Total surplus always falls by $4
q.feedback: The loss includes continuing and exiting sellers.

labels: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.

q.q: Consumer surplus falls $60, producer surplus rises $44, and revenue rises $10. Total surplus:
options: Falls by $16
Rises by $54
Falls by $6
Falls by $26
q.feedback: Include government revenue once: −$60 + $44 + $10 = −$6. The $10 received by government is a transfer of surplus, not another loss. Total surplus falls by $6.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: Consumer surplus rises $35, producer surplus falls $50, and administration uses $4 of resources. Total surplus:
options: Falls by $15
Rises by $31
Falls by $54
Falls by $19
q.feedback: The consumer and producer changes sum to $35 − $50 = −$15. Administration consumes another $4 of real resources, so the total change is −$19. A resource cost reduces surplus; it is not just a payment transferred to another participant.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: Why is “a higher price always benefits society” wrong?
options: A higher price can redistribute surplus and alter quantity; total surplus is what matters
Higher prices always reduce producer surplus
Higher prices erase willingness to pay
Society benefits only when consumer surplus is zero
q.feedback: Price alone does not determine efficiency.

labels: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.

q.q: Why is “a lower price always benefits society” wrong?
options: Lower prices always raise cost
Consumers may gain while producers lose, and quantity effects can change total gains
Lower prices erase demand
Society benefits only when producer surplus is zero
q.feedback: Count both sides and quantity effects.

labels: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.

q.q: Marginal willingness to pay is $18 and marginal cost is $12. Which adjustment raises surplus?

Keep output fixed because price is absent
Increase output; the next unit adds $6
Raise price without changing output

q.q: Marginal willingness to pay is $14 and marginal cost is $21. Which adjustment raises surplus?

Keep output fixed because both are positive
Lower price without changing output

q.feedback: MC exceeds MB by $7.

labels: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

q.q: Allocation A gives two units to buyers valuing them at $40 and $32; B gives them to buyers valuing them at $35 and $28. Costs are equal. Which is better?

q.feedback: A costs $24 versus $31.

q.q: Buyer value is $50, seller cost is $20, and price is $47. Which statement is correct?

Marginal cost includes all fixed costs
q.feedback: Fixed cost can exceed producer surplus.

q.q: Why is a triangle formula wrong for a step-shaped demand curve?

q.q: Which statement is an efficiency claim?

q.q: A tax leaves $40 consumer surplus, $30 producer surplus, and $20 revenue. Without it, total surplus is $100. Deadweight loss is:
q.feedback: Post-tax total is $90.

q.q: A ceiling increases surplus for continuing buyers by $25, but buyers who lose access forfeit $5 of prior surplus. Producer surplus falls by $40. There are no search costs or other effects. What happens to total surplus?
options: It falls by $15
It rises by $20
It falls by $20
It falls by $70
q.feedback: Count all consumers: their net change is +$25 − $5 = +$20. Adding the $40 producer loss gives a $20 total-surplus loss. Counting only successful buyers understates the loss.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: Why is the entire producer loss from a price ceiling not necessarily deadweight loss?
options: Producer losses never matter
All consumer gains are deadweight loss
Deadweight loss equals price
Part may be transferred to buyers; only net destroyed gains are deadweight loss
q.feedback: Separate transfers from destroyed gains.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: Consumer surplus falls by $70 and producer surplus falls by $50 after a tax, while tax revenue equals $100. What is the reduction in total surplus?
q.feedback: The $120 decline in private surplus includes $100 transferred as revenue, leaving a $20 reduction in total surplus.

labels: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

q.q: A student calls the highest-surplus buyer the marginal buyer. What is wrong?

The marginal buyer is at the cutoff and usually has the smallest nonnegative surplus

The highest-value buyer never buys
q.feedback: The marginal buyer is just willing to purchase.

q.q: Refer to the asymmetric-market graph. Suppose a ceiling of $12 permits six units to trade, allocated to the highest-value buyers and produced by the lowest-cost sellers. How does consumer surplus compare with its value at E?

q.q: Refer to the underproduction graph. A rule holds output at the marked quantity left of E. Repealing it restores E but also transfers $9 from producers to consumers on units still traded. What is the total-surplus change, assuming efficient allocation and no other effects?

A $4 increase; the $9 changes distribution
A $5 decrease; the transfer costs more than the recovered gains
A $9 increase; only the transfer changes welfare
