Opportunity cost matters only for consumers
Owner-supplied resources can have implicit opportunity costs even without a cash payment
q.feedback: Economic cost includes the value of the next-best use of owner-supplied resources.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: A learner subtracts the owner’s forgone salary when calculating accounting profit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The forgone salary should be added to revenue
Accounting profit ignores explicit costs
Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs; the forgone salary is implicit
Accounting profit subtracts all opportunity costs
q.feedback: Implicit costs matter for economic profit, not the accounting-profit calculation.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: A learner says economic profit equals accounting profit plus implicit costs. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Economic profit and accounting profit are always equal
Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs
Economic profit equals accounting profit plus explicit costs
Economic profit ignores owner opportunity costs
q.feedback: Implicit costs reduce economic profit relative to accounting profit.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: A learner calls zero economic profit a “loss.
options: Zero economic profit means all explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered
Zero economic profit means revenue is zero
Zero economic profit means explicit costs exceed revenue
Zero economic profit excludes owner compensation
q.feedback: Normal profit is included in economic cost, so zero economic profit can be a sustainable outcome.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: A learner finds accounting profit of $50,000 and implicit cost of $70,000, then reports economic profit of $20,000. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: $20,000 is correct because profit cannot be negative
Economic profit is $120,000
Implicit cost should be ignored
Economic profit is −$20,000
q.feedback: Economic profit equals $50,000 − $70,000 = −$20,000.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: A learner writes TC = TFC − TVC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: TC = MC + AFC
TC = revenue − profit
TC = TFC + TVC
TC = TVC − TFC
q.feedback: Total cost combines the fixed and variable components.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A learner says fixed cost must fall when output falls. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Fixed cost is another name for marginal cost
Within the short run, total fixed cost does not vary with output
Fixed cost moves one-for-one with output
Fixed cost equals zero below capacity
q.feedback: A fixed input creates a cost that remains even as current output changes.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A learner reports positive TVC when output is zero in the standard short-run schedule. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: At zero output, TVC is zero; any remaining cost is fixed
TVC equals TFC at zero output
TVC is always greater than TC
TVC is an implicit cost only
q.feedback: Variable costs arise from producing output, while fixed costs remain at zero output.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A row has TFC = $90 and TC = $250, but a learner records TVC = $340. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: TVC is $250
TVC is $90
TVC is $340
TVC is $160
q.feedback: TVC = TC − TFC = $250 − $90.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A learner divides output by TFC to calculate AFC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: AFC = TFC/Q
AFC = Q/TFC
AFC = TVC/Q
AFC = ΔTC/ΔQ
q.feedback: Average fixed cost is fixed cost per unit of output.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A learner calculates AVC using TC/Q. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: AVC = TC/Q
AVC = TFC/Q
AVC = ΔTVC/Q
AVC = TVC/Q
q.feedback: TC/Q is ATC; AVC uses total variable cost only.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A learner says ATC = AVC − AFC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: ATC = MC + AFC
ATC = TC − Q
ATC = AVC + AFC
ATC = AFC − AVC
q.feedback: Average total cost contains both average variable and average fixed cost.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A learner says AFC eventually rises because “all U-shaped costs rise.
options: AFC rises whenever MC rises
AFC keeps falling as fixed cost is spread over more output
AFC is U-shaped like AVC
AFC equals MC at its minimum
q.feedback: AFC is not U-shaped in the standard model; it declines as quantity increases.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: At Q = 10, AFC = $6 and AVC = $14. A learner reports ATC = $8. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: ATC is $20
ATC is $8
ATC is $14
ATC is $60
q.feedback: ATC = AFC + AVC = $6 + $14.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A learner calculates MC as TC/Q. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: MC = ΔTC/ΔQ
MC = TC/Q
MC = TFC/Q
MC = TVC/Q
q.feedback: TC/Q is average total cost; marginal cost uses changes.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A learner says a higher fixed property tax must raise MC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Every fixed-cost increase raises MC one-for-one
MC equals AFC after a tax
Fixed costs are part of TVC
A pure fixed-cost increase does not change MC
q.feedback: MC depends on changes in cost as output changes, and a fixed amount is present at every output.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A learner says falling marginal product causes MC to fall. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Marginal product and MC always move together
Marginal product affects fixed cost only
With a constant input price, falling marginal product raises MC
Falling marginal product lowers both MC and AVC automatically
q.feedback: Less extra output from the same variable-input expense raises cost per additional unit.

labels: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.

q.q: TC rises by $50 when output rises by 5 units, but a learner reports MC = $50. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: MC cannot use total cost
MC is $10 per unit
MC is $55 per unit
MC is $250 per unit
q.feedback: Divide the cost change by the output change: $50/5 = $10.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A worker costs $100 and adds 10 units. A learner reports MC from labor as $100 per unit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The labor cost per marginal unit is $10
The labor cost per marginal unit is $100
Marginal product should be added to the wage
The worker’s wage is a fixed cost
q.feedback: Divide the worker’s cost by the worker’s marginal product: $100/10 = $10 per unit.

labels: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.

q.q: A learner says MC must be falling whenever ATC is falling. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: ATC can fall only if MC is zero
MC and ATC always have the same slope
ATC falls only when AFC rises
MC can be rising while ATC is still falling, as long as MC remains below ATC
q.feedback: The direction of the average depends on whether the marginal is above or below it, not on whether the marginal is itself rising.

labels: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.

q.q: A learner says a higher fixed insurance premium shifts AVC and MC upward. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: All short-run curves shift by the same amount
A fixed-cost increase lowers ATC
A pure fixed-cost increase shifts AFC and ATC, not AVC or MC
A fixed-cost increase shifts only MC
q.feedback: Fixed cost does not change the variable cost of current output or the incremental cost of another unit.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: A learner says, “Fixed cost and sunk cost mean the same thing.
options: A fixed cost can be avoidable in a future decision; a sunk cost is unrecoverable
Every sunk cost varies with output
Every fixed cost has already been paid forever
Sunk costs are always implicit
q.feedback: Fixed describes how cost behaves with current output; sunk describes whether it can be recovered.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: A learner includes a nonrefundable past payment when comparing two current options that both leave the payment unchanged. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Double the payment to reflect risk
Treat it as marginal cost
Convert it into future revenue
Ignore the payment because it is sunk and identical across the options
q.feedback: Only costs and benefits that differ across current alternatives should affect the choice.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: A learner calls a cancelable future lease payment sunk because the lease is a fixed cost. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Only variable costs can be avoided
A lease payment is always implicit
The future payment is avoidable if canceling the lease eliminates it
All fixed costs are sunk
q.feedback: A cost can be fixed with respect to output yet avoidable with respect to a future decision.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: A learner treats LRAC as the ATC curve of one fixed plant. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: LRAC is total variable cost per unit only
LRAC reflects the lowest attainable ATC across alternative plant sizes
LRAC is the same as AFC
LRAC fixes every input forever
q.feedback: The long run permits plant adjustment, so LRAC summarizes least-cost choices across plants.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: A learner says economies of scale mean total cost must fall as output rises. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Economies of scale mean average cost falls; total cost can still rise
Economies mean output falls
Economies mean fixed cost becomes zero
Economies require marginal product to be negative
q.feedback: The concept concerns cost per unit, not necessarily the level of total cost.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: A learner says diseconomies of scale begin when marginal product first falls in the short run. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Diseconomies and diminishing marginal product are the same event
Diseconomies require one input to remain fixed
Diseconomies mean LRAC is falling
Diseconomies concern long-run expansion of all inputs and rising LRAC
q.feedback: The two concepts refer to different horizons and different input adjustments.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: A learner reads a downward-sloping LRAC segment as diseconomies of scale. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: LRAC slope says nothing about scale
A downward-sloping LRAC segment requires negative output
A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents economies of scale
A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents constant returns
q.feedback: Falling long-run average cost as output expands is economies of scale.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: A learner says rising LRAC means output itself must be falling. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Rising LRAC means total cost is falling
LRAC can rise while output expands; the issue is rising cost per unit at larger scale
Rising LRAC requires zero output
Output and LRAC always move in opposite directions
q.feedback: Diseconomies describe a higher average cost at greater output, not a fall in output.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: A learner chooses the largest output on a flat minimum-LRAC segment as MES. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: MES is always the largest efficient output
MES is where LRAC first begins to fall
MES is where total cost is smallest
MES is the smallest output that attains the minimum LRAC
q.feedback: The definition focuses on the minimum scale required to achieve the lowest long-run unit cost.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: A learner says a flat LRAC means output is not changing. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Flat LRAC means economies of scale
Flat LRAC means fixed cost is constant in the short run
Output can rise while LRAC stays constant; that range reflects constant returns to scale
Flat LRAC means output must be zero
q.feedback: Constant returns refers to proportional changes in all inputs and output, leaving long-run cost per unit unchanged.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: A proprietor uses a personally owned storefront. How does opportunity cost enter production cost?
options: The building has no cost
Only depreciation counts
Forgone market rent is an implicit cost
Forgone rent is revenue
q.feedback: Owner-supplied property has an opportunity cost.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: An entrepreneur leaves a $70,000 job to run a firm. In economic-cost analysis, the $70,000 is:
options: An explicit wage payment
A sunk cost
Producer surplus
An implicit cost
q.feedback: The forgone salary is the next-best alternative.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: Why can economic profit be lower than accounting profit?
options: Economic profit subtracts opportunity costs of owner resources
It ignores fixed costs
It adds revenue twice
Accounting profit includes all implicit costs
q.feedback: Implicit opportunity costs create the gap.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: Zero economic profit signals that owner resources earn:
options: Nothing
Their opportunity cost
Only explicit cost
Maximum monopoly profit
q.feedback: Normal profit keeps owner resources in their current use.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: A firm asks how much cost rises when output expands slightly. Which measure is relevant?
options: Average fixed cost
Total fixed cost
Marginal cost
Accounting profit
q.feedback: Marginal analysis focuses on incremental changes.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: Why does MC below ATC lower ATC?
options: Fixed cost rises
Demand shifts
Revenue exceeds cost
The added unit costs less than the current average
q.feedback: A below-average marginal observation pulls the average down.

labels: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.

q.q: A worker adds 10 units and costs $200. The labor-based MC is:
options: $20 per unit
$200 per unit
$10 per unit
$2,000 per unit
q.feedback: Divide the input cost by marginal product.

labels: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.

q.q: Which cost is irrelevant to the marginal cost of one more unit?
options: Additional materials
A fixed payment that does not change with output
Additional labor
A per-unit royalty
q.feedback: A cost that does not change has zero marginal contribution.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: A productivity improvement raises output per worker. With wages unchanged, what happens to labor cost per unit?
options: It rises
It becomes fixed
It falls
It equals revenue
q.feedback: More output from the same wage lowers unit cost.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: A factory produces the same output with fewer labor hours. Which cost most directly falls?
options: Sunk cost
Past fixed cost
Forgone owner salary
Variable cost
q.feedback: Labor-hours savings lower current variable cost.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: How can better organization create economies of scale?
options: Specialization and coordination may lower LRATC over an output range
It guarantees negative MP
It raises every input price
It eliminates opportunity cost
q.feedback: Scale can permit productive specialization.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: For a competitive firm considering a change in output, which cost curve measures the incremental production cost?
options: AFC
Marginal cost
TFC
Accounting profit
q.feedback: Marginal cost measures the additional cost of producing more output and is the relevant cost measure for incremental output decisions.

labels: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.

q.q: Why does distinguishing AVC from ATC matter for a firm’s short-run production decisions?
options: They are always identical
AVC includes fixed cost
The two averages contain different cost components
ATC excludes variable cost
q.feedback: AVC excludes fixed cost; ATC includes it.

labels: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.

q.q: Cost curves can be reused across market structures because:
options: Every firm faces the same price
All firms earn zero profit
Market structure determines fixed cost
Production technology and input costs determine cost independently of the firm’s demand conditions
q.feedback: Revenue conditions differ, but cost construction follows production and input prices.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: A higher wage paid for labor directly raises:
options: Variable and marginal production costs
Only implicit cost
Only TFC
Consumer surplus
q.feedback: Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: If the rental price of an adjustable machine service rises, what happens to cost?
options: All sunk costs fall
The cost of outputs using that service rises
Marginal product automatically doubles
Economic cost excludes it
q.feedback: An input-price increase raises production cost.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: Why can a supply curve reflect marginal cost in a competitive setting?
options: Supply measures fixed cost only
Consumer surplus equals cost
A seller’s minimum acceptable price is tied to the cost of the marginal unit
Demand determines production technology
q.feedback: Marginal cost helps define willingness to accept.

labels: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.

q.q: Producer surplus differs from accounting profit partly because:
options: Producer surplus subtracts consumer surplus
Accounting profit excludes revenue
They are always identical
Producer surplus is tied to variable or marginal costs, while accounting profit also subtracts fixed costs
q.feedback: The measures use different cost concepts.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: A monopoly and a competitive firm may use the same cost schedule. What differs later?
options: Their revenue and demand conditions, not the cost identities
TC=TFC+TVC only for competition
Monopoly has no marginal cost
Competition has no fixed cost
q.feedback: Cost machinery is shared even when revenue conditions differ.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: Why is marginal cost relevant to a competitive firm’s supply decision?
options: It measures total demand
It measures the additional resource cost of another unit
It equals consumer surplus
It is fixed at every output
q.feedback: Marginal cost measures the additional production cost of another unit and therefore helps determine whether expanding output is worthwhile at a given market price.

labels: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.

q.q: How does the general idea of opportunity cost carry into a firm’s production-cost analysis?
options: Opportunity cost is replaced by accounting profit
A firm counts only costs that change with output
Resources supplied by the owner are valued by the best alternative return sacrificed
Only purchased inputs have opportunity cost
q.feedback: The same next-best-alternative principle applies to labor, capital, land, and other resources used by a firm.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: How does opportunity cost explain the difference between accounting profit and economic profit?
options: Economic profit ignores explicit expenses
The two measures differ only when fixed cost changes
Economic profit subtracts the forgone returns of owner-supplied resources
Accounting profit subtracts more opportunity costs than economic profit
q.feedback: Economic profit extends accounting profit by charging the firm for owner resources at their next-best use.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: Why is normal profit connected to the idea of opportunity cost?
options: It is identical to producer surplus
It compensates entrepreneurial resources for what they could earn in their next-best use
It is a tax on accounting profit
It measures consumer willingness to pay
q.feedback: Normal profit is the implicit opportunity cost required to keep entrepreneurial resources in the firm.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: How does marginal decision-making differ from comparing total economic profit?
options: Marginal analysis focuses on changes from one more action, while economic profit compares total revenue with all opportunity costs
Marginal analysis compares total revenue with total explicit costs, while economic profit isolates the value of the next unit
Economic profit evaluates the next incremental action, while marginal analysis measures the return on the entire project
Both methods compare total revenue and total cost, but marginal analysis reports the result per unit of output
q.feedback: The two tools answer different questions: one about incremental choices and one about overall return after opportunity costs.

labels: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.

q.q: How does marginal product connect the production function to marginal cost when the wage is unchanged?
options: A higher marginal product necessarily raises marginal cost
Marginal product determines fixed cost
Marginal cost and marginal product move together in the same direction
A higher marginal product generally means a lower marginal cost of additional output
q.feedback: When each worker adds more output for the same wage, the labor cost per additional unit falls.

labels: Analyze short-run production using total, marginal, and average product.

q.q: Why does diminishing marginal product help explain the upward-sloping portion of short-run marginal cost?
options: Total product must fall as soon as diminishing returns begin
Average fixed cost becomes negative
Additional variable input eventually adds less output, so each extra unit of output becomes more costly
Fixed cost rises with every worker
q.feedback: With a fixed input, falling marginal product raises the variable-input cost of producing additional output.

labels: Analyze short-run production using total, marginal, and average product.

q.q: How does average product connect to average variable cost when labor is the only variable input and the wage is constant?
options: Average product equals total fixed cost per worker
Higher average product tends to imply lower average variable cost
Higher average product raises average fixed cost
Average product and average variable cost are unrelated
q.feedback: More output per worker spreads the wage cost across more units of output.

labels: Analyze short-run production using total, marginal, and average product.

q.q: Why does the short-run/long-run distinction matter when interpreting cost curves?
options: Some inputs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs can vary in the long run
All costs are variable in both horizons
The long run is always exactly one year
Fixed costs rise only in the long run
q.feedback: Short-run cost curves reflect at least one fixed input; long-run cost analysis allows plant size and all other inputs to change.

labels: Analyze short-run production using total, marginal, and average product.

q.q: How does the marginal-versus-average rule connect product curves to cost curves?
options: Marginal and average values always move in opposite directions
A marginal below an average always raises the average
The rule applies to product but never to cost
A marginal value above an average pulls the average up; a marginal cost below an average cost pulls that average down
q.feedback: The same arithmetic relationship governs MP versus AP and MC versus AVC or ATC.

labels: Analyze short-run production using total, marginal, and average product.

q.q: How does identifying fixed and variable inputs help classify short-run costs?
options: Fixed inputs create marginal revenue
Variable inputs determine accounting profit but not cost
Payments tied to fixed inputs generate fixed cost, while costs of variable inputs change with output
Every input creates only variable cost
q.feedback: Input flexibility is the production-side basis for distinguishing fixed and variable cost.

labels: Analyze short-run production using total, marginal, and average product.

q.q: How does a fixed input in the production model connect to fixed cost?
options: Fixed inputs determine revenue rather than cost
A fixed input makes marginal cost zero
A payment associated with an input that cannot be changed in the short run contributes to fixed cost
Every fixed input creates variable cost only
q.feedback: The production distinction between fixed and variable inputs carries directly into short-run cost classification.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: How does hiring additional labor connect production decisions to variable cost?
options: Variable cost falls automatically whenever workers are added
If labor is variable, more labor raises total variable cost
Hiring labor changes total fixed cost only
Labor cost is sunk by definition
q.feedback: Payments to adjustable inputs are part of total variable cost.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: Why is the vertical distance between TC and TVC constant in a standard short-run total-cost graph?
options: The distance equals TFC, which does not vary with output
The distance equals MC, which is constant
TVC and TC have different output units
The distance equals profit
q.feedback: Because TC = TFC + TVC, the fixed-cost amount separates the two curves at every output.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: How does a cost schedule support marginal analysis?
options: A cost schedule eliminates the need to compare changes
Only TFC is needed to calculate marginal cost
Marginal cost is found by adding TC and TVC
Changes in TC or TVC between output levels can be used to calculate marginal cost
q.feedback: Cost schedules provide the change in cost associated with a change in output.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: How does TC = TFC + TVC relate to average total cost?
options: It implies ATC equals TFC at every output
It makes AVC independent of variable cost
Dividing each component by output gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by output gives MC = AFC + AVC
q.feedback: The total-cost identity becomes the average-cost identity after dividing by quantity.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: Why does a pure increase in TFC leave the change in total cost between two output levels unchanged?
options: The increase reduces TVC by the same amount
The same fixed amount is added to TC at both output levels
TFC becomes variable after the increase
MC is defined as total fixed cost per unit
q.feedback: Marginal cost depends on cost differences across output, so a constant fixed-cost addition cancels out.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: How does the fixed-cost concept connect to the downward slope of AFC?
options: TFC falls automatically as output rises
Variable cost is spread across fewer units
AFC is determined by marginal product only
The same TFC is spread across more units as output rises
q.feedback: AFC falls because the numerator stays fixed while the denominator grows.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: How can rising average product of labor affect AVC when the wage is constant?
options: It tends to raise AVC because a worker producing more output increases total wage cost faster than output
It leaves AVC unchanged because a constant wage fixes variable cost per unit regardless of worker productivity
It tends to lower AVC because each worker produces more output per dollar of wage cost
It lowers average fixed cost rather than AVC because labor productivity affects the spreading of fixed cost
q.feedback: Higher output per worker reduces variable labor cost per unit.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: How does the identity TC = TFC + TVC connect to ATC?
options: ATC excludes fixed cost
Dividing by Q gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by Q gives ATC = MC + AVC
ATC equals TC minus output
q.feedback: The average-cost identity follows directly from the total-cost identity.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: Why can ATC fall even when AVC is flat?
options: Falling AFC can pull ATC downward
ATC never includes fixed cost
MC must be zero
TVC must be falling
q.feedback: Because ATC = AVC + AFC, a declining fixed-cost component can reduce ATC.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: Why is AVC often more relevant than AFC for understanding the cost of current production activity?
options: AFC determines how much extra output one worker adds
AVC includes all sunk costs
AFC changes directly with every unit produced
AVC reflects variable resources used to produce the current output
q.feedback: Variable cost is tied to inputs adjusted as production changes.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: How does a below-average marginal cost affect ATC?
options: It leaves ATC unchanged by definition
It makes AFC rise
It pulls ATC downward
It pushes ATC upward
q.feedback: The marginal-versus-average rule applies to costs just as it does to other averages.

labels: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.

q.q: How does the sunk-cost rule connect to marginal analysis?
options: Both rules say fixed costs are always irrelevant
Both focus the current choice on additional costs and benefits that change across alternatives
Marginal analysis requires adding all past costs
Sunk cost is another term for marginal cost
q.feedback: Past unrecoverable costs do not change the marginal consequences of the current decision.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: How can a cost be fixed with respect to current output but still relevant to a future decision?
options: It may be avoidable if choosing a different plan eliminates the future payment
Every fixed cost is permanently sunk
Fixed costs always change one-for-one with output
Future fixed costs are excluded from economic cost
q.feedback: Cost behavior with output and recoverability across decisions are different classifications.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: Why is “recovering what we already spent” a poor reason by itself to continue a project?
options: Continuing can convert past spending into a relevant marginal benefit if enough future revenue is earned
Past spending should be added to expected future benefits because the project needs to recover its historical cost
A project should continue when accounting profit remains positive, even if future incremental costs exceed benefits
Past unrecoverable spending is unchanged by the current choice, so the decision should compare future incremental benefits and costs
q.feedback: The relevant comparison is forward-looking, not an attempt to reverse an unrecoverable past payment.

labels: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

q.q: How does specialization connect to economies of scale?
options: A larger scale can support specialized workers or capital that lowers cost per unit
Specialization always creates diminishing marginal product
Specialization raises fixed cost per unit forever
Specialization eliminates opportunity cost
q.feedback: Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: How do coordination problems connect organizational size to diseconomies of scale?
options: Coordination problems reduce all input prices
They guarantee constant returns to scale
They turn fixed cost into sunk cost
Communication and management complexity can raise cost per unit as the organization grows
q.feedback: Very large scale can create managerial inefficiencies that push LRAC upward.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: How does the short-run/long-run distinction connect SRATC curves to LRAC?
options: SRATC includes implicit cost but LRAC does not
The curves differ only because of revenue
Each SRATC holds a plant size fixed, while LRAC allows the firm to choose the least-cost plant for each output
LRAC fixes plant size while SRATC changes every input
q.feedback: Long-run flexibility over plant size is what lets LRAC trace the least-cost envelope.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: How is economies of scale different from spreading a fixed short-run cost over more units?
options: Falling AFC is a long-run scale effect only
Economies of scale is a long-run change in cost per unit when all inputs can vary; falling AFC is a short-run arithmetic effect
They are identical concepts
Economies of scale requires one input to remain fixed
q.feedback: Both can lower average cost, but they arise from different mechanisms and horizons.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: How can productivity improvements affect long-run average cost?
options: If the same inputs can produce more output, attainable cost per unit can fall
Higher productivity necessarily raises LRAC
Productivity affects revenue but never cost
Productivity makes all costs sunk
q.feedback: More output from a given bundle of resources can lower the cost required per unit.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: How does MES build on the idea of economies of scale?
options: MES is the largest feasible plant regardless of cost
MES marks the smallest output at which the firm has exhausted the available LRAC reductions
MES is where diseconomies first begin at zero output
MES measures short-run AFC
q.feedback: Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: How does constant returns to scale differ from short-run diminishing marginal product?
options: Constant returns is a long-run proportional change in all inputs; diminishing marginal product varies one input with others fixed
They are identical concepts
Constant returns requires a fixed plant
Diminishing marginal product requires all inputs to change proportionally
q.feedback: The concepts apply to different production experiments and time horizons.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: Why can MES matter when comparing efficient firm scale with the size of a market?
options: It determines consumer demand directly
It fixes the market price by law
It measures accounting profit rather than cost
It indicates the minimum output needed to achieve the lowest available long-run unit cost
q.feedback: MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.

labels: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

q.q: The law of demand says that, other things equal:
options: As price falls, quantity demanded rises
As price falls, demand always shifts left
As price rises, supply shifts left
As price rises, quantity demanded rises
q.feedback: The law of demand says price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: When the price of a good falls, what happens to quantity demanded?
options: Quantity demanded increases
Demand decreases
Supply increases
The demand curve shifts left
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the demand curve.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A change in which factor would shift the demand curve?
options: Consumer income
The good's own price
Movement along the curve
Quantity supplied
q.feedback: Income is a demand shifter. The good's own price changes quantity demanded.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: If income rises and tablets are a normal good, what happens to demand for tablets?
options: Demand increases
Demand decreases
Quantity demanded decreases because price changed
Supply decreases
q.feedback: For a normal good, higher income increases demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Two goods are substitutes when:
options: One good can be used in place of the other
The goods are typically consumed together
The goods use the same raw material in production
A price change for one good leaves demand for the other unrelated
q.feedback: Substitutes are goods that can replace one another.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Two goods are complements when:
options: They are commonly used together
One good can be used in place of the other
The goods are produced using the same inputs
A price change for one good leaves demand for the other unchanged.
q.feedback: Complements are goods used together.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: If the price of a substitute for iPhones falls, what happens to demand for iPhones?
options: Demand for iPhones decreases
Demand for iPhones increases
Supply of iPhones increases
Quantity demanded of iPhones increases because iPhone price fell
q.feedback: If a substitute gets cheaper, buyers shift away from the original good.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: If the price of printer ink rises, what likely happens to demand for printers?
options: Demand for printers decreases
Demand for printers increases
Supply of printers increases
Quantity supplied of printers increases
q.feedback: Printers and ink are complements, so higher ink prices reduce demand for printers.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: On the displayed gourmet-donut demand curve, what price and quantity are shown at point A?
options: $10 and 100 thousand donuts
$5 and 225 thousand donuts
$10 and 225 thousand donuts
$14 and 100 thousand donuts
q.feedback: At point A, the demand curve pairs a price of $10 with a quantity demanded of 100 thousand donuts.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: In the displayed coffee market, the move from D0 to D1 represents:
options: A decrease in demand
An increase in quantity demanded caused only by a lower price
An increase in demand
A decrease in supply
q.feedback: D1 lies to the right of D0, showing that consumers demand more coffee at each common price.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: How should the change in the tea demand curve from D0 to D1 be classified?
options: A decrease in demand
An increase in demand
A decrease in quantity demanded caused only by a higher price
An increase in supply
q.feedback: D1 lies to the left of D0, showing that consumers demand less tea at each common price.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of streaming subscriptions rises, and consumers buy fewer subscriptions. What happened?
options: Quantity demanded decreased
Demand decreased
Supply increased
Demand shifted right
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity demanded, not demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Consumers expect laptop prices to rise next month, so more laptops are purchased today. What happens to current demand for laptops?
options: Demand increases
Quantity demanded decreases
Supply decreases
Demand stays fixed because only current price matters
q.feedback: Expectations about higher future prices can increase demand today.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A popular celebrity endorsement makes more buyers want a product at every price. What happens?
options: Demand shifts right
Quantity demanded falls
Supply shifts left
The product's own price changed
q.feedback: A change in tastes shifts demand; more buyers wanting the product shifts demand right.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of tablets rises. What happens in the market for tablet cases, a complement?
options: Demand for tablet cases decreases
Demand for tablet cases increases
Supply of tablet cases increases
Quantity supplied of tablets decreases
q.feedback: If tablets become more expensive, fewer tablets are bought, reducing demand for tablet cases.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of tea rises. If coffee is a substitute for tea, what happens to demand for coffee?
options: Demand for coffee increases
Demand for coffee decreases
Quantity demanded of coffee decreases because coffee price changed
Supply of coffee decreases
q.feedback: When a substitute becomes more expensive, demand for the other good rises.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. Consumer income rises for a normal good while production conditions remain unchanged. Which equilibrium movement provides evidence of the resulting demand change?
options: From P1, Q2 to P2, Q3 along S2, showing demand shifts right from D1 to D2
From P2, Q1 to P1, Q2 along D1, showing supply shifts right from S1 to S2
From P3, Q2 to P2, Q3 along D2, showing supply shifts right from S1 to S2
From P2, Q3 to P1, Q2 along S2, showing demand shifts left from D2 to D1
q.feedback: Higher income raises demand for a normal good. With supply fixed at S2, the equilibrium moves along S2 from D1/S2 at P1, Q2 to D2/S2 at P2, Q3.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The market moves from point A to point B on the displayed demand curve. What is the most precise description?
options: Demand increases, shifting D to the right.
Price falls, causing an increase in quantity demanded along D.
Price falls, causing quantity demanded to decrease along D.
Supply increases, shifting S to the right.
q.feedback: A and B lie on the same demand curve. The lower price is associated with a larger quantity demanded, so this is a movement along demand, not a shift.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Moving from point A to point B on the displayed demand curve changes quantity demanded by:
options: A decrease of 125 thousand donuts
An increase of 5 thousand donuts
An increase of 125 thousand donuts
An increase of 225 thousand donuts
q.feedback: Quantity demanded rises from 100 thousand at A to 225 thousand at B, an increase of 125 thousand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: At a price of $10 on the displayed coffee graph, how does quantity demanded change when demand shifts from D0 to D1?
options: It decreases from 125 thousand to 50 thousand
It increases from 100 thousand to 175 thousand
It stays at 125 thousand
It increases from 50 thousand to 125 thousand
q.feedback: At $10, D0 shows 50 thousand units and D1 shows 125 thousand, so quantity demanded at that price rises by 75 thousand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: If coffee is a normal good, which event is consistent with the shift from D0 to D1 shown in the graph?
options: Consumer income rises
The price of coffee falls while all demand shifters stay unchanged
Coffee producers adopt cheaper technology
The price of coffee rises and buyers move up D0
q.feedback: For a normal good, higher income increases demand, shifting the entire demand curve to the right.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. At a price of $4, how does quantity demanded change as demand shifts from D0 to D1?
options: It increases from 100 thousand to 200 thousand
It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
It decreases from 300 thousand to 200 thousand
It stays at 100 thousand
q.feedback: At $4, D0 shows 200 thousand units while D1 shows 100 thousand, a decrease of 100 thousand at the same price.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: For a normal good such as tea, which change in a demand shifter could generate the illustrated curve movement?
options: The price of tea rises while all demand shifters stay unchanged
Tea producers receive a subsidy
Consumer income falls
The price of tea falls and buyers move down D0
q.feedback: For a normal good, lower income decreases demand and shifts the entire demand curve left.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: How does equilibrium change as demand moves from D0 to D1?
options: Demand decreases, lowering price and quantity
Demand increases, raising price and quantity
Supply decreases, raising price and reducing quantity
Supply increases, lowering price and raising quantity

q.feedback: Demand shifts right; price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity rises from 200 to 250 thousand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A market survey shows that at every possible price consumers now plan to buy more electric bikes than before. Which event cannot explain the change?
options: A subsidy to buyers
A rise in gasoline prices
A fall in the price of electric bikes itself
Stronger preferences for low-emission travel
q.feedback: A change in the good’s own price causes movement along demand, not a shift of the entire demand curve.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A student says, 'Demand increased because the price rose.' What is the correct response?
options: A demand increase can raise price; a price rise alone moves along demand.
That is correct because demand always means the current price
That describes a supply increase
That proves the good is inferior
q.feedback: A price rise can be caused by a demand increase, but the price rise itself does not shift demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of headphones falls from $80 to $60, and consumers buy more headphones. What is the most precise statement?
options: Quantity demanded increases
Demand increases
Supply increases
Demand shifts right
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along demand, so quantity demanded changes.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A consumer's income rises, and meal delivery is a normal good. At every price, consumers now want more meal delivery. What happened?
options: Demand increased
Quantity demanded increased because price fell
Supply increased
Demand decreased
q.feedback: Income is a demand shifter. For a normal good, higher income increases demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A survey shows buyers want more electric scooters at every listed price than they did last month. Which statement is most precise?
options: Quantity demanded increased because the scooter price fell.
Demand increased, so the entire demand schedule shifted right.
Demand increased only at the market price.
The law of demand stopped applying to electric scooters.
q.commonError: Calling an across-the-board schedule change a movement along demand.
q.feedback: Wanting more at every price is a rightward shift of demand, not a change in quantity demanded caused by the good’s own price.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Which comparison best captures the difference between moving from D1 to D2 and moving along D1?
options: D1 to D2 is a demand shift; movement along D1 is a quantity demanded change
D1 to D2 is a quantity demanded change; movement along D1 is a demand shift
D1 to D2 is a supply shift; movement along D1 is a supply decrease
D1 to D2 is a price ceiling; movement along D1 is a price floor
q.feedback: A non-price determinant shifts demand; a price change causes movement along a demand curve.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of tablets falls, and consumers buy more tablets. No non-price determinant changed. What happened?
options: Quantity demanded increased along the existing demand curve.
Demand increased and the curve shifted right
Supply increased and the curve shifted right
Demand decreased because price fell
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along demand, not a demand shift.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of peanut butter rises. If jelly is a complement, what happens in the jelly market?
options: Demand for jelly decreases
Demand for jelly increases
Supply of jelly decreases
Quantity demanded of jelly increases
q.feedback: Peanut butter and jelly are complements. If peanut butter gets more expensive, demand for jelly falls.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of bus rides rises. If subway rides are substitutes, what happens in the subway market?
options: Demand for subway rides increases
Demand for subway rides decreases
Supply of subway rides decreases
Quantity supplied of bus rides increases
q.feedback: When the price of a substitute rises, demand for the other good increases.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Consumers expect the price of coffee to fall next month. What happens to current demand for coffee, other things equal?
options: Current demand decreases
Current demand increases
Current quantity supplied increases
Supply shifts left
q.feedback: If buyers expect a lower future price, they delay purchases, reducing current demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. The price of a substitute rises, shifting demand from D1 to D2 while supply remains S1. Which chain of graph evidence explains the resulting equilibrium change?
options: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2, so both price and quantity rise
Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q1, so both price and quantity fall
Supply shifts right; equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2, so price falls as quantity rises
Supply shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, so price rises as quantity falls
q.feedback: The higher substitute price increases demand. With supply fixed at S1, the graph moves from the D1/S1 intersection at P2, Q1 to the D2/S1 intersection at P3, Q2.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. A close substitute becomes cheaper, reducing demand from D2 to D1 while supply remains S2. Which explanation correctly traces the change in equilibrium?
options: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2, reducing both price and quantity
Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3, increasing both price and quantity
Supply shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, increasing price and reducing quantity
Supply shifts right; equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3, reducing price and increasing quantity
q.feedback: A cheaper substitute reduces demand for this good. With S2 unchanged, the equilibrium moves from D2/S2 at P2, Q3 to D1/S2 at P1, Q2.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. Calculate the quantity response per $1 price decrease from A to B, then infer which demand relationship that calculation illustrates.
options: Quantity demanded rises 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating movement along a downward-sloping demand curve
Demand rises 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating a rightward shift of the demand curve
Quantity demanded falls 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating movement up the demand curve
Demand falls 125 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating a leftward shift of the demand curve
q.feedback: From A to B, price falls $5 and quantity demanded rises 125 thousand, or 25 thousand per dollar. Because the good's own price changes, this is movement along the demand curve, not a curve shift.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. At $6, compare D0 with D1. If this is a normal good, which change could explain the difference, and how large is it?
options: A fall in the good’s own price; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
Higher consumer income; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
Higher consumer income; 100 thousand more units demanded at that price.
A cheaper substitute; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
q.feedback: At $6, D0 shows 150 thousand and D1 shows 225 thousand: a 75-thousand increase at the same price. Higher income shifts demand right for a normal good; an own-price fall moves along a curve, and a cheaper substitute shifts demand left.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the tea graph. Compare D0 with D1 at both $4 and $6. Which inference is supported by the repeated horizontal gap?
options: Demand decreases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a leftward curve shift
Quantity demanded decreases by 100 thousand solely because tea's own price rises
Demand increases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a rightward curve shift
Supply decreases by 100 thousand units, causing movement from D0 to D1
q.feedback: At both $4 and $6, D1 lies 100 thousand units left of D0. A repeated horizontal difference at fixed prices identifies a decrease in demand rather than movement along one curve.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the movie-ticket graph. Streaming subscriptions are substitutes for theater visits. With production conditions unchanged, which event could take equilibrium from A to B?
options: Streaming subscriptions become more expensive, increasing demand for movie tickets.
Streaming subscriptions become cheaper, increasing demand for movie tickets.
The movie-ticket price rises by itself, shifting demand for movie tickets right.
Theaters face lower operating costs, shifting supply of movie tickets right.
q.imageAlt: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. S0 is an upward-sloping supply curve. D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.
q.feedback: A lies on D0 and S0; B lies on D1 and S0. Demand has increased while supply stays fixed. A higher substitute price can cause that shift; the higher ticket price is a result, not a demand shifter.

D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A product gets cheaper because supply increases. Students say demand increased because quantity sold rose. What is the error?
options: They confused an increase in quantity demanded with an increase in demand
They correctly identified a demand shift
They confused a price floor with a price ceiling
They ignored that supply can never change price
q.feedback: If price falls because supply increases, buyers move along the demand curve. Quantity demanded rises, but demand itself does not shift.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A product becomes cheaper and sales rise. A follow-up survey finds that buyers now want more at EVERY unchanged price after a favorable health report. A student attributes all extra purchases to movement along the old demand curve. Which correction uses the survey evidence?
options: Demand is unchanged; every increase in sales is a movement along demand.
Demand shifts left; lower prices mean buyers want less at each fixed price.
Supply must shift left; buyer surveys establish producers’ costs.
Demand shifts right; the price change alone cannot explain greater planned purchases at a fixed price.
q.feedback: Unlike a supply-driven price fall alone, the survey reports greater demand at fixed prices after new health information. That identifies a demand shift, although the survey alone does not determine the separate supply change or how much of observed sales growth each cause explains.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Suppose the only change in the gourmet-donut market is that the good's own price falls from $10 to $5. The displayed graph shows the market moving from A to B. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Quantity demanded rises 125 thousand; demand is unchanged.
Demand rises 125 thousand; D shifts right.
Quantity demanded falls 125 thousand; demand is unchanged.
Demand falls 125 thousand; D shifts left.
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along a fixed demand curve. Quantity demanded rises from 100 thousand to 225 thousand, but demand does not shift.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of a substitute for coffee rises. What happens in the coffee market, holding other factors constant?
options: Demand for coffee increases, raising equilibrium price and quantity
Quantity demanded of coffee decreases along the same curve
Supply of coffee increases because coffee is now profitable
Demand for coffee decreases because substitutes are now expensive
q.feedback: When a substitute becomes more expensive, demand for the original good rises.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of peanut butter falls. What happens to the demand for jelly, assuming they are complements?
options: Demand for jelly increases
Quantity demanded of jelly falls along the same curve
Supply of jelly decreases
Demand for jelly decreases because peanut butter is cheaper
q.feedback: A lower price for a complement increases demand for the related good.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Income rises for a normal good while the price of a close substitute falls. What can be concluded about demand for the normal good?
options: The net demand shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.
Demand must rise because income rises for a normal good.
Demand must fall because the substitute becomes cheaper.
Demand stays fixed; both changes are movements along the original curve.
q.commonError: Assuming one of two opposing demand shifters must dominate.
q.feedback: Higher income raises demand for the normal good; a cheaper substitute lowers it. Either effect can dominate, or they can offset. Own-price movements do not describe these determinants.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. A buyer group starts on D0 at $6. After demand changes to D1, price is $10. Which statement reconciles the demand change with the final quantity?
options: Demand decreased, causing final quantity to be 25 thousand below the starting quantity.
Demand increased, so final quantity must be 75 thousand above the starting quantity.
Demand increased, yet final quantity is 25 thousand below the starting quantity.
Demand was unchanged, and the price increase reduced quantity by 100 thousand.
q.feedback: The initial quantity is 150 thousand and the final quantity is 125 thousand. D1 is right of D0, but movement up the new demand curve offsets more than the 75-thousand rightward shift.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compare the initial point on D0 at $6 with the final point on D1 at $4. Which explanation correctly separates the demand shift from the subsequent price movement?
options: The shift to D1 lowers quantity at each price; moving down D1 then raises quantity to 100 thousand, only partly offsetting the shift
The shift to D1 raises quantity at each price; moving down D1 then lowers quantity to 100 thousand
Demand stays on D0 because the price fall accounts for the entire move to 100 thousand
Supply shifts left first, and movement along D1 restores quantity to 150 thousand
q.feedback: At $6, shifting from D0 to D1 reduces quantity demanded. The later price decline produces movement down D1 to 100 thousand, but that movement does not fully undo the demand decrease.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which description correctly separates the demand shift from the movement along supply?
options: Quantity demanded rises only because price falls along D0
Supply shifts right and demand stays fixed
Both curves shift right equally
Demand shifts D0 to D1, and equilibrium moves upward along S0
q.imageAlt: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. S0 is an upward-sloping supply curve. D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.
q.feedback: Demand changes curves; the higher equilibrium is also a movement along unchanged supply.
