D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. A report attributes the entire A-to-B change to stronger tastes for donuts. A second survey finds the quantity desired at every fixed price is unchanged. Which diagnosis fits both pieces of evidence?
options: The report is supported; quantity rises 125 thousand because demand shifted right.
The report confuses movement with a shift; quantity rises 125 thousand because price is lower.
The report confuses movement with a shift; quantity falls 125 thousand because price is lower.
The report is supported; demand shifted right even though the fixed-price schedule is unchanged.
q.feedback: A and B are on the same demand curve, at 100 and 225 thousand. The unchanged fixed-price schedule rules out a taste-driven demand shift. The graph shows an increase in quantity demanded caused by a lower price.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. First compare D0 with D1 at a price of $10. Then follow D1 as price falls from $10 to $6. Which option correctly decomposes the two quantity changes into a demand shift and a movement along D1?
options: 50→125 from the price fall; 125→225 from a supply shift.
50→150 from the demand shift; 150→225 from the price fall.
50→25 from the demand shift; 25→225 from the price fall.
50→125 from the demand shift; 125→225 from the price fall.
q.feedback: At $10 the shift from D0 to D1 raises quantity demanded from 50 to 125 thousand. Moving down D1 from $10 to $6 raises it again from 125 to 225 thousand, for a total increase of 175 thousand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The market begins on D0 at $6 and 150 thousand units. Demand shifts to D1 while price is still $6, and then price falls to $4. Which decomposition matches the graph?
options: 150→250 from the demand shift; 250→100 from the price fall.
150→50 from the demand shift; 50→100 from the price fall.
150→50 from the price fall; 50→100 from the demand shift.
150→100 from the demand shift; 100→50 from the price fall.
q.feedback: At $6, D0 shows 150 thousand and D1 shows 50 thousand. Moving down D1 to $4 raises quantity demanded to 100 thousand. Final quantity remains 50 thousand below the starting level.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Coffee is a normal good. Consumer income rises, buyers expect coffee prices to fall next month, and the current price of tea, a substitute, rises. What can be concluded about current coffee demand?
options: Demand must rise: two favorable determinants outweigh one unfavorable determinant regardless of their sizes.
Demand must fall: an expected future price decline outweighs current income and substitute-price effects.
Demand is indeterminate: income and the substitute price raise it, while waiting for a lower future price reduces it.
Demand is unchanged: income, expectations, and related-good prices affect only movement along the curve.
q.commonError: Adding demand shifters mechanically without recognizing opposing effects.
q.feedback: The two positive demand effects need not outweigh the negative expectations effect. Counting determinants cannot replace comparing their magnitudes.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A shop cuts a product’s price and sells more. A separate survey finds the quantity buyers want at every fixed price is unchanged. Which account fits both observations?
options: Movement down the same curve; unchanged fixed-price plans provide no evidence of a demand shift.
A rightward demand shift; rising purchases provide evidence of stronger demand despite unchanged fixed-price plans.
Movement up the same curve; a lower price reduces the quantity buyers desire at that price.
A leftward demand shift; unchanged fixed-price plans provide evidence that consumers now want fewer units.
q.feedback: A price cut raises quantity demanded along the same curve. An unchanged fixed-price schedule rules out attributing the increase to a demand shift.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Coffee buyers remain on the same downward-sloping demand curve. Their quantity demanded falls from 80 to 60 cups per day. With non-price determinants unchanged, which price change is consistent with this movement?
options: A rise in coffee’s own price.
A fall in coffee’s own price.
An unchanged coffee price.
A change in coffee’s production cost with its price unchanged.
q.feedback: Moving to a smaller quantity on the same downward-sloping demand curve requires a higher own price. A demand shift would change the curve rather than move along it.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A household’s income rises. With tablet prices, tastes and all other demand determinants unchanged, it plans to buy fewer tablets. How should tablets be classified for this household over this income range?
options: Normal, because any income change shifts demand.
Inferior, because higher income reduces its demand.
Normal, because the tablet price has not changed.
Inferior, because the tablet price must have risen.
q.feedback: An inferior good has lower demand when income rises, other things equal. This is an income-driven demand shift; the unchanged tablet price rules out an own-price movement.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The good’s own price declines while every non-price determinant stays fixed. Which demand-side change occurs?
options: Demand increases through a rightward shift of the curve.
Demand decreases through a leftward shift of the curve.
Quantity demanded stays fixed because the curve did not shift.
Quantity demanded increases through a movement along the existing curve.
q.commonError: Using demand and quantity demanded as interchangeable terms.
q.feedback: A change in the good’s own price causes movement along the demand curve and changes quantity demanded.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Which event shifts demand for bus rides to the right?
options: The price of subway rides, a substitute, increases.
The price of bus rides decreases while all non-price determinants remain fixed.
Bus companies add routes and lower their operating costs.
The cost of diesel fuel decreases for bus operators.
q.commonError: Selecting an own-price movement or a supply shifter as a demand shifter.
q.feedback: A higher price for a substitute makes bus rides more attractive at every bus fare and shifts demand right.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Income falls and purchases of instant noodles rise. What does this evidence suggest?
options: Instant noodles are a normal good for these consumers
Instant noodles are an inferior good for these consumers
A lower noodle price caused movement along the demand curve
A supply decrease raised purchases despite the income change
q.commonError: Treating all goods as normal or confusing demand evidence with supply.
q.feedback: Demand for an inferior good rises when income falls, holding other determinants constant.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Electric scooters are normal goods. Household incomes rise, but a close substitute becomes cheaper. At an unchanged scooter price, can we predict the direction of scooter purchases without knowing the strength of each effect?
options: Yes, purchases rise; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand right.
Yes, purchases fall; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand left.
No; higher income pushes demand right while the cheaper substitute pushes it left.
No change occurs; an unchanged scooter price prevents any change in quantity purchased.
q.commonError: Explaining a full demand-schedule change as movement along one curve.
q.feedback: Income growth increases normal-good demand, while a cheaper substitute reduces scooter demand. Their unknown relative strengths make the net fixed-price quantity effect ambiguous.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Movie tickets are a normal good. Income rises, but the price of streaming subscriptions, a substitute, falls. What is the strongest conclusion about movie-ticket demand?
options: Demand rises because higher income and a cheaper substitute both increase demand for movie tickets.
Demand falls because the cheaper substitute lowers ticket demand while income does not shift demand for a normal good.
Quantity demanded changes along one curve because both events change the ticket price
The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other
q.commonError: Claiming certainty when opposing demand shifters act simultaneously.
q.feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good, while a cheaper substitute reduces demand for movie tickets. The effects oppose each other and their relative sizes are not supplied, so the net shift cannot be determined. These are demand shifters, not changes caused by the ticket’s own price.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Concert attendance falls after ticket prices rise. A fan claims demand decreased. Surveys show fans’ planned purchases at each fixed price are unchanged, but later a popular performer joins the tour. Which sequence is supported?
options: The first decline is movement along demand; the later performer change can shift demand right.
The first decline is a leftward demand shift; the later performer change is movement down that curve.
Both events are movements along demand because each changes the number of tickets sold.
Both events shift demand left because ticket price and performer popularity are market conditions.
q.commonError: Calling an own-price movement a change in demand.
q.feedback: Unchanged fixed-price plans imply the first attendance decline is due to movement along demand. Greater performer appeal changes a nonprice determinant and can shift the demand schedule right.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Streaming subscriptions are normal goods. Incomes rise, a rival streaming service lowers its price, and broadband needed for both services becomes more expensive. A manager credits income alone for rising subscriptions. Which inference is defensible?
options: Income and the rival-price cut push demand right; broadband cost changes supply, so observed growth isolates the two demand effects.
Income pushes demand right; rival-price and broadband-cost changes push left, so observed growth need not measure the income effect alone.
Income pushes demand left; the rival-price cut and broadband cost push right, so observed growth rules out normal-good status.
All three changes push demand right; an unchanged subscription price would show that subscriptions rose along the old demand curve.
q.feedback: Income raises normal-good demand. A cheaper substitute and a dearer complement reduce it. Observed growth is the net result and cannot identify the isolated income effect; a fixed own price does not prevent a demand shift.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Tea and coffee are substitutes. Coffee prices rise while consumer income falls, and tea is a normal good. What can be concluded about tea demand without knowing effect sizes?
options: Tea demand rises because the substitute-price effect is larger than the income effect
Tea demand falls because the income effect is larger than the substitute-price effect
The direction of the tea-demand shift is ambiguous
Tea demand is unchanged because tea's own price did not change
q.commonError: Assuming one of two opposing demand shifters must dominate.
q.feedback: The higher coffee price raises demand for tea, while lower income reduces demand for tea because it is normal. Without relative effect sizes, the net shift cannot be determined.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Which event shifts demand?
options: Consumer income changes
The good's own price changes
Quantity supplied changes
There is movement along the demand curve.
q.feedback: Income is a demand shifter. The good's own price causes movement along demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: If consumer income rises and tablets are a normal good, what happens?
options: Demand for tablets increases
Quantity demanded falls
Supply of tablets increases
Demand for tablets decreases
q.feedback: For a normal good, higher income increases demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: When only the price of a good changes, what happens on the demand curve?
options: There is movement along the demand curve
The demand curve shifts right
The demand curve shifts left
Supply shifts right
q.feedback: A good's own price changes quantity demanded, not demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of coffee falls. What is the most precise result?
options: Quantity demanded of coffee increases
Demand for coffee increases
Supply of coffee decreases
Demand for coffee decreases
q.feedback: Because coffee's own price changed, buyers move along the demand curve.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Consumers expect the price of laptops to rise next month, so they buy more laptops today. What happens today?
options: Current demand increases
Current quantity demanded falls
Supply decreases
Demand stays fixed because only current price matters
q.feedback: Expectations about future prices can shift current demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: A recession lowers consumer income. If restaurant meals are a normal good, what happens to demand for restaurant meals?
options: Demand decreases
Demand increases
Quantity demanded increases because price changed
Supply increases
q.feedback: For a normal good, lower income decreases demand.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of streaming subscriptions rises, and fewer subscriptions are purchased. What is the most precise explanation?
options: Quantity demanded decreased because the good's own price changed
Demand decreased because the curve shifted left
Supply increased because sellers charged more
Demand increased because price rose
q.feedback: The good's own price changed, so this is a movement along demand and a change in quantity demanded.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: Bus fares fall, while a campus adds students who use the bus. Considering each change separately, how does it affect demand for bus rides?
options: Lower fares shift demand right; more students move buyers along demand.
Lower fares move buyers along demand; more students shift demand left.
Both changes move buyers along the same demand curve.
Lower fares move buyers along demand; more students shift demand right.
q.feedback: The fare is the ride's own price, so its fall increases quantity demanded along a curve. More potential riders are a non-price determinant: at each fare, the campus buys more rides, shifting demand right.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of peanut butter rises. If jelly is a complement, what happens to demand for jelly?
options: Demand for jelly decreases
Demand for jelly increases
Supply of jelly decreases
Quantity supplied of jelly increases
q.feedback: Complements are used together. If peanut butter becomes more expensive, demand for jelly falls.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: The price of bus rides rises. If subway rides are substitutes, what happens to demand for subway rides?
options: Demand for subway rides increases
Demand for subway rides decreases
Supply of subway rides increases
Quantity demanded of bus rides increases
q.feedback: When the price of a substitute rises, demand for the other good increases.

labels: LO4.2

q.q: An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption. What two roles appear?
options: Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation
Adviser for both because policy is mentioned
Scientist for both because evidence is used
Legislator for the estimate and judge for the advice
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: When an economist estimates how a tax will affect employment, the economist is primarily:
options: Making a moral judgment about fairness.
Providing positive analysis about likely consequences.
Guaranteeing the policy will pass.
Setting the tax rate by law.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences without deciding the policy.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: When policymakers ask an economist to compare costs and benefits, the economist should:
options: Hide uncertainty to sound decisive.
Replace evidence with personal preference.
State assumptions and identify relevant tradeoffs.
Ignore who bears the costs.
q.feedback: Good advice makes assumptions, tradeoffs, and uncertainty visible.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: Which activity is most clearly part of an economist’s policy role?
options: Voting on behalf of the legislature.
Enforcing the final regulation.
Declaring one value judgment scientifically correct.
Evaluating evidence about likely behavioral responses.
q.commonError: Giving economists powers they do not possess.
q.feedback: Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: An economist estimates how a bus fee changes ridership. What role is primary?
options: Scientist analyzing a testable consequence
Adviser making a value judgment about whether the fee is fair
Policymaker deciding whether the fee should be adopted
Administrator responsible for enforcing the fee.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: An adviser compares costs borne by commuters and taxpayers. What should the adviser make explicit?
options: The combined cost alone, without showing how it is divided between the two groups.
The costs each group bears and the tradeoffs between the policy alternatives.
The adviser’s preferred outcome alone, without showing the costs of other choices.
The taxpayers’ costs alone, without including the costs borne by commuters.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: An informative comparison identifies which costs fall on commuters and which fall on taxpayers, and how those costs change across policy alternatives. A single total can conceal the distribution of costs and the tradeoffs facing the decision maker.

q.q: Why can economics inform but not dictate a school policy?
options: Economics cannot measure the effects of school policies
School policies have no economic tradeoffs
The final choice also depends on social values
Evidence cannot help identify the likely consequences of alternative policies.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: A forecast gives a range rather than one number. Why?
options: The range identifies which policy society should prefer
A range means the evidence is too weak to be useful
Every value inside the range is equally likely.
Policy effects are uncertain, not guaranteed
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: Two economists use different estimates of demand elasticity and reach different tax projections. What best explains the disagreement?
options: They may share the same framework but use different empirical assumptions.
One of them must reject opportunity cost.
Economic analysis cannot use evidence.
Normative values are the only possible source of disagreement.
q.commonError: Assuming disagreement proves the discipline has no method.
q.feedback: Different estimates and assumptions can produce different forecasts.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: An economist reports that a policy raises total surplus but imposes concentrated losses on one group. What should the report do next?
options: Conclude that everyone benefits.
Separate the efficiency finding from the distributional consequence.
Ignore the losing group because total surplus rose.
Call the distributional judgment a positive fact.
q.commonError: Collapsing efficiency and equity into one claim.
q.feedback: Policy analysis should distinguish aggregate efficiency from distribution.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: A forecast is highly sensitive to one uncertain parameter. The best policy advice is to:
options: Use only the most favorable value.
Present one estimate as certain.
Report the sensitivity and show results under plausible values.
Remove the parameter from the model.
q.feedback: Decision makers need to know when conclusions depend heavily on uncertain inputs.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: A mayor asks whether rent control is “good.” What is the economist’s most useful first response?
options: Answer solely from personal ideology.
Promise there will be no unintended consequences.
Treat the word good as a measurable price.
Clarify the objectives and analyze likely effects and tradeoffs.
q.commonError: Treating vague policy goals as self-defining.
q.feedback: Policy evaluation requires explicit objectives and evidence about consequences.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: Two economists use different demand estimates. What can explain different forecasts?
options: Different scientific judgments about evidence
One economist must have made an arithmetic mistake
Different forecasts can only come from different value judgments
Empirical disagreements cannot be informed by additional evidence.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: Two advisers share one forecast but rank equity differently. What differs?
options: Their estimates of the policy’s effects
Their normative values
Their definitions of the economic variables
One adviser must have interpreted the data incorrectly.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: A policy raises total surplus but harms one region. What should analysis report?
options: Only the increase in total surplus
Only the regional loss, because any loser makes the policy inefficient
Efficiency and distribution separately
A single efficiency conclusion without reporting who gains and loses.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

q.q: A rule changes incentives in an unexpected way. What should advisers examine?
options: Only the response the rule was intended to create
Treat unexpected behavior as irrelevant to the policy analysis
Assume the original behavioral prediction remains correct.
Likely behavioral responses and unintended effects
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: A model omits enforcement costs. What should the policy estimate do?
options: Include feasible implementation and administration costs
Ignore enforcement costs if the policy objective is worthwhile
Count only the direct statutory cost of the program
Assume administration uses no scarce resources.
q.commonError: Confusing statutory design with actual implementation.
q.feedback: Enforcement and administration use scarce staff time, equipment and other resources. A feasible policy estimate must include those implementation costs when comparing benefits with costs. Omitting them can overstate net benefits even if the policy’s stated goal is desirable.

q.q: A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period. What is the central concern?
options: Whether the evidence generalizes to the current setting.
Whether the policy has a money price.
Whether economists may use models.
Whether positive analysis is always normative.
q.commonError: Assuming evidence transfers automatically across settings.
q.feedback: Policy advice must consider whether evidence is applicable to the target population and context.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: An economist is employed by an agency that benefits from a favorable estimate. What practice best protects credibility?
options: Publish the preferred specification with full calculations, omitting the agency relationship to keep the report technical.
Disclose the agency interest, assumptions, alternatives and uncertainty so others can assess the estimate.
Have an agency colleague check the arithmetic, then report one point estimate to avoid confusing readers.
Report an interval from the chosen model, leaving model selection and alternative specifications to the agency.
q.feedback: Disclosure must address both the institutional interest and methodological discretion. Arithmetic review or an uncertainty interval alone does not reveal how model selection could favor the agency.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: A policy has a positive expected net benefit but a small chance of catastrophic loss. Which addition is necessary?
options: A claim that averages eliminate risk.
Removal of all low-probability outcomes.
Risk analysis beyond the expected-value calculation.
A conclusion based only on sunk costs.
q.commonError: Treating expected value as a complete policy criterion.
q.feedback: Low-probability, high-cost outcomes may matter even when expected net benefits are positive.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: A pilot worked elsewhere but institutions differ locally. What is the key warning?
options: A successful pilot automatically generalizes to other settings
Institutional differences matter only for normative judgments
A large effect elsewhere guarantees a large local effect.
Evidence may not transfer to the new setting
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: An efficient proposal conflicts with a legal-rights goal. What follows?
options: The efficient proposal must be adopted
Efficiency evidence does not uniquely decide social desirability
The legal-rights goal is irrelevant to policy evaluation
The conflict proves the proposal is economically inefficient.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

q.q: A recommendation changes under plausible assumptions. What should the economist do?
options: Report only the baseline estimate
Use the assumption that produces the most favorable result
Report sensitivity rather than one certain answer
Delay all advice until uncertainty is eliminated.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: Two advisers accept the same estimate: consolidating offices saves staff time but lengthens rural travel. One favors consolidation and the other opposes it. Which information best explains their different recommendations?
options: Which adviser used more decimal places in the shared estimate
Whether the two advisers agree that travel is measurable
Whether consolidation is being proposed by a public institution
How each weighs staff savings against rural access
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Agreement about effects leaves room for different weights on efficiency and access. Those priorities can explain the recommendations without inventing a forecast disagreement.

q.q: An economist recommends a policy because it maximizes total surplus, while citizens prioritize equal treatment. The disagreement is primarily about:
options: The arithmetic definition of surplus.
The normative criterion used to rank outcomes.
Whether incentives exist.
The distinction between micro and macro topics.
q.commonError: Calling a value disagreement an empirical error.
q.feedback: Economic analysis can measure consequences, but ranking competing values requires a normative criterion.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: Two studies estimate opposite effects because one uses a credible natural experiment and the other compares self-selected groups. The strongest appraisal emphasizes:
options: Differences in causal identification.
Which result has the larger number.
Which author supports the preferred policy.
Whether both studies use percentages.
q.commonError: Treating all empirical designs as equally informative.
q.feedback: Policy advice should weigh evidence by its ability to identify causal effects.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: Volunteers in a training pilot earn more later. A second study assigns training by lottery and finds little effect. Before recommending expansion, what should the adviser resolve?
options: Whether volunteer enthusiasm proves the training caused their earnings
Whether the lottery result makes all participant preferences irrelevant
Whether selection explains the first result and whether the lottery setting fits expansion
Whether the larger positive estimate is easier to communicate
q.commonError: Treating all empirical designs as equally informative.
q.feedback: Volunteers can differ before training. The lottery helps separate selection from treatment, while its population and implementation still need to fit the expansion setting.

q.q: A report favors plan A because paid-work savings exceed its cash cost. A requires relatives to provide unpaid care; plan B purchases the same care. What comparison would correct the scope of the advice?
options: Value caregiving time under both plans alongside cash and paid-work effects
Add unpaid care only to B because B records an invoice
Treat unpaid care as free because relatives are not paid
Remove paid-work savings so both plans contain only budget costs
q.feedback: Unpaid time has alternative uses. Comparable benefit-cost scope includes caregiving burdens for A and avoids ignoring a resource merely because B buys it explicitly.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: A model favors a recycling program if most households sort correctly. A pilot reports high collection but does not measure contamination; sorting is harder in the rollout area. What should precede the recommendation?
options: Declare the program undesirable solely because compliance is uncertain
Measure correct sorting and test whether the ranking survives realistic rollout compliance
Treat collected tonnage as proof of the required compliance
Use the pilot average unchanged because the same program name is used
q.commonError: Confusing statutory design with actual implementation.
q.feedback: Collection is not the assumed correct sorting. Advice needs the relevant compliance measure and sensitivity to the more difficult rollout setting.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: A consolidation plan has aggregate gains but losses for remote users. A report says compensation makes everyone better off, although no compensation is funded. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: An unfunded transfer can be counted as income already received
Any remote loss proves aggregate gains are mathematically impossible
Potential compensation does not establish actual gains for remote users; report the implemented distribution
Positive total gains mean the remote users must gain indirectly
q.feedback: Aggregate gains can create scope for compensation. Without an implemented transfer, the remote users' losses remain part of the actual policy outcome.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: Two access plans have the same total measured benefit. One imposes concentrated losses on residents with few alternatives; the other spreads smaller losses. What additional step supports a defensible recommendation?
options: Choose either plan because equal totals establish identical welfare for every resident
Increase numerical precision until one value criterion becomes unnecessary
Count only beneficiaries because costs are already reflected in the total
State how concentrated hardship is weighed, and show each plan's distribution
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Equal totals conceal different distributions. A recommendation needs an explicit evaluation of concentrated hardship and evidence about who gains and loses.

q.q: A permit reform saves time for compliant firms but increases inspections. It has positive net benefit at high compliance and negative net benefit at low compliance. Local compliance is unmeasured. What advice is best supported?
options: Present the conditional ranking and seek local compliance evidence before a firm recommendation
Recommend adoption because the favorable scenario is feasible
Reject because one plausible scenario has losses
Average the two outcomes without assessing how likely each is
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: The sign depends on an unresolved local behavior. Reporting that dependence and obtaining relevant evidence is more defensible than selecting or mechanically averaging scenarios.

q.q: A school schedule saves paid staff hours but shifts supervision to families. The measured gain disappears when family time is valued at its next-best use. Which revision follows?
options: Treat the original cash saving as false because the wider net gain disappeared
Report the wider resource comparison and explain why a budget saving need not be a social gain
Keep the original conclusion because only paid hours use scarce resources
Count the family time twice, once as cost and once as a separate loss of the same activity
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: The budget saving can be real while the wider net benefit vanishes. Count the forgone family activity once and distinguish fiscal effects from resource effects.

q.q: An adviser reports a narrow forecast interval based on one assumed take-up rate. Credible alternative take-up rates reverse the recommendation. What uncertainty is missing?
options: A value judgment proving which take-up rate is true
Evidence that no economic forecast can ever inform a choice
Uncertainty about the behavioral assumption, beyond precision conditional on that assumption
Only rounding uncertainty in the reported forecast
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: A precise estimate conditional on one rate does not capture uncertainty about the rate itself. Report the alternative assumptions and the recommendation reversal.

q.q: Two policy models fit the pilot. One attributes improved attendance to transport; the other to reminders sent at the same time. The rollout can fund only one. What evidence most directly helps the adviser choose?
options: A larger pilot that always combines both services
The political popularity of the combined pilot as proof of causality
The pilot's total attendance without a breakdown of interventions
Comparable groups receiving transport alone and reminders alone
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Separating the interventions tests the competing mechanisms relevant to the actual funding choice. More bundled observations cannot identify which component drove the gain.

q.q: An economist identifies the schedule with the highest total measured benefit. Citizens prefer another because it guarantees a minimum service level to every district. Which advice respects both roles?
options: Explain the cost of the service guarantee and make the ranking criterion explicit
Treat the citizens' preference as a statistical error in the benefit estimate
Describe the maximizing schedule as morally required by the calculation
Alter the benefit numbers until both schedules receive the same ranking
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economic analysis can estimate the tradeoff created by the guarantee. Deciding how strongly to value equal minimum access goes beyond identifying the aggregate maximum.

q.q: A small pilot pays shops to repair items and records strong gains. Nationwide adoption induces shops to relabel routine maintenance as repairs. What should a follow-up evaluation change?
options: Infer zero genuine gains solely because some reporting changed
Measure additional genuine repairs and account for the changed reporting incentive
Use reimbursement counts unchanged because the pilot already validated the measure
Treat all repairs after adoption as caused by the payment
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Scaling changes incentives and can change what the metric measures. Estimate genuine additional repairs against a credible comparison rather than equating paid claims with benefits.

q.q: What can an economist contribute without choosing society’s values?
options: Evidence about likely consequences
Choose society’s moral priorities
Decide which policy lawmakers must adopt
Guarantee that the chosen policy will succeed.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: A projection includes a confidence range. What does it acknowledge?
options: The true effect is guaranteed to lie inside the range
Uncertainty in the predicted effect
The range identifies the policy society should prefer
Every value in the range is equally likely.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: A policy creates winners and losers. What should analysis show?
options: Only the total effect on surplus
Only which groups lose
The distribution as well as the total effect
Ignore distribution whenever the aggregate effect is positive.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

q.q: Policy A creates $40 million of gains for high-income households and $10 million of losses for low-income households. Policy B creates $22 million of gains for low-income households and costs high-income households $5 million. With no other effects, which advice distinguishes efficiency from distribution?
options: A has the larger unweighted net gain, while B favors low-income households; the ranking depends on the stated social criterion.
B has the larger unweighted net gain, while A favors low-income households; efficiency alone therefore selects B.
A has the larger unweighted net gain, so it necessarily satisfies a goal of improving low-income households’ welfare.
B favors low-income households, so A cannot have a positive unweighted net gain even if its benefits exceed losses.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Unweighted net gains are 40-10=30 for A and 22-5=17 for B. Efficiency totals and incidence differ. Choosing between them requires stating how distribution enters the social ranking.

q.q: A subsidy model estimated that firms would add 100 jobs when credit was available at 5%. Credit is now rationed and borrowing costs 12%; the model still predicts 100 jobs because it treats financing as fixed. What is the best next analysis?
options: Keep the 100-job forecast because the subsidy is unchanged; treat financing as an unrelated macroeconomic detail.
Reestimate firms’ financing responses and compare predictions under feasible credit conditions before transferring the old forecast.
Replace 100 jobs with the latest observed hiring total; that difference directly measures the subsidy’s causal effect.
Reject all subsidy models because one institutional change means simplified forecasts cannot provide policy evidence.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Credit conditions affect the mechanism through which firms finance expansion. The old forecast is conditional on assumptions that changed; observed hiring alone does not identify a counterfactual subsidy effect.

q.q: Two advisers agree that a flood barrier yields $60 million in avoided damage, costs $35 million and relocates 200 households. One favors it; the other rejects involuntary relocation. Which further step would clarify rather than merely repeat their disagreement?
options: Collect a more precise construction-cost estimate until both advisers must adopt the same view of relocation.
Add the number of relocated households directly to the dollar cost and select the policy with the smallest sum.
State the relocation criterion, examine feasible less-displacing alternatives and show how each changes net benefits and affected households.
Treat the shared positive net benefit as evidence that objections to relocation are errors in economic forecasting.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: The advisers share the main predictions but differ over a social criterion. Examining feasible alternatives and explicit tradeoffs informs the choice; greater forecast precision cannot itself settle the value judgment.

q.q: Economists disagree because one trusts a different study. What differs?
options: Their scientific judgment about evidence
Their normative values must differ
One economist must be irrational
Evidence becomes irrelevant once economists disagree.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: They agree on effects but rank fairness differently. What differs?
options: Their scientific forecasts
Their normative evaluation
One economist must have misread the data
Economic analysis cannot distinguish factual claims from value judgments.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: Why examine enforcement before recommending a rule?
options: Enforcement affects legality but not economic outcomes
Assume full compliance when evaluating a proposed rule
Implementation changes costs and behavior
Implementation costs are irrelevant before adoption.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: A proposed tax is projected to create $80 million in national efficiency gains but $50 million in losses concentrated in one region. Those regional losses are already included in the national estimate. A domestic transfer could offset them at $8 million of administrative cost, but the regional loss estimate is uncertain. Which advice is sound?
options: Net expected national gain after administration is $72 million; test regional-loss scenarios and compensation feasibility before making a distributional recommendation.
Net expected national gain after compensation is $22 million; subtract the regional losses again because concentration makes them additional costs.
Net expected national gain after compensation is $122 million; add the transfer because recipients experience it as a benefit.
Net expected national gain is $80 million under every scenario; positive national gains guarantee each region can implement compensation itself.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: The $50 million loss is already in the national ledger and a domestic transfer is redistribution. Administration reduces expected gain to 72. Uncertain regional effects still matter for funding, implementation and social priorities.

q.q: Model A predicts a transit subsidy raises ridership mainly by attracting former drivers. Model B predicts the same total increase mainly by shifting riders from unsubsidized buses. Both fit current totals. The policy goal is fewer car trips. What evidence best discriminates between the models for this decision?
options: Collect more precise total ridership counts after the subsidy; equal predictions imply either model establishes equal car-trip reductions.
Track prior travel modes and changes against a credible untreated comparison; total ridership fit alone cannot identify car-trip displacement.
Choose A because its mechanism matches the goal; a policy-relevant mechanism needs no separate test once totals fit.
Average the predicted ridership increases; averaging identical totals also identifies how many riders switched from cars.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Identical ridership predictions can hide different substitution channels. Prior-mode and counterfactual evidence tests whether observed new riders actually displaced car travel.

q.q: A school policy has estimated net benefits of $12 million and reduces access for rural pupils. An alternative yields $8 million and preserves access. The adopted charter requires preserving rural access unless no feasible alternative exists. What conclusion follows from the estimates and criterion together?
options: The first policy must satisfy the charter because its larger net benefit proves no economically feasible alternative exists.
The alternative’s access benefit proves its unweighted net benefit exceeds $12 million even though the estimate is $8 million.
The first policy leads on unweighted net benefits, but the feasible alternative satisfies the stated access constraint; surplus alone does not justify overriding it.
Neither estimate is positive analysis because the access constraint makes factual policy comparisons inherently normative.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: The estimates are factual claims about consequences; the charter supplies a normative constraint. A feasible access-preserving alternative exists, so maximizing the listed net benefit is not the only decision rule.

q.q: A safety rule would prevent $10 million of harm with full compliance and require $4 million of compliance resources. Current enforcement induces only half the affected firms to comply; assume benefits and compliance costs scale proportionally. An extra $1 million enforcement program would raise compliance to 80%. Which assessment is correct?
options: Net benefit rises from $3 million to $4.8 million; enforcement spending is a transfer and should not reduce the gain.
Net benefit falls from $6 million to $3.8 million; compare actual enforcement with the original full-compliance forecast.
Net benefit stays $6 million; the legal rule fixes compliance benefits regardless of enforcement behavior.
Net benefit rises from $3 million to $3.8 million; the extra enforcement gains $0.8 million despite falling short of full compliance.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Current net benefit is 0.5(10-4)=3. With stronger enforcement it is 0.8(10-4)-1=3.8. The incremental gain is 0.8, and the correct baseline is current feasible compliance rather than the full-compliance forecast.

q.q: Positive policy analysis asks:
options: What consequences are likely to occur.
Which outcome is morally best.
Which party should win.
Which value judgment is scientifically true.
q.feedback: Positive analysis describes or predicts consequences.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: When a policy conclusion depends on an assumption, the economist should:
options: Hide it from decision makers.
State the assumption and test how much it matters.
Treat it as a proven fact.
Replace it with a slogan.
q.feedback: Transparent assumptions and sensitivity checks strengthen policy advice.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: Can economists scientifically determine society’s values?
options: Yes; economic expertise identifies the morally best outcome
Yes; estimating consequences also determines which values society should hold
No; they can clarify consequences and tradeoffs
Yes; economists receive decision-making authority from their technical expertise.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: Does efficiency prove a policy is socially best?
options: Yes; efficiency incorporates every social objective
Yes; distribution does not matter when total surplus rises
Yes; economists can rank competing social values scientifically.
No; other values and distribution may matter
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

q.q: Is a policy forecast a guarantee?
options: No; it depends on evidence and assumptions
Yes, if the forecast comes from a strong model
Yes, if the confidence interval is narrow
Yes, if the economist has no conflict of interest.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: Must economist disagreement be political?
options: Yes; all disagreement among economists is ideological
No; evidence, models, or values can differ
Yes; economists using the same field must otherwise agree
Yes; empirical evidence cannot produce different interpretations.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: The economist's role in policy analysis is primarily to:
options: Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
Choose everyone's values
Guarantee a policy works
Eliminate scarcity
q.feedback: Economics can analyze consequences and tradeoffs, while value judgments remain separate choices.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: A faculty committee asks whether a new attendance rule will improve learning. An economist would first:
options: Identify the behavioral mechanism and evidence needed to test it.
Declare the rule fair or unfair without analysis.
Assume attendance and learning are identical.
Ignore incentives created by the rule.
q.commonError: Failing to transfer policy-analysis logic outside government.
q.feedback: Economic policy reasoning applies to any rule that changes incentives and outcomes.

labels: LO2.5

q.q: A policy forecast is testable, but the economist also recommends adoption. How should the forecast and recommendation be distinguished?
options: Both are positive claims because the recommendation follows evidence
Positive analysis informs a separate normative choice
Both are normative because the topic is public policy
The forecast itself determines whether the policy should be adopted.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: A model works only under one assumption. What should advice report?
options: Report only the baseline result
Drop the assumption from the analysis
How the conclusion changes when the assumption changes
Delay all advice until the assumption can be proven true.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: A subsidy changes behavior beyond its intended target. Which economic idea helps explain these additional responses?
options: Only the directly targeted behavior should be included in the analysis
Responses outside the target are irrelevant to the policy’s effects
Unintended responses occur only when enforcement fails.
Incentives can create unintended consequences
q.feedback: A subsidy changes the payoff from an action. People may adjust related choices as well as the behavior the policy targets, creating effects the designer did not intend. Those responses belong in the policy’s benefit-and-cost analysis even when the subsidy is enforced as designed.

q.q: Economists use elasticity to measure:
options: How strongly one variable responds to a change in another
Only whether a variable rises or falls
The dollar value of every market transaction
The slope of any line without regard to units
q.feedback: Elasticity is a responsiveness measure: percentage response divided by percentage change in a driver.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Why is an elasticity coefficient usually unit-free?
options: It always uses dollars
It compares percentage changes
It divides quantity by price levels
It converts all values to index numbers
q.feedback: Because both numerator and denominator are percentage changes, measurement units cancel.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: A price elasticity of demand equal to 1.8 is classified as:
options: Inelastic
Unit elastic
Elastic
Perfectly inelastic
q.feedback: A demand elasticity greater than one means quantity responds proportionally more than price.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: A price elasticity of demand equal to 0.45 is classified as:
options: Elastic
Unit elastic
Perfectly elastic
Inelastic
q.feedback: A coefficient between zero and one is inelastic.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: A price elasticity of demand equal to 1 is:
options: Unit elastic
Perfectly elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Necessarily negative income elasticity
q.feedback: Unit elasticity means equal proportional changes in price and quantity demanded.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: A vertical demand curve represents demand that is:
options: Perfectly elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unit elastic everywhere
Elastic only at high prices
q.feedback: Quantity does not respond to price on a vertical demand curve, so elasticity is zero.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: A horizontal demand curve represents demand that is:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Unit elastic everywhere
Perfectly elastic
Inelastic because slope is zero
q.feedback: A tiny price increase eliminates quantity demanded along a perfectly elastic demand curve.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Demand is generally more elastic when consumers have:
options: Fewer alternatives
Less time to adjust
A smaller share of income at stake
Many close substitutes
q.feedback: Close substitutes make it easier to switch away when price rises.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Compared with luxuries, necessities generally have demand that is:
options: Less elastic
More elastic
Perfectly elastic
Always unit elastic
q.feedback: Consumers have less ability to reduce purchases of necessities after a price increase.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Compared with a broadly defined market, a narrowly defined market usually has:
options: Less elastic demand
More elastic demand
The same elasticity by definition
Perfectly inelastic demand
q.feedback: Narrow markets have more close substitutes, which raises demand elasticity.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Demand tends to be more elastic for a good that takes up:
options: A tiny share of the buyer’s budget
No time to compare alternatives
A large share of the buyer’s budget
A fixed legal quantity
q.feedback: Large budget shares give buyers a stronger reason to adjust.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Over a longer time horizon, demand for gasoline is likely to become:
options: Less elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unrelated to available alternatives
More elastic
q.feedback: Over time, drivers can change vehicles, locations, and travel habits.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Which feature most directly makes demand for one brand of bottled water elastic?
options: Many nearly identical brands
Water is necessary for life
The product is sold in liters
The market price is positive
q.feedback: Brand-level demand is elastic because buyers can switch among close substitutes.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Which purchase is most likely to have inelastic demand in the short run?
options: A vacation package
A required medication with few substitutes
A premium restaurant meal
One brand of breakfast cereal
q.feedback: Necessity, limited substitutes, and short adjustment time all reduce elasticity.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Total revenue equals:
options: Price divided by quantity sold
Quantity sold minus price
Price multiplied by quantity sold
Elasticity multiplied by price
q.feedback: Total revenue is P × Q.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: When demand is elastic, a price increase usually causes total revenue to:
options: Rise
Remain unchanged
Become zero
Fall
q.feedback: With elastic demand, the percentage drop in quantity is larger than the percentage price increase.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: When demand is inelastic, a price increase usually causes total revenue to:
options: Rise
Fall
Remain unchanged
Equal marginal revenue
q.feedback: With inelastic demand, quantity falls proportionally less than price rises.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: When demand is unit elastic, a price change leaves total revenue:
options: Always higher
Approximately unchanged
Always lower
Equal to zero
q.feedback: Equal proportional price and quantity changes offset in total revenue.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: Price elasticity of supply measures how quantity supplied responds to a change in:
options: Consumer income
The price of a complement in consumption
The good’s price
Buyer preferences
q.feedback: Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: Why is supply generally more elastic over a longer time horizon?
options: Less time to adjust production
No unused capacity
Inputs fixed by law
More time to adjust production
q.feedback: A longer time horizon gives producers more time to expand capacity, change inputs, and otherwise adjust production.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: A firm with substantial unused capacity is likely to have short-run supply that is:
options: More elastic supply
Less elastic supply
Perfectly inelastic supply
No possible quantity change
q.feedback: Unused capacity makes output easier to expand.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: Which product is likely to have more elastic short-run supply?
options: Seats at tonight’s sold-out concert
A storable manufactured good
Fresh fish already caught today
Land in a fixed downtown block
q.feedback: Storage and adjustable production make supply more responsive.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: A positive income elasticity usually identifies a:
options: Inferior good
Complement
Normal good
Perfectly inelastic good
q.feedback: Demand for a normal good rises as income rises.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: A negative income elasticity usually identifies an:
options: Normal good
Substitute good
Unit-elastic good
Inferior good
q.feedback: Demand for an inferior good falls as income rises.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: A positive cross-price elasticity indicates that two goods are:
options: Substitutes
Complements
Both inferior
Both perfectly inelastic
q.feedback: When the price of one rises, demand for its substitute rises.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: A negative cross-price elasticity indicates that two goods are:
options: Substitutes
Complements
Both normal
Both elastic
q.feedback: When the price of one rises, demand for its complement falls.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: A per-unit tax is generally borne more heavily by the side of the market that is:
options: More elastic
Legally required to mail the payment
Less elastic
Represented by the flatter curve in every case
q.feedback: The less elastic side has fewer ways to avoid the taxed transaction.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: Refer to the graph. D2 is steeper than D1. Why isn’t slope alone a valid measure of elasticity?
options: Slope and elasticity measure the same response in the same units.
A negative slope makes demand inelastic at every point.
A steeper-looking curve has the same elasticity at every point.
Slope uses units; elasticity compares percentage changes.
q.feedback: Slope measures units of price per unit of quantity and changes when axis units change. Elasticity measures percentage responsiveness; classification also depends on the price and quantity being compared.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: On the displayed linear demand curve, as you move downward from C through B toward A, price elasticity of demand generally:
options: Declines from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic
Remains constant because slope is constant
Rises from inelastic to elastic
Becomes zero immediately after B
q.feedback: C lies in the elastic region, B is the unit-elastic midpoint, and A lies in the inelastic region.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: The midpoint method calculates percentage changes using:
options: Only the starting value
The average of the starting and ending values
Only the ending value
The larger value in both denominators
q.feedback: Using averages makes the elasticity estimate symmetric for increases and decreases.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand

q.q: At point B on the displayed linear demand curve, what price and quantity are shown?
options: $8 and 60 units
$12 and 30 units
$4 and 90 units
$8 and 90 units
q.feedback: Point B is marked at P = $8 and Q = 60.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand

q.q: Which labeled point is the midpoint of the displayed linear demand curve?
options: Point A
Point B
Point C
None of the labeled points
q.feedback: The line runs from P = $16, Q = 0 to P = $0, Q = 120, so its midpoint is P = $8, Q = 60 at B.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand

q.q: Which labeled point lies in the inelastic portion of the displayed linear demand curve?
options: Point B
Point C
Point A
All three points are equally elastic
q.feedback: Below the midpoint of a linear demand curve, quantity is relatively large and price relatively small, so demand is inelastic; A is in that region.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand

q.q: At a price of $10 in the displayed graph, which curve shows the larger quantity demanded?
options: D2, at 45 units
D1, at 35 units
D1, at 45 units
D2, at 55 units
q.feedback: At P = $10, point B on D1 is Q = 45 while point D on D2 is Q = 35.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand

q.q: When price is $6, which demand curve shows the larger quantity demanded?
options: D2, at 95 units
D1, at 55 units
D2, at 45 units
D1, at 95 units
q.feedback: At P = $6, D1 is at point A with Q = 95, while D2 is at point C with Q = 55.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand

q.q: A horizontal demand curve is the graphical form of:
options: Perfectly inelastic demand
Unit-elastic demand
Perfectly elastic demand
A supply curve
q.feedback: A horizontal demand curve is the limiting case of perfectly elastic demand.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: What elasticity case is represented by the vertical demand curve?
options: Perfectly elastic demand
Unit-elastic demand
A perfectly elastic supply curve
Perfectly inelastic demand
q.feedback: A vertical demand curve means quantity demanded does not change when price changes.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: At a price of $8, what quantity is supplied on the short-run supply curve?
options: 60 units
100 units
70 units
40 units
q.feedback: Point A on the short-run supply curve is Q = 70 at P = $8.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: Refer to the graph. Starting from P = $4 and Q = 60, which supply curve shows the larger increase in quantity supplied when price rises to $8?
options: Short-run supply
Both show the same response
Neither curve responds
Long-run supply
q.feedback: Long-run supply reaches Q = 100, compared with Q = 70 in the short run.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: A bakery owns an unused oven and can add a second production shift quickly. Other things equal, its short-run supply is likely to be:
options: More elastic because output can expand without major new investment
More inelastic because unused capacity prevents adjustment
Perfectly inelastic because the bakery has fixed equipment
Unit elastic because capacity and price are unrelated
q.feedback: Unused capacity makes it easier to raise output when price rises.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: Which situation generally makes supply more price elastic?
options: Production requires a fixed harvest already in the ground
All firms are operating at absolute capacity
The good must be supplied at one fixed quantity
Inputs can be moved easily into the industry
q.feedback: Mobile inputs let producers expand or contract output more readily.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: A fresh strawberry farmer has only today to respond to a sudden price increase. Compared with supply over several growing seasons, today’s supply is usually:
options: Perfectly elastic
Exactly unit elastic
Less elastic
More elastic
q.feedback: The very short run gives the farmer little time to change acreage, plants, or harvest capacity.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: A seller can store a product cheaply and release inventory when price rises. Cheap storage generally makes supply:
options: Unrelated to price
More elastic
Less elastic
Perfectly inelastic
q.feedback: Inventory can be shifted toward periods with higher prices, increasing quantity responsiveness.

labels: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

q.q: Household income rises and demand for bus rides falls. This pattern is most consistent with bus rides being:
options: A normal good with positive income elasticity
A luxury with income elasticity above one
A substitute good identified by cross-price elasticity
An inferior good for these consumers
q.feedback: Demand moving opposite income implies negative income elasticity and an inferior good.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: Demand for restaurant meals rises when consumer income rises. The income elasticity of demand is therefore most likely:
options: Exactly zero by definition
A measure of supply responsiveness
Positive
Negative
q.feedback: Normal goods have positive income elasticity because demand moves with income.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: If demand for a good changes very little when income changes, its income elasticity is likely to be:
options: The same as its price elasticity
Close to zero
Necessarily greater than one
Necessarily negative
q.feedback: A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: The price of butter rises and demand for margarine rises. Butter and margarine are most likely:
options: Unrelated because cross-price effects cannot shift demand
Substitutes
Complements
Inferior goods
q.feedback: Demand for one good moving in the same direction as the other good’s price implies positive cross-price elasticity.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: The price of game consoles falls and demand for compatible games rises. Consoles and games are most likely:
options: Complements
Substitutes
Both inferior goods
Goods with zero cross-price elasticity
q.feedback: Demand for games moves opposite the console price, indicating negative cross-price elasticity.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: If a change in the price of one good has almost no effect on demand for another, their cross-price elasticity is probably:
options: Strongly positive
Strongly negative
Always equal to one
Near zero
q.feedback: Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: A seller cuts price and total revenue rises. Over that price range, demand is most likely:
options: Inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unrelated to price
Elastic
q.feedback: When demand is elastic, the percentage quantity increase outweighs the percentage price decrease, raising total revenue.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: A seller cuts price and total revenue falls. Over that price range, demand is most likely:
options: Perfectly elastic
Necessarily unit elastic
Inelastic
Elastic
q.feedback: With inelastic demand, quantity rises proportionally less than price falls, so total revenue declines.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: If a price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged, demand over that range is closest to:
options: Income elastic
Unit elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Perfectly elastic
q.feedback: At unit elasticity, the percentage price and quantity effects approximately offset.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: A firm sells 200 units at $15 each. Which expression gives total revenue?
q.feedback: Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity sold.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: On a linear demand curve, total revenue is typically highest near the point where demand is:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Most inelastic possible
Defined only by income elasticity
Unit elastic
q.feedback: For a standard linear demand curve, total revenue reaches its maximum around unit elasticity.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: A price increase raises total revenue. Which demand condition is consistent with that result?
options: Demand must be perfectly elastic
Demand must have positive income elasticity
Demand is inelastic over the relevant range
Demand is elastic over the relevant range
q.feedback: With inelastic demand, the price effect dominates the smaller quantity decline.

labels: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue

q.q: If demand is much less elastic than supply, buyers usually bear:
options: None of the tax burden
Exactly half of every tax by rule
More of a per-unit tax burden
Less of a per-unit tax burden
q.feedback: The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: If supply is much less elastic than demand, sellers usually bear:
options: Only the administrative cost of the tax
More of a per-unit tax burden
Less of a per-unit tax burden
None of the tax burden
q.feedback: The less elastic side has fewer alternatives and bears more of the tax burden.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: A business facing highly elastic demand should be especially cautious about:
options: Raising price
Expanding output
Tracking competitors
Estimating variable cost
q.feedback: With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: A business facing very inelastic demand can raise price with a relatively small percentage decline in:
options: Fixed cost
Supply elasticity
Producer technology
Quantity demanded
q.feedback: Inelastic demand means quantity demanded responds proportionally less than price.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: Other things equal, a tax reduces the quantity traded by more when demand and supply are:
options: Perfectly vertical
Unrelated to price
More elastic
More inelastic
q.feedback: More responsive buyers and sellers reduce traded quantity more when a tax wedge is introduced.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: A policy that raises price will reduce consumption most strongly when demand is:
options: Independent of price
More elastic
More inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
q.feedback: Elastic demand produces a larger percentage quantity response to a given percentage price change.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: An export industry can expand output more after a world-price increase when its supply is:
options: More elastic
More inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Measured only by income elasticity
q.feedback: More elastic supply allows producers to respond more strongly to the higher price.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: If employers can easily substitute machines for a type of labor when wages rise, demand for that labor is likely to be:
options: More inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unrelated to substitution possibilities
More elastic
q.feedback: Availability of substitutes makes factor demand more responsive to its price.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: A city wants a fee to sharply reduce use of a service. The fee is more likely to change behavior when demand for the service is:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Vertical at every price
Elastic
Inelastic
q.feedback: Elastic demand means usage responds strongly to a price-like charge.

labels: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

q.q: A commuter has few alternatives this week but can relocate or change vehicles over several years. Demand for gasoline is likely to be:
options: More elastic in the short run than in the long run
Equally elastic in both periods by definition
More elastic in the long run than in the short run
Perfectly elastic in both periods
q.feedback: Longer adjustment periods create more substitution possibilities.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: Demand for “food” is less elastic than demand for “restaurant lunches” mainly because:
options: Restaurant lunches are always necessities
Food has a steeper curve in every graph
Broad markets always have lower prices
Food is a broader market with fewer substitutes outside the category
q.feedback: Narrower definitions expose more alternatives within the broader category.

labels: Foundations and determinants of elasticity

q.q: A streaming service raises price by 5 percent and subscriptions fall by 12 percent. Demand is:
options: Elastic
Inelastic
Unit elastic
Perfectly inelastic

q.q: Holding prices fixed, a 4% income increase raises demand for Product A by 6% and lowers demand for Product B by 2%. If income next falls 2%, use the same local elasticities to forecast the two demands approximately.

A falls 3% and B falls 1%; discard both income-elasticity signs.

Income elasticity is -0.4; the product is an inferior good
The product cannot be classified because price is not provided

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

The product cannot be classified because price is not provided
Income elasticity is 0.83; the product is an income-inelastic normal good

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

options: +0.75; lenses and cameras are substitutes, and lens demand falls about 3%.
-0.75; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand falls about 3%.
-0.75; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand rises about 3%.
-1.33; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand rises about 5.33%.
q.feedback: Cross-price elasticity is -6/8 = -0.75. The negative sign indicates complements. Applying the same local estimate to a -4% camera-price change gives (-0.75)(-4%) = +3% lens demand.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: A controlled price test finds that an 8% increase in Service Y’s price raises demand for Service X by 10%. If Y next cuts price 4%, which estimate, relationship, and approximate forecast follow?

+1.25, substitutes; demand for X rises about 5%.
+0.80, substitutes; demand for X falls about 3.2%.
+1.25, substitutes; demand for X falls about 5%.
q.feedback: Cross-price elasticity is 10/8 = +1.25. Its positive sign indicates substitutes. Applying that signed estimate to -4% gives a -5% change in X demand, with other factors fixed.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: The price of tablet cases changes by 15 percent, and demand for tablets changes by -18 percent. Which cross-price result is correct?
options: Cross-price elasticity is -1.2; the goods are complements
Cross-price elasticity is -0.83; the reciprocal defines the relationship
Cross-price elasticity is 1.2; the goods are substitutes regardless of sign
The goods are unrelated because neither quantity supplied nor income is given

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: Two rival brands have cross-price elasticity +0.8 for A’s demand with respect to B’s price. Brand A expects B to cut price 5%, while income and A’s own price remain fixed. A proposes stocking 4% more units because the coefficient is positive. Evaluate the plan.
options: The sign identifies substitutes and predicts a 4% demand increase, so the stock increase matches the forecast.
The sign identifies substitutes, but the forecast is a 4% demand decrease, so the proposed stock increase reverses the response.
The sign identifies complements and predicts a 4% demand decrease, so the stock increase reverses the response.
The sign identifies substitutes but predicts a 6.25% demand decrease, so division gives the correct forecast.
q.feedback: A positive cross-price coefficient means X demand moves in the same direction as the other product’s price. Here 0.8 × (-5%) = -4%. A cheaper substitute reduces demand for A; positive elasticity does not mean demand always increases.

labels: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity

q.q: The price of coffee creamer changes by 20 percent, and demand for coffee changes by -7 percent. Which cross-price result is correct?
options: Cross-price elasticity is -2.86; the reciprocal defines the relationship
Cross-price elasticity is 0.35; the goods are substitutes regardless of sign
Cross-price elasticity is -0.35; the goods are complements
The goods are unrelated because neither quantity supplied nor income is given
q.feedback: The coefficient is -7% ÷ 20% = -0.35. Its sign identifies complements.

options: Quantity demanded falls about 3.3 percent and revenue rises

Quantity demanded falls about 10.8 percent and revenue likely falls

Elasticity remains one and marginal revenue remains zero

The more elastic base has no substitutes
q.feedback: A less responsive base distorts fewer trades for a given revenue target.

Supply elasticity alone caused substitution
The statutory payer should be changed
q.feedback: Close substitutes generate a strong demand response and can erode a narrow tax base.

options: Machinery makes labor supply more elastic
Wages become a smaller unit of measurement
Firms can change input mix more strongly after a wage increase
The output demand curve becomes vertical
q.feedback: Input substitutability raises the responsiveness of labor demanded.

No change because exchange rates affect only supply

q.q: Import supply to a small country is nearly perfectly elastic at the world price. A tariff is introduced. Which side is likely to bear most of the tariff?

options: The equilibrium wage changes
