A discouraged worker
Market allocation
q.feedback: In market allocation, households and firms use prices and voluntary exchange to guide resource use.

labels: LO1.6

q.q: The Signal Breaker asks: 'Which statement is positive?'
options: Investment spending raises GDP, other things equal
The government should spend more
GDP is the fairest possible measure
Every country should maximize GDP at all costs
q.feedback: A positive statement is testable. If investment rises and other components stay fixed, GDP rises.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: In the circular-flow model, households usually provide which resource to firms?
options: Final goods and services
Factors of production
Price ceilings
GDP deflators
q.feedback: Households provide factors of production such as labor, land, and capital to firms.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: The Signal Breaker asks which question is macroeconomic.
options: How many workers should one coffee shop hire?
How should one consumer spend a gift card?
How fast is the nation's GDP growing?
How should one firm price one sandwich?
q.feedback: GDP growth is an economy-wide issue, so it is macroeconomic.

labels: LO2.3

q.q: The Signal Breaker's final gate asks: which pairing is correct?
options: GDP growth is micro; one firm's hiring decision is macro
Both are always micro
Both are always normative
GDP growth is macro; one firm's hiring decision is micro
q.feedback: GDP growth concerns the whole economy, while one firm's hiring decision is about an individual firm.

labels: LO2.3

q.q: The Market Marshal shows wages rising from $20 to $21 while the price index rises from 100 to 110. What happened to the worker's real wage?
options: It fell because nominal wages rose 5% while prices rose 10%
It rose because the worker earns one more dollar per hour
It stayed constant because both wages and prices increased
It cannot be analyzed without GDP components
q.feedback: The wage rose 5%, but prices rose 10%, so the worker's purchasing power fell.

q.q: A city indexes wages to CPI, but the CPI overstates inflation because consumers substitute away from expensive goods. What is the likely result?
options: Real compensation must fall
Real compensation may rise more than intended
Nominal wages cannot change
Workers leave the labor force automatically
q.feedback: If CPI overstates inflation, indexing wages to CPI can raise real compensation more than intended.

q.q: Workers receive a 4% COLA, inflation is reported at 4%, but actual cost-of-living inflation is closer to 2.5% because quality improved and substitution occurred. What happened to real wages?
options: They definitely fell because reported inflation was positive
They stayed exactly constant because CPI inflation and COLA match
They likely increased because the COLA exceeded the true rise in living costs
They became a transfer payment
q.feedback: If true living costs rose less than the CPI-based COLA, workers gained purchasing power.

q.q: A borrower signs a loan at 7% nominal interest expecting 3% inflation. Actual inflation turns out to be 8%. Who benefits compared with expectations?
options: The lender, because inflation makes repayment more valuable
Neither side, because nominal interest determines all real outcomes
The government, because unemployment must fall
The borrower, because the real repayment burden is lower than expected
q.feedback: Unexpectedly high inflation reduces the real value of fixed nominal repayments, helping borrowers and hurting lenders.

q.q: A saver earns 6% nominal interest. Inflation is 9%. At the same time, the saver receives a 4% nominal wage increase. Which statement best connects the two effects?
options: Both the real return on savings and the real wage fell
Both the real return and real wage rose
The real return rose but the real wage fell
The real wage rose because any raise beats inflation
q.feedback: The real interest rate is about -3%, and the wage increase is below inflation, so both real values fell.

q.q: The Market Marshal says: 'Nominal interest is high, but the real reward for saving is low.' Which situation fits that statement?
options: Nominal interest is 4% and inflation is 0%
Nominal interest is 10% and inflation is 9%
Nominal interest is 3% and inflation is -2%
Nominal interest is 8% and inflation is 1%
q.feedback: A 10% nominal rate with 9% inflation gives only about a 1% real return.

q.q: Imported oil prices rise sharply, but prices of domestically produced goods are mostly unchanged. Which measure is more directly affected?
options: GDP deflator, because it includes all imported goods
Both measures rise equally by definition
CPI, because imported consumer goods can be in the consumer basket
Neither measure can change unless unemployment changes
q.feedback: CPI can include imported goods bought by consumers, while the GDP deflator tracks prices of domestically produced output.

q.q: A domestic technology boom lowers the price of U.S.-made computers and raises output. Which statement best separates CPI from the GDP deflator?
options: CPI measures only exports while the deflator measures only imports
The GDP deflator is fixed-basket while CPI automatically changes with GDP
Both ignore technology-related price changes
The GDP deflator reflects domestic production prices; CPI reflects consumer basket prices
q.feedback: The GDP deflator follows prices of domestically produced output, while CPI follows the cost of the consumer basket.

q.q: The Market Marshal shows CPI rising faster than the GDP deflator after imported food and fuel become more expensive. What is the best interpretation?
options: Consumer prices rose partly because imported items became more expensive
Domestic production prices must have risen faster than consumer prices
Real GDP must have increased faster than nominal GDP
Unemployment must be structural
q.feedback: CPI can rise faster when imported consumer items rise in price, because imports affect CPI more directly than the GDP deflator.

q.q: Country A doubles nominal wages while prices also double. Country B raises output per worker by 25% with stable prices. Which country has the clearer improvement in living standards?
options: Country A, because nominal wages doubled
Country B, because productivity and real output per worker increased
Both improved equally because wages and output are both economic variables
Neither can improve living standards without a price ceiling
q.feedback: Higher nominal wages do not help if prices rise equally. Higher productivity supports higher real living standards.

q.q: A country increases capital per worker for several decades. Growth is strong at first, then slows even though investment continues. What explains the slowdown?
options: Substitution bias in CPI
A discouraged-worker effect
Diminishing returns to capital
A binding price ceiling
q.feedback: As capital becomes more abundant, each additional unit tends to add less extra output.

q.q: A poorer country adopts existing technology and attracts foreign investment. Its growth rate rises above that of richer countries for a time. What concept fits best?
options: Cost-of-living bias because the CPI is fixed
Cyclical unemployment because the economy is in recession
Tax equivalence because buyers and sellers share taxes
Catch-up growth because returns to capital can be higher when capital is scarce
q.feedback: Poorer countries can grow quickly when they add capital and technology because the return to new investment can be high.

q.q: Automation raises output per worker but displaces workers whose skills fit the old production process. What is the best synthesis?
options: Productivity may rise while structural unemployment increases for some workers
Productivity must fall because some workers lose jobs
Unemployment disappears because machines create output
The CPI must overstate inflation
q.feedback: Technology can raise productivity while creating structural unemployment for workers whose skills no longer match available jobs.

q.q: A recession reduces demand for restaurant meals, so restaurants lay off workers. Later, demand returns and many are rehired. What type of unemployment best describes the initial layoffs?
options: Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Discouraged employment
q.feedback: Layoffs caused by a recession or weak demand are cyclical unemployment.

q.q: A worker quits to search for a better job in a growing industry, while another worker loses a job because their old industry has permanently declined. Which pairing is correct?
options: First is structural; second is frictional
Both are cyclical
First is frictional; second is structural
Both are not in the labor force
q.feedback: Job search unemployment is frictional. Mismatch caused by lasting industry change is structural.

q.q: A binding minimum wage raises pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces hiring for low-skill labor. What is the strongest policy interpretation?
options: The policy eliminates scarcity in labor markets
The policy guarantees higher employment and higher wages for all workers
The policy only changes CPI and has no employment effects
The policy creates a tradeoff between higher wages for some and job loss for others
q.feedback: A binding wage floor can help workers who remain employed while making it harder for others to find jobs.

labels: LO6.2

q.q: A city imposes rent control below equilibrium. Rent is lower for some tenants, but apartments become scarce and quality declines. Which chain is best?
options: Binding ceiling → shortage → rationing and weaker maintenance
Binding floor → surplus → higher apartment quality
Tax wedge → higher seller revenue → no shortage
CPI bias → labor force exit → real wage growth
q.feedback: A binding ceiling creates shortages and changes incentives, often producing waiting, rationing, black markets, or quality decline.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A price ceiling is imposed during an inflation spike. Official prices stop rising, but buyers wait longer and pay side fees. What is the best interpretation?
options: Inflation is fully eliminated because the listed price cannot rise
The posted price is capped, but the full economic cost to buyers may still rise.
The good becomes less scarce because the posted price is lower.
The CPI must perfectly capture waiting time
q.feedback: A price ceiling can hide costs in waiting time, side payments, lower quality, or black markets.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A tax is placed on a good with very inelastic demand and elastic supply. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Sellers bear most of the burden and quantity rises
Buyers and sellers split the burden exactly equally by law
Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
The tax has no effect because supply is elastic
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. With inelastic demand, buyers bear more and quantity changes less.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: A tax on sellers shifts supply upward, raises the price buyers pay, lowers the price sellers receive, and reduces quantity. What is the best overall description?
options: The tax creates a price floor and expands the market
The tax only affects sellers because they mail the check
The tax eliminates deadweight loss
The tax creates a wedge and shrinks the market
q.feedback: A tax wedge separates buyer and seller prices and reduces the equilibrium quantity traded.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: The Market Marshal asks why a tax on buyers and an equal tax on sellers lead to similar market outcomes. What is the best answer?
options: Both create the same wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive
Only seller taxes reduce quantity
Only buyer taxes change demand
The legal taxpayer always bears the full burden
q.feedback: Whether the tax is legally placed on buyers or sellers, the market adjusts around the wedge between buyer and seller prices.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: Employment rises by 100,000, unemployment rises by 50,000, and labor-force participation rises. What likely happened?
options: The labor force must have shrunk
More people entered the labor force, and not all found jobs immediately
The unemployment rate must be zero
Everyone who entered the labor force became employed
q.feedback: Unemployment can rise when more people enter the labor force and some are still searching.

q.q: The unemployment rate falls, but employment does not rise and labor-force participation falls. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: The labor market definitely improved
Productivity must have risen
People may have stopped searching
Inflation must have fallen
q.feedback: A lower unemployment rate is not always good news if people left the labor force instead of finding jobs.

q.q: Adult population is 250 million, employed workers are 155 million, and unemployed workers are 10 million. What are the unemployment rate and labor-force participation rate?
options: Unemployment rate = 4%; labor-force participation rate = 62%
Unemployment rate ≈ 6.5%; labor-force participation rate = 60%
Unemployment rate = 10%; labor-force participation rate = 66%
Unemployment rate ≈ 6.1%; labor-force participation rate = 66%
q.feedback: Labor force = 155 + 10 = 165 million. Unemployment rate = 10/165 ≈ 6.1%. LFPR = 165/250 = 66%.

q.q: The price of beef rises while chicken remains cheaper, and consumers buy more chicken. Which CPI problem does this expose?
options: GDP double counting because beef is an intermediate good
Substitution bias from a fixed basket
Structural unemployment because workers lack skills
A binding price ceiling because suppliers produce too much
q.feedback: The CPI uses a fixed basket, so it can overstate inflation when consumers substitute toward relatively cheaper goods.

q.q: A price index rises from 125 to 150. What is the inflation rate?
q.feedback: Inflation is calculated as (150 - 125) / 125 x 100 = 20%.

q.q: An economist says inflation is 8%, but many consumers avoided the goods whose prices rose the most. What is the best interpretation?
options: Measured CPI inflation must equal zero
Measured CPI inflation only tracks unemployment
Measured CPI inflation proves real income rose
CPI may overstate true living-cost inflation
q.feedback: If consumers substitute away from goods with large price increases, a fixed CPI basket can overstate the true rise in the cost of living.

q.q: A worker receives a 5 percent raise while prices rise 8 percent. What happens to the worker's real wage?
options: It fell because prices rose faster than the nominal wage
It rose because any nominal raise increases purchasing power
It stayed exactly the same because wages and prices are unrelated
It became a transfer payment
q.feedback: A nominal raise does not guarantee higher purchasing power. If prices rise faster than wages, the real wage falls.

q.q: A loan pays 9% nominal interest while inflation is 4%. What is the approximate real interest rate?
q.feedback: The approximate real interest rate is nominal interest minus inflation: 9% - 4% = 5%.

q.q: A saver earns 6 percent interest while inflation is 7 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: The saver has fewer dollars but more purchasing power
The saver must be unemployed
The saver has more dollars but less purchasing power
The saver caused a price ceiling
q.feedback: The nominal balance rises, but because inflation is higher than the interest rate, purchasing power falls.

q.q: Which factor best explains how a country can support higher wages and living standards over time?
options: Higher productivity allows workers to produce more output per hour
Higher nominal prices automatically create more real wealth
A price ceiling always increases available goods
Unemployment insurance directly raises productivity
q.feedback: Long-run living standards depend heavily on productivity, meaning output produced per worker or per hour.

q.q: A country invests in better machines, worker training, and new technology. Which productivity factors are being strengthened?
options: Only natural resources
Only transfer payments
Physical capital, skills, and technology
Only the CPI basket
q.feedback: Machines are physical capital, training is human capital, and new production methods reflect technological knowledge.

q.q: An economist shows a PPF shifting outward after years of investment in capital and technology. What is the best interpretation?
options: The economy's productive capacity has increased
The economy moved inside the PPF because resources are idle
The CPI basket became fixed
A tax wedge disappeared
q.feedback: An outward PPF shift means the economy can produce more because resources, technology, or productivity improved.

q.q: An economist finds a worker who lost a job, has not worked this week, and has actively searched for work in the last four weeks. How is that worker classified?
options: Employed
Not in the labor force
Unemployed
Structurally impossible to classify
q.feedback: A person without a job who is actively looking for work is counted as unemployed and remains in the labor force.

q.q: An unemployed worker becomes discouraged and stops looking for work. What happens immediately in the official labor-force statistics?
options: The unemployment rate must rise because the person still lacks a job
The person becomes employed
The labor force must increase
The person leaves the labor force and is no longer counted as unemployed
q.feedback: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed because they are no longer actively looking for work.

q.q: The unemployment rate falls because many jobless workers stop searching. What is the most careful interpretation?
options: The labor market definitely improved because a lower unemployment rate is always good
The labor market may not have improved even though the official unemployment rate fell
The economy must have higher productivity
The CPI must have fallen
q.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if people stop looking for work and leave the labor force.

q.q: A minimum wage is raised above the equilibrium wage for low-skill labor. What is the expected market result?
options: A shortage of labor, meaning firms cannot find enough workers
No change because price floors never bind
An automatic increase in productivity
A surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire
q.feedback: A binding minimum wage is a price floor. It raises the wage above equilibrium and can create a surplus of labor.

labels: LO6.2

q.q: At $10 per hour, firms hire 1,000 workers and 1,000 workers want jobs. At a $15 minimum wage, firms want 800 workers and 1,200 workers want jobs. What is the labor surplus?
options: 400 workers
200 workers
800 workers
1,200 workers
q.feedback: The surplus is workers wanting jobs minus workers firms want to hire: 1,200 - 800 = 400.

labels: LO6.2

q.q: Why can a minimum wage help some workers while hurting others?
options: All workers are guaranteed jobs at the higher wage
Workers who keep jobs earn more, but some workers may be priced out of employment
Firms hire more workers because labor is now more expensive
The CPI stops measuring prices
q.feedback: A higher minimum wage can raise earnings for workers who remain employed, but reduce hiring for others.

q.q: A tax is imposed on sellers. Buyers pay a higher price, sellers receive a lower price, and fewer units are sold. What concept ties these effects together?
options: A price floor that creates a labor surplus
A tax wedge that shrinks the market
Substitution bias in the CPI
Discouraged-worker measurement
q.feedback: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, reducing the quantity sold.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A tax is legally imposed on buyers instead of sellers. What does tax-incidence analysis imply?
options: Buyers always bear 100% of the burden
Legal assignment alone does not determine the burden
Sellers always bear 100% of the burden
The tax disappears from the market
q.feedback: Tax incidence depends on market responses, not simply on whether the law says buyers or sellers pay the tax.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: Demand is less elastic than supply. Which side bears more of a per-unit tax?
options: Sellers bear more because buyers can easily leave
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because taxes do not affect prices
Buyers bear more because they respond less to the price change
q.feedback: The less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax burden because it has fewer good alternatives.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: An economist observes that gasoline prices rise after a supply disruption. A city responds with a binding price ceiling. What is the most likely result?
options: A surplus because suppliers produce more at the lower price
No effect because ceilings above equilibrium are always binding
A shortage because the legal price is held below the market-clearing price
Higher productivity because gasoline is cheaper
q.feedback: A binding price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A storm reduces supply while demand stays the same. Before any price control, what happens in the market?
options: Equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity rises
Both price and quantity rise
Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls
Both price and quantity fall
q.feedback: A decrease in supply shifts supply left, raising equilibrium price and lowering equilibrium quantity.

labels: LO4.4

q.q: A binding price ceiling holds the posted price below equilibrium. What happens to the underlying scarcity?
options: Scarcity disappears when prices are legally capped
All consumers get more of the good
Shortages cause waiting, side markets, favoritism, or lower quality
The CPI cannot measure any price change
q.feedback: A ceiling can hold down the legal money price, but scarcity still appears through shortages and nonprice rationing.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: An economist says a country spends more on education and infrastructure today to raise future productivity. What core economic idea is present?
options: A guarantee that inflation becomes zero
A binding price ceiling in labor markets
A discouraged-worker effect
Current resources versus future capacity
q.feedback: Policies that build future productivity often require giving up resources that could have been used elsewhere today.

q.q: A country has more machines per worker, but each additional machine adds less extra output than the one before. What explains this pattern?
options: Substitution bias
Frictional unemployment
A binding price ceiling
Diminishing returns to capital
q.feedback: Diminishing returns means each additional unit of capital adds less extra output once capital is already abundant.

q.q: A policy raises productivity over time but temporarily displaces workers in old industries. Which statement best describes the tradeoff?
options: Long-run growth can coexist with short-run structural unemployment
Productivity growth means no one ever loses a job
Structural unemployment only happens when CPI rises
Worker displacement proves the economy cannot grow
q.feedback: Productivity growth can raise long-run living standards while creating short-run adjustment costs for workers whose skills no longer match available jobs.

q.q: The Market Marshal shows a worker's wage rising from $28 to $30 while the CPI rises from 250 to 275. The worker says, 'I got a raise, so I am better off.' What is the best answer?
options: No; nominal wages rose about 7.1%, but prices rose 10%, so the real wage fell
Yes; nominal wages rose by $2, so purchasing power must have increased
No; real wages fell exactly 10% because the CPI rose 10%
Yes; any wage increase above zero raises real income
q.feedback: The wage rose about 7.1%, while prices rose 10%. Since prices rose faster than wages, the worker's real wage fell.

q.q: A CPI basket costs $100 in the base year and $140 this year. But consumers shifted toward cheaper substitutes, so their actual cost of maintaining a similar standard of living rose closer to $128. What is the best interpretation?
options: The CPI reports 28% inflation because consumers changed baskets
Fixed-basket CPI likely overstates true inflation
The CPI reports 12% inflation because $140 minus $128 equals $12
The CPI cannot be calculated because substitution occurred
q.feedback: The fixed CPI basket gives 40% inflation, but if consumers substitute toward cheaper goods, the CPI can overstate the true rise in living costs.

q.q: A union contract gives workers a CPI-based 6% raise. The CPI overstates inflation because of substitution bias and quality improvements. Which result is most likely?
options: Real wages must fall because CPI inflation is positive
Real wages must stay unchanged because the contract uses CPI
Indexed raises can lift real wages if CPI overstates inflation
Nominal wages fall because quality improvements reduce prices
q.feedback: If CPI overstates true inflation, a CPI-indexed raise can increase real wages more than intended.

q.q: A lender issues a loan at 11% nominal interest expecting 4% inflation. Actual inflation turns out to be 9%. Which statement is correct?
options: The actual real return is about 7%, so the lender receives exactly what was expected
The actual real return is about 20%, so both borrower and lender gain
The actual real return is about -5%, so the borrower pays more in real terms
The actual real return is about 2%, so the borrower gains relative to what the lender expected
q.feedback: Expected real return was about 7%, but actual real return was about 2%. Unexpected inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders.

q.q: A saver earns 8% nominal interest, inflation is 6%, and their wage rises 4%. Which statement best connects the two real effects?
options: The saver earns a positive real return on savings, but the real wage falls
The saver earns a negative real return, but the real wage rises
Both the real return and real wage rise
Both the real return and real wage fall
q.feedback: The real interest rate is about 2%, but the wage increase is below inflation, so the real wage falls.

q.q: The Market Marshal offers four economies. Which has the highest approximate real interest rate?
options: Nominal interest 11%, inflation 8%
Nominal interest 7%, inflation -1%
Nominal interest 5%, inflation 2%
Nominal interest 9%, inflation 7%
q.feedback: Approximate real interest equals nominal interest minus inflation. With 7% nominal interest and -1% inflation, the real rate is about 8%.

q.q: In Year 1, employed = 150 million, unemployed = 10 million, and not in labor force = 90 million. In Year 2, employed = 152 million, unemployed = 8 million, and not in labor force = 95 million. What is the best interpretation?
options: Employment rose, unemployment rose, and labor-force participation rose
Employment fell because not-in-labor-force increased
Employment rose, the unemployment rate fell, but labor-force participation fell
The unemployment rate stayed constant because the labor force stayed at 160 million
q.feedback: Employment rises from 150 to 152. The unemployment rate falls from 10/160 to 8/160. But participation falls because adult population rises while the labor force stays at 160.

q.q: The unemployment rate falls from 6% to 4.8%, but employment does not increase and labor-force participation falls sharply. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: The labor market definitely improved because the unemployment rate fell
Productivity must have increased because the unemployment rate fell.
Inflation must have fallen because labor-force participation fell
The labor market may be weaker than the unemployment rate suggests because people exited the labor force
q.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if people stop looking for work and leave the labor force.

q.q: A recession ends. Some discouraged workers begin searching again before finding jobs. What can happen to the unemployment rate and why?
options: It can rise temporarily because people reenter the labor force and are counted as unemployed while searching
It must fall because reentering workers are automatically employed
It must stay constant because discouraged workers were already unemployed
It can rise only if employment falls.
q.feedback: When discouraged workers resume searching, they reenter the labor force and may be counted as unemployed until they find jobs.

q.q: At a $12 equilibrium wage, firms hire 1,000 workers and 1,000 workers want jobs. A $16 minimum wage leads firms to demand 850 workers while 1,250 workers want jobs. Prices then rise 20%. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: The nominal wage floor creates a 250-worker shortage, and inflation raises the real wage further
The nominal wage floor creates a 400-worker surplus, but the real value of the $16 wage is partly eroded by inflation
The nominal wage floor creates no unemployment because 1,250 workers want jobs
The nominal wage floor creates a 150-worker surplus because employment falls from 1,000 to 850
q.feedback: The labor surplus is 1,250 - 850 = 400 workers. Inflation also reduces the purchasing power of the higher nominal wage.

labels: LO6.2

q.q: A binding minimum wage raises labor costs in restaurants. Restaurants hire fewer low-skill workers and raise menu prices. Which chain best synthesizes the effect?
options: Price ceiling in labor market → labor shortage → lower production costs → lower CPI
Tax wedge in output market → more labor demanded → lower unemployment
Price floor in labor market → lower labor demanded → higher production costs → higher output prices
Substitution bias → higher labor productivity → no job loss
q.feedback: A binding wage floor can reduce labor demanded and raise firms' costs, which can push output prices upward.

labels: LO6.2

q.q: The Market Marshal says: 'This policy improves pay for some workers, worsens access to jobs for others, and may raise consumer prices.' Which policy is most likely being described?
options: A nonbinding price ceiling above equilibrium
A decrease in CPI caused by quality improvements
A tax cut on sellers in a competitive market
A binding minimum wage above equilibrium
q.feedback: A binding minimum wage helps some workers who keep jobs, can reduce employment for others, and may raise business costs and consumer prices.

labels: LO1.1

q.q: During a supply shock, equilibrium rent would rise to $1,400, but a city caps rent at $1,000. Quantity demanded is 70,000 units and quantity supplied is 45,000 units. Tenants also spend more time searching. What is the best answer?
options: There is a 25,000-unit shortage, and the full economic cost includes nonmoney costs like search time
There is a 25,000-unit surplus, and the full economic cost falls to exactly $1,000
There is a 45,000-unit shortage, and search time is counted perfectly in CPI
There is no shortage because the legal rent is lower
q.feedback: The shortage is 70,000 - 45,000 = 25,000 units. Search time and rationing raise the full cost even if legal rent is capped.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A government caps gasoline prices below equilibrium during an oil shock. Official gasoline prices stop rising, but stations run out, drivers wait in long lines, and black-market resale appears. What is the deepest problem with saying inflation was solved?
options: Inflation is solved because CPI captures all waiting costs perfectly
A binding cap shifts scarcity into nonprice rationing
The market has a surplus because buyers want more gas
The price ceiling shifts supply right by lowering the posted price
q.feedback: A price ceiling can suppress the posted price while increasing nonmoney costs and creating shortages or black markets.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A binding price ceiling causes landlords to reduce maintenance. Rent is cheaper for lucky tenants, but housing quality falls. Which pair of concepts best explains these effects?
options: Tax incidence and real interest rates
Catch-up growth and discouraged workers
Price control incentives and CPI quality-measurement limits
GDP final-goods accounting and nominal wages
q.feedback: A lower legal price can come with worse quality, and quality changes are one reason cost-of-living measurement gets messy.

q.q: A $4 tax is placed on a good. After adjustment, buyers pay $2.75 more and sellers receive $1.25 less. Which conclusion is best?
options: Sellers bear more of the burden, so supply is likely less elastic than demand
Buyers and sellers split the burden equally because the tax is $4
The legal taxpayer must be the buyer because buyers pay $2.75 more
Buyers bear more of the burden, so demand is likely less elastic than supply
q.feedback: Buyers bear $2.75 of the $4 tax. The side bearing more burden is usually less elastic.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: A tax reduces quantity only slightly but raises the buyer price substantially. Which market condition best explains this?
options: Demand is relatively inelastic, so buyers keep purchasing despite the higher price
Demand is relatively elastic, so buyers leave the market completely
Supply is perfectly elastic, so sellers bear the full burden
The tax must be legally assigned to buyers
q.feedback: When demand is inelastic, buyers do not reduce quantity much, so they can bear much of the tax through higher prices.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: The Market Marshal compares two taxes. Tax A is on insulin with very inelastic demand. Tax B is on restaurant meals with more elastic demand. Which tax likely creates less quantity reduction but places more burden on buyers?
options: Tax B, because restaurant meals are easier to avoid
Tax A, because insulin demand is less elastic
Both taxes have identical effects because all taxes create wedges
Neither tax affects quantity if sellers legally pay it
q.feedback: A tax on a good with very inelastic demand causes less quantity reduction and places more burden on buyers.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Country A has nominal wages rise 12% while prices rise 12%. Country B has nominal wages rise 5%, prices rise 1%, and output per worker rises. Which country shows the stronger evidence of improved real living standards?
options: Country A, because nominal wages rose faster
Both are equal because both have wage growth
Country B, because real wages and productivity rose
Country A, because inflation confirms higher productivity
q.feedback: Country B has real wage growth and rising productivity. Country A's nominal wage gain is wiped out by inflation.

q.q: Automation raises output per worker and lowers production costs, but some workers in the old process lose jobs and need retraining. Which statement best describes the combined effect?
options: Automation must reduce living standards because some workers lose jobs
Automation eliminates unemployment because higher output creates jobs for every displaced worker.
Automation only affects CPI and not labor markets
Productivity can improve long-run living standards while causing short-run structural unemployment
q.feedback: Technology can raise productivity and living standards over time while displacing some workers whose skills no longer match the market.

q.q: A poor country attracts capital investment and adopts existing technology. Growth accelerates, but after decades the growth rate slows as capital becomes abundant. Which paired concepts best explain the pattern?
options: Catch-up growth followed by diminishing returns to capital
Substitution bias followed by cyclical unemployment
Price ceilings followed by tax incidence
Discouraged workers followed by CPI quality bias
q.feedback: Poorer countries can grow quickly through catch-up, but growth can slow as capital accumulation faces diminishing returns.

q.q: A supply shock raises food prices. The government caps prices below equilibrium. Official prices rise less, but shortages emerge, quality falls, and households spend more time searching. What is the best synthesis?
options: The ceiling eliminates inflation and improves allocation because prices are lower
The ceiling suppresses posted prices but worsens allocation and hides part of the full cost of scarcity
The ceiling creates a surplus because the lower price encourages producers to supply more.
The ceiling shifts demand left because consumers want more food
q.feedback: A ceiling can reduce the posted price while causing shortages, lower quality, waiting costs, and misallocation.

labels: LO6.1

q.q: A government raises the minimum wage during high inflation. Nominal wages rise for workers who keep jobs, firms reduce low-skill hiring, and consumer prices rise in labor-intensive sectors. Which answer best captures the whole chain?
options: The policy guarantees real wage growth and higher employment because legal wages increased
The policy has no price effect because only labor markets change
Some gain higher pay; others lose jobs; real gains depend on prices
The policy lowers unemployment because more workers want jobs at the higher wage
q.feedback: The real effect depends on employment, prices, and purchasing power. A higher legal wage is not the whole story.

labels: LO6.2

q.q: The Market Marshal presents a final scenario: unemployment falls, CPI inflation slows because price ceilings cap posted prices, real wages appear stable, and productivity is flat. Which warning is most important?
options: The economy is clearly stronger because unemployment and CPI inflation both fell
Stable real wages prove productivity increased because purchasing power did not fall.
Price ceilings improve welfare whenever they slow posted-price inflation.
The indicators may be distorted by labor-force exits, hidden price-control costs, and lack of productivity growth
q.feedback: Headline indicators can mislead. Falling unemployment may reflect labor-force exits, capped prices may hide shortages, and flat productivity weakens long-run living standards.

q.q: A scenario mentions scarcity and opportunity cost. What makes analysis integrated?
options: It uses scarcity to identify the forgone next-best alternative
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: Scarcity forces a choice, and opportunity cost identifies the value of the next-best alternative given up. Connecting those two ideas turns vocabulary recognition into economic reasoning.

q.q: A policy changes incentives and marginal benefits. What reasoning is required?
options: Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Compare the changed marginal benefit and cost created by incentives
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: The policy changes incentives, which changes expected marginal benefits or costs. The behavioral prediction comes from comparing those changed marginal benefits and marginal costs.

q.q: A PPF move is described. What connection should be made?
options: Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
The slope or tradeoff reveals opportunity cost
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: Movement along a PPF shows a production tradeoff. The slope or quantities given up reveal the opportunity cost of producing more of the other good.

q.q: A market failure is identified. What policy step remains?
options: Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Compare feasible remedies and their tradeoffs
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: Identifying a market failure does not automatically identify the best remedy. Policy analysis must compare feasible interventions, their benefits, costs, and possible unintended consequences.

q.q: A policy claim mixes prediction and advice. What should be separated?
options: The positive effect claim and normative recommendation
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: The prediction about what the policy will do is a positive claim that can be tested. The recommendation about what should be done is normative and depends on values as well as evidence.

q.q: Two producers specialize. What completes the reasoning?
options: Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Compare opportunity costs and feasible terms of trade
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: Specialization should follow comparative advantage, which requires comparing opportunity costs. For both sides to gain from exchange, the terms of trade must fall between their opportunity costs.

q.q: A policy proposal claims it will “improve fairness” and also predicts that employment will rise. What should an analyst do first?
options: Separate the fairness judgment from the testable employment prediction.
Treat both statements as positive because they concern policy.
Reject both statements because models cannot study policy.
Combine both statements into one numerical forecast.
q.commonError: Mixing a value judgment with a testable economic prediction.
q.feedback: Fairness is a normative criterion, while the employment effect is a positive claim that can be tested with evidence.

labels: INTEGRATED

q.q: A worker receives a 4 percent nominal wage increase while consumer prices rise 6 percent. What calculation is needed before judging the change in living standards?
options: Add wage and price growth to obtain a 10 percent real gain.
Adjust the wage for inflation; the real wage fell about 2 percent.
Use the unemployment rate as the wage deflator.
Compare the nominal wage only with nominal GDP.
q.commonError: Evaluating purchasing power from nominal wages without adjusting for inflation.
q.feedback: Approximate real wage growth equals nominal wage growth minus inflation: 4 - 6 = -2 percent.

labels: INTEGRATED

q.q: Limited resources force a city to choose projects. Which ideas connect?
options: The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
No causal or tradeoff connection is required
Scarcity creates an opportunity cost equal to the best forgone project
Opportunity cost is unrelated to scarcity once the city has chosen a project.
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: Scarcity means the city cannot fund every project. Choosing one project therefore creates an opportunity cost equal to the value of the best forgone alternative.

q.q: A bonus changes effort until added benefit no longer exceeds added cost. Which ideas connect?
options: No causal or tradeoff connection is required
Incentives determine behavior without any need to compare marginal benefits and costs.
The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
Incentives alter behavior evaluated at the margin
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: The bonus changes the incentive to exert effort, while marginal analysis explains why effort expands only while the added benefit exceeds the added cost.

q.q: A PPF shows a lower opportunity cost for one producer. What follows?
options: Comparative advantage can guide specialization and trade
The lower-opportunity-cost producer should avoid specialization because both producers can trade.
The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
No causal or tradeoff connection is required
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: Lower opportunity cost identifies comparative advantage. Specializing according to comparative advantage can raise combined output and create gains from trade.

q.q: A pollution rule is predicted to cut emissions but raise bills and is recommended as fair. What must be combined?
options: Once the rule reduces emissions, no further economic analysis is needed.
Market-failure logic, positive evidence, and normative policy judgment
The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
No causal or tradeoff connection is required
q.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
q.feedback: Market-failure analysis explains why intervention may be considered, positive analysis evaluates predicted effects such as emissions and bills, and the claim that the policy is fair is normative.

q.q: In the small-country trade model, what is the world price?
options: The price available in the world market that the country takes as given
The price selected by the domestic government
The domestic autarky price after trade opens
The tariff-inclusive domestic price
q.feedback: A small country takes the world price as given.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: A country becomes an importer of a good when:
options: The world price is above its no-trade domestic equilibrium price
The world price is below its no-trade domestic equilibrium price
Domestic supply is greater than domestic demand at the world price
The government sets a quota equal to zero
q.feedback: A lower world price creates excess domestic demand that is filled by imports.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: A country becomes an exporter of a good when:
options: The world price is below its no-trade domestic equilibrium price
Domestic demand is greater than domestic supply at the world price
The world price is above its no-trade domestic equilibrium price
Domestic consumers refuse to buy the good
q.feedback: A higher world price creates excess domestic supply that is sold abroad.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Imports are calculated as:
options: Domestic quantity supplied minus domestic quantity demanded
Domestic quantity demanded plus domestic quantity supplied
World quantity demanded minus domestic quantity demanded
Domestic quantity demanded minus domestic quantity supplied
q.feedback: Imports fill the gap between domestic consumption and domestic production.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: Exports are calculated as:
options: Domestic quantity supplied minus domestic quantity demanded
Domestic quantity demanded minus domestic quantity supplied
Domestic quantity supplied plus domestic quantity demanded
World supply minus domestic supply
q.feedback: Exports are the domestic production not purchased by domestic consumers.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: When an importing country opens to trade and the domestic price falls, domestic quantity demanded generally:
options: Decreases
Increases
Stays fixed by definition
Becomes equal to domestic quantity supplied
q.feedback: A lower price causes a movement down the domestic demand curve.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: When an importing country opens to trade and the domestic price falls, domestic quantity supplied generally:
options: Increases
Stays fixed by definition
Decreases
Becomes equal to domestic quantity demanded
q.feedback: A lower price causes a movement down the domestic supply curve.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: When an exporting country opens to trade and the domestic price rises, domestic quantity demanded generally:
options: Increases
Becomes zero in every case
Must equal domestic quantity supplied
Decreases
q.feedback: A higher price reduces domestic quantity demanded.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: When an exporting country opens to trade and the domestic price rises, domestic quantity supplied generally:
options: Increases
Decreases
Becomes zero in every case
Must equal domestic quantity demanded
q.feedback: A higher price raises domestic quantity supplied.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: Opening an importing market to a lower world price normally causes domestic consumer surplus to:
options: Decrease
Increase
Remain unchanged
Become equal to producer surplus
q.feedback: Consumers pay less and purchase more.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: Opening an importing market to a lower world price normally causes domestic producer surplus to:
options: Increase
Remain unchanged
Decrease
Become tariff revenue
q.feedback: Domestic producers receive a lower price and sell less.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: Opening an exporting market to a higher world price normally causes domestic consumer surplus to:
options: Increase
Remain unchanged
Become quota rent
Decrease
q.feedback: Domestic consumers pay the higher world price and buy less.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: Opening an exporting market to a higher world price normally causes domestic producer surplus to:
options: Increase
Decrease
Remain unchanged
Become government revenue
q.feedback: Domestic producers receive a higher price and sell more.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: What does “gains from trade” mean in the standard surplus model?
options: Every domestic consumer and producer gains
Total surplus is higher with trade than without trade
Imports become larger than domestic production
The government receives tariff revenue
q.feedback: Gains from trade are measured by the increase in total surplus.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: Which statement is correct when total surplus rises after trade opens?
options: Every domestic person must be better off
Domestic producers must always gain
Some domestic groups may still lose even though the aggregate gain is positive
Domestic consumers must always lose
q.feedback: Aggregate gains do not imply universal gains.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: A tariff is:
options: A legal maximum on exports
A payment to domestic consumers
A tax on all domestic production
A tax on imported goods
q.feedback: A tariff taxes imported units.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: In the basic small-country import model, a tariff normally causes the domestic price to:
options: Rise above the world price
Fall below the world price
Remain at the world price
Become equal to the no-trade quantity
q.feedback: The tariff creates a wedge between the world price and domestic price.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: A tariff that raises the domestic price generally causes imports to:
options: Increase
Decrease
Remain unchanged
Equal domestic quantity demanded
q.feedback: Domestic production rises and domestic consumption falls, shrinking imports.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: Tariff revenue equals:
options: Domestic price multiplied by domestic production
Consumer surplus minus producer surplus
Tariff per imported unit multiplied by the number of imported units
The two tariff deadweight-loss triangles
q.feedback: Government revenue is the tariff rate times post-tariff imports.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: Why is tariff revenue not deadweight loss?
options: Tariff revenue is retained by domestic firms, so it remains part of producer surplus rather than a social loss
Deadweight loss is the portion of consumer surplus transferred to producers and the government after the tariff
Tariff revenue offsets the production distortion, leaving the consumption distortion as the remaining deadweight loss
Revenue is a transfer to the government, while deadweight loss is surplus that disappears
q.feedback: A transfer changes who receives surplus; deadweight loss is a net loss.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: An import quota is:
options: A legal limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
A tax collected on every domestic sale
A subsidy for foreign producers
A minimum price set below the world price
q.feedback: A quota directly limits import quantity.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: A binding import quota normally causes the domestic price to:
options: Fall below the world price
Rise above the world price
Remain permanently at the world price
Equal zero
q.feedback: Restricted imports create scarcity in the domestic market.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: Quota rents are:
options: The government’s tariff revenue in every quota system
The entire loss of consumer surplus
The price gap created by the quota multiplied by the permitted import quantity
Domestic producers’ total revenue
q.feedback: Quota rents accrue to whoever holds the valuable import rights.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: When does the government receive quota rents?
options: Whenever any quota is binding
Only when imports fall to zero
Whenever foreign exporters own the licenses
When it auctions the import licenses and keeps the proceeds
q.feedback: Rent distribution depends on who owns or sells the import rights.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: At an importing country's request, a foreign government caps shipments and gives its exporters the rights free. Which restriction is this?
options: A voluntary export restraint (VER)
An import tariff collected by the importing treasury
An import-license auction held by the importing treasury
A subsidy paid on domestic production
q.feedback: A VER limits exports from the supplying country. With free rights assigned to foreign exporters, those exporters can capture the scarcity rents.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: Why is “a tariff protects jobs” incomplete economic analysis?
options: The statement is sufficient because preserving employment in the protected sector captures the main national welfare effect
It ignores higher consumer costs, resource shifts, and jobs affected in other industries
Employment effects can be evaluated from the protected industry because tariff costs are unlikely to spill into other sectors
The key missing issue is the effect on foreign workers; domestic consumer and input costs are secondary to that effect
q.feedback: A complete analysis traces costs and effects beyond the protected industry.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: Which is the strongest way to evaluate a national-security argument for protection?
options: Assume every industry is essential
Reject the argument because trade is always harmless
Compare the security benefit with the policy cost and less costly alternatives
Count only the protected firms’ profits
q.feedback: Security can be legitimate, but the claim still requires evidence and comparison.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: New domestic pump makers request temporary protection while they learn to match established foreign firms' costs. Which argument are they using?
options: National-security argument
Jobs argument based only on existing employment
Retaliation against a partner's trade barrier
Infant-industry argument
q.feedback: The infant-industry argument claims temporary learning can make a new industry competitive. The label alone does not establish that future benefits exceed current costs.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: Why can retaliation make a tariff more costly?
options: Trading partners may restrict the country’s exports, harming additional producers and workers
Trading partners may tax imports from the country, but the proceeds go into the original country’s treasury.
Trading partners may tax imports from the country, making its goods cheaper for foreign customers to buy.
Trading partners may restrict imports from the country, increasing sales opportunities for the country’s exporters.
q.feedback: Retaliation can restrict sales of the country’s exports in foreign markets. Export producers and their workers can therefore lose business in addition to the costs created by the original tariff.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: Which statement separates efficiency from equity in trade analysis?
options: An efficient outcome must divide gains equally
Trade can raise total surplus while distributing gains and losses unevenly
Equity is measured only by import quantity
If consumers gain, fairness is settled
q.feedback: Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: Using the displayed trade graph, is the domestic economy an importer or exporter when the world price is $5?
options: Importer
Exporter
Neither; trade does not occur
The graph does not determine the trade direction
q.feedback: The $5 world price lies below the $7 autarky price, so domestic demand exceeds domestic supply and the country imports.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At a world price of $5, how many thousand avocados do domestic producers supply?
options: 175 thousand
125 thousand
225 thousand
100 thousand
q.feedback: The world-price line intersects domestic supply at Q = 125 thousand.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At a world price of $5, how many thousand avocados do domestic consumers demand?
options: 125 thousand
175 thousand
225 thousand
350 thousand
q.feedback: The world-price line intersects domestic demand at Q = 225 thousand.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: At the $10 world price, does this market export or import?
options: Exporter
Importer
Neither; trade does not occur
The graph does not determine the trade direction
q.feedback: The $10 world price lies above the $7 autarky price, so domestic production exceeds domestic consumption and the country exports.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At Pw = $10, how many thousand avocados do domestic consumers demand?
options: 175 thousand avocados
100 thousand avocados
250 thousand avocados
150 thousand avocados
q.feedback: The world-price line intersects demand at Q = 100 thousand.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At Pw = $10, how many thousand avocados do domestic producers supply?
options: 100 thousand avocados
175 thousand avocados
250 thousand avocados
150 thousand avocados
q.feedback: The world-price line intersects supply at Q = 250 thousand.

labels: Determine domestic production, domestic consumption, and trade quantities.

q.q: In the displayed trade graph, what domestic price results from the $4 world price plus the tariff?
q.feedback: The graph marks the tariff-inclusive domestic price at $6.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: What is the per-unit tariff shown in the displayed trade graph?
q.feedback: The domestic price rises from the $4 world price to $6, so the tariff is $2 per unit.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: In the displayed trade graph, what domestic price results under the import quota?
q.feedback: The graph marks the domestic price under the quota at $6.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: What world price is shown in the displayed trade graph?
q.feedback: The green world-price line is drawn at $3.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: When an importing country opens to a lower world price, domestic buyers generally:
options: Lose because imports reduce choice
Are unaffected because only producers trade
Pay the old domestic price by definition
Gain because they pay a lower price
q.feedback: The lower domestic price raises consumer surplus for buyers.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: When an importing country opens to trade at a lower price, domestic producers generally:
options: Are unaffected by the lower domestic price
Receive tariff revenue automatically
Lose some producer surplus
Gain producer surplus because imports raise price
q.feedback: Domestic sellers receive a lower price and sell less, reducing producer surplus.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: When an exporting country opens to a higher world price, domestic producers generally:
options: Pay the world price to consumers
Gain producer surplus
Lose producer surplus
Are unaffected because exports go abroad
q.feedback: The higher domestic price and larger domestic production raise producer surplus.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: The standard small-country model predicts that opening to free trade:
options: Raises total surplus even though some domestic groups can lose
Makes every domestic person better off
Always lowers consumer surplus
Always lowers producer surplus
q.feedback: Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: In a small importing country, a tariff usually causes domestic production of the protected good to:
options: Decrease
Remain fixed by definition
Fall to zero
Increase
q.feedback: The tariff raises the domestic price, encouraging domestic producers to supply more.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: In a small importing country, a tariff usually causes domestic consumption of the protected good to:
options: Remain fixed by definition
Become equal to exports
Decrease
Increase
q.feedback: The higher domestic price reduces quantity demanded.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: Government tariff revenue is generated by:
options: The tariff multiplied by domestic consumption whether imported or not
The tariff per imported unit multiplied by the quantity imported
The world price multiplied by domestic production
Consumer surplus multiplied by producer surplus
q.feedback: Tariff revenue equals the tax rate per imported unit times the number of units still imported.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: A binding import quota directly limits:
options: Domestic supply at every price
The quantity that may be imported
The world price in every country
Domestic demand at every price
q.feedback: A quota is a quantitative restriction on imports.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: When a binding quota raises the domestic price above the world price, domestic producers generally:
options: Gain producer surplus
Lose producer surplus
Receive no price effect
Become foreign producers
q.feedback: The higher domestic price benefits domestic sellers.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: Quota rent is the value created by:
options: The gap between domestic demand and domestic supply at autarky only
Total consumer surplus before trade
Government tax revenue collected on all domestic production
The gap between the domestic price and world price on the units allowed to be imported
q.feedback: Import licenses can carry value because permitted imports can be bought at the world price and sold at the higher domestic price.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: In Arden's market for solar panels, the no-trade equilibrium price is $50 and the world price is $30. What trade position follows?
options: Arden exports the good
No trade occurs because the prices differ
Arden imports the good
The country must impose a tariff before trade occurs
q.feedback: Because $30 is below the domestic equilibrium price $50, the country imports.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Bellora’s no-trade coffee price is $60; the world price is $76. Which trade position follows?
options: Bellora imports because world price exceeds its no-trade price.
Bellora has no net trade because world and no-trade prices differ.
Bellora exports because world price exceeds its no-trade price.
Bellora imports because domestic demand exceeds supply at $76.
q.feedback: The world price exceeds the $60 autarky price. At $76, domestic output rises and domestic consumption falls relative to autarky; surplus production is exported.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Caspia’s no-trade bicycle price and world price are both $42. With ordinary upward-sloping supply and downward-sloping demand, what initial net trade is implied?
options: Net exports, because producers can now sell abroad.
Net imports, because buyers can now purchase abroad.
Net exports equal to all domestic production.
No net trade, because domestic supply and demand remain equal.
q.feedback: At the unchanged equilibrium price of $42, domestic quantity supplied equals domestic quantity demanded. Opening trade creates no initial net export or import gap in this model.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Demer becomes a net importer of tablets. Relative to its no-trade equilibrium price, where must the world price lie?
options: Below the no-trade price.
Above the no-trade price.
Exactly at the no-trade price.
Its position cannot be inferred from net imports.
q.feedback: Net imports mean domestic demand exceeds domestic supply at the world price. With ordinary demand and supply, that gap occurs below the autarky equilibrium price.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Estara’s no-trade wool-blanket price is $53, and the world price is $30. Relative to autarky, what happens to domestic production and consumption?
options: Production rises; consumption falls.
Production falls; consumption rises.
Both production and consumption rise.
Both production and consumption fall.
q.feedback: Opening to the lower world price moves domestic producers down supply and consumers down demand: domestic production falls, consumption rises, and imports fill the gap.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. At the world price, Faron’s firms produce 90 batches of tiles and its residents consume 60. What is the trade position?
options: Imports of 30 batches.
Exports of 60 batches.
Imports of 150 batches.
Exports of 30 batches.
q.feedback: Domestic production exceeds domestic consumption by 90 - 60 = 30 batches. Those excess batches are exported.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Galena exports medical gloves at a world price of $58. What does this imply about its no-trade equilibrium price?
options: It must have been above $58.
It must have equaled $58.
It must have been below $58.
It could have been either above or below $58.
q.feedback: Exports occur when the world price is above autarky: domestic supply exceeds domestic demand. Therefore the no-trade price was below $58.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Haven’s no-trade garden-tool price is $60 and Ilyria’s is $35. Both face a world price of $44. Which prediction follows?
options: Haven imports and Ilyria exports.
Both countries import.
Haven exports and Ilyria imports.
Both countries export.
q.feedback: Compare each domestic no-trade price with the same world price: $44 < $60 makes Haven an importer; $44 > $35 makes Ilyria an exporter. Comparing the two countries’ prices only to one another is insufficient.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. At the world price, Ilyria’s residents consume 70 paper rolls while domestic firms supply 45. Which statement reconciles those quantities?
options: Imports provide the remaining 25 rolls.
Exports absorb the remaining 25 rolls.
Imports provide all 70 rolls.
Exports equal all 45 domestically supplied rolls.
q.feedback: Imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production: 70 - 45 = 25 rolls. Domestic production still supplies part of consumption.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Juno’s no-trade olive-oil price is $62. The world price first is $38, then rises to $70. Which change in trade position follows?
options: Exporter at both world prices.
Importer at $38, exporter at $70.
Exporter at $38, importer at $70.
Importer at both world prices.
q.feedback: At $38 below autarky, domestic demand exceeds supply and Juno imports. At $70 above autarky, domestic supply exceeds demand and Juno exports. The position must be reassessed when the world price crosses $62.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: At the world price of $30, Arden's consumers demand 50 units of solar panels and domestic firms supply 10. How many units are imported?

q.q: A tariff and a quota initially reduce imports to the same amount. Demand then rises. Which policy automatically permits more imports?

Both always preserve the same price and imports
q.feedback: A fixed quota holds imports constant; a tariff allows quantity to adjust.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.feedback: The argument requires a temporary, evidence-based learning mechanism and net benefits.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: Workers in an import-competing industry lose jobs while consumers gain from lower prices. Which conclusion is strongest?

q.feedback: Aggregate gains and adjustment costs can coexist.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: After an importing market opens, domestic consumers gain $90 of surplus while domestic producers lose $55. Which statement describes the national welfare effect in the standard model?

Total surplus rises by $35 even though producers lose

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

options: There is no national gain because both groups must benefit
Consumers gain $24 because the world price is higher
The country has a $24 net gain while consumers lose
The country has a $116 net loss because consumers lose
q.feedback: Producer gains exceed consumer losses by $24, illustrating how trade can raise total surplus without making every group better off.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: Why can free trade raise total surplus even when domestic producers in an importing industry lose?

Consumer gains can exceed producer losses
Producer losses are not counted in welfare analysis
Imports automatically create government revenue
q.feedback: The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: Why can free trade raise total surplus even when domestic consumers in an exporting industry lose?

q.feedback: Higher export prices redistribute surplus toward producers while creating a positive net gain in the standard model.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: After trade opens, one group gains $120 and another loses $85. Which statement is best?

There is no net gain because someone loses
The losing group’s loss should not be counted
There is a $35 net gain, but the distributional conflict is real
q.feedback: Net welfare is the gain minus the loss, while distribution identifies who bears the loss.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

q.q: A policy analyst says “trade is beneficial, so nobody can be harmed by opening the market.” What is wrong with the statement?

Consumer and producer surplus never change with trade

Trade can never raise total surplus
q.feedback: The standard result is aggregate: winners can gain more than losers lose.

labels: Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

Foreign competition always raises domestic producer surplus
q.feedback: A complete welfare analysis includes costs to consumers, resource reallocation, and economy-wide effects.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: A new domestic battery industry asks for five years of protection while firms learn a production process. Which finding would give the request the strongest economic case?

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
