A repair shop owns a patented machine that lowers the cost of each service call
A shop sells an identical commodity
q.feedback: The guarantee changes the service experience.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: What does branding differentiation primarily create?
options: A perfectly horizontal demand curve
A legal prohibition on all entry
A perceived identity that may make buyers view close substitutes differently
A legal franchise that prevents rival brands from entering the relevant market
q.feedback: Branding can shape perceived differences and loyalty.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: Products in monopolistic competition are best described as:
options: Perfect complements
Identical commodities
Products that buyers regard as identical commodities from interchangeable sellers
Close but imperfect substitutes
q.feedback: Consumers can switch, but they may not view every variety as identical.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: Why does an individual firm face downward-sloping demand?
options: Some buyers prefer its particular variety
The firm takes price as given
Every buyer views all rival products as identical and refuses to switch among sellers
The government assigns each customer
q.feedback: Differentiation allows price to affect quantity demanded for the firm’s variety.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: For a monopolistically competitive firm, average revenue equals:
options: Marginal cost
Price
Average total cost
Economic profit
q.feedback: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: Why is marginal revenue below price for the firm?
options: Marginal cost is rising
Average total cost falls as fixed cost is spread across a larger number of units
Selling another unit generally requires a lower price on units sold
Entry is legally blocked
q.feedback: The price effect makes added revenue smaller than the new unit’s price.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: A firm’s close substitutes become more numerous. Its demand will generally become:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Vertical
Less responsive to price
More elastic
q.feedback: More alternatives make switching easier.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: What output rule does a monopolistically competitive firm use in the short run?
options: Produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost on rising MC
Produce where demand intersects average total cost at the lowest attainable unit cost
Produce at minimum average fixed cost
Produce where price is highest
q.feedback: The firm applies the same marginal rule as other profit-maximizing firms.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: After choosing output where MR equals MC, where does the firm find its price?
options: On the marginal-revenue curve at the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
On its demand curve at that output
At minimum AVC
On the market supply curve
q.feedback: Demand gives the price buyers will pay for the chosen quantity.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: A firm earns positive economic profit when, at its chosen output:
options: Price exceeds marginal revenue
Marginal cost exceeds price
Price exceeds average total cost
Average variable cost exceeds price
q.feedback: Profit per unit is price minus ATC.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: A firm incurs an economic loss when, at its chosen output:
options: Marginal revenue lies below demand even though price still covers average total cost
Price is above marginal cost
Demand slopes downward
Price is below average total cost
q.feedback: A price below ATC means revenue does not cover total economic cost.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: In the short run, a loss-making firm should continue producing when:
options: Price covers average variable cost
Price falls below minimum average variable cost but remains above average total cost
Price equals zero
Fixed cost is positive
q.feedback: Production can cover variable cost and part of fixed cost.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: What usually happens when firms earn short-run economic profit?
options: Existing firms gain customers because a larger number of sellers expands demand for every variety
Entry creates more close substitutes
Market demand disappears
All products become identical
q.feedback: Profit attracts entry when entry is relatively easy.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: How does entry usually affect an existing firm’s demand?
options: It becomes vertical
It shifts right
It shifts left
It becomes the market supply curve
q.feedback: New varieties take some customers from existing firms.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: How does entry usually affect an existing firm’s demand elasticity?
options: Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
Demand becomes less elastic
Elasticity becomes unrelated to substitutes
Demand becomes more elastic
q.feedback: More substitutes make buyers more responsive.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: What usually happens when firms experience persistent economic losses?
options: Some firms exit
More firms enter
Existing firms’ demand shifts left indefinitely
Products become identical by law
q.feedback: Exit removes varieties and relieves losses for survivors.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: How does exit usually affect a surviving firm’s demand?
options: It shifts left
It shifts right
It becomes horizontal at zero
It disappears
q.feedback: Fewer substitutes leave more demand for surviving varieties.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: In long-run monopolistic-competition equilibrium, firms earn:
options: Guaranteed monopoly profit
Zero accounting profit
Zero economic profit
A loss equal to fixed cost
q.feedback: Entry and exit eliminate economic profit while normal profit remains.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: What geometric relationship characterizes long-run equilibrium?
options: MR is tangent to demand
Demand crosses ATC at minimum ATC
Marginal cost becomes horizontal and coincides with demand at minimum average total cost
The firm’s demand curve is tangent to ATC at its chosen output
q.feedback: Tangency makes price equal ATC at the chosen output.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: In long-run equilibrium, price is typically:
options: Greater than marginal cost
Equal to marginal cost
Below average variable cost
Equal to zero
q.feedback: Differentiation leaves a markup even when economic profit is zero.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: What is excess capacity in this model?
options: Any unused chair in a store
The gap between equilibrium output and the output minimizing ATC
The vertical distance between the firm’s price and marginal revenue at equilibrium
The firm’s fixed cost
q.feedback: The firm produces below the output that minimizes average total cost.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Which condition shows productive inefficiency?
options: Price equals ATC
MR equals MC
Output is below the quantity at minimum ATC
Economic profit is zero because price equals average total cost at the chosen output
q.feedback: Productive efficiency requires production at minimum ATC.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Which condition shows allocative inefficiency?
options: Price equals ATC
Demand is tangent to average total cost at the firm’s long-run equilibrium output
Entry is possible
Price exceeds marginal cost
q.feedback: Allocative efficiency requires price equal MC.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Which is an example of informational advertising?
options: An ad lists a clinic’s hours, prices, and services
An ad uses only an emotional celebrity image
A group of rival firms secretly coordinates prices and promotional messages
A government bans competing brands
q.feedback: The ad provides facts that reduce search costs.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: Which statement best captures the welfare tradeoff?
options: Variety has no value
Differentiation can add valued variety while markup and excess capacity create inefficiency
Zero profit guarantees full efficiency
Advertising and differentiation always destroy more value than product variety can create
q.feedback: The model involves both variety benefits and efficiency costs.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: An advertisement lists a store’s prices, hours, and warranty terms. What type of advertising is this primarily?
options: Predatory pricing
Price discrimination
Informational advertising
Persuasive advertising
q.feedback: The message mainly reduces consumers’ information costs by providing facts.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A perfume ad links the brand with status and excitement but provides almost no factual product information. What type of advertising is this primarily?
options: Perfectly competitive promotion
Persuasive advertising
Informational advertising
Marginal-cost pricing
q.feedback: The ad is trying to shape preferences and brand perception rather than mainly transmit facts.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A café upgrades ingredients and service rather than cutting price. Which strategy is it using?
options: Nonprice competition through quality
A price ceiling
Perfect price discrimination
Market exit
q.feedback: Monopolistically competitive firms often compete through quality and service as well as price.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A shoe company introduces custom colors and faster delivery while leaving its posted price unchanged. This is an example of:
options: Collusive pricing
A shutdown decision
Perfect competition
Nonprice competition
q.feedback: The firm is competing through product features and service rather than changing price.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A firm buys a one-time advertising campaign that does not change demand. If the expense is fixed, which cost curve does it directly raise?
options: Average variable cost
Marginal revenue
Average total cost
Marginal cost
q.feedback: A fixed selling cost raises fixed and average total cost but does not directly raise MC or AVC.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A platform charges a promotional fee on every unit a seller sells. The fee acts most like an increase in:
options: Market demand
Variable cost
Fixed cost
Consumer income
q.feedback: A per-unit selling expense rises with output, so it behaves like a variable cost.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A successful brand campaign causes more buyers to want the firm’s product at every price. What happens to the firm’s demand curve?
options: It shifts to the right
There is a movement down the same demand curve
It becomes the market supply curve
It shifts left because advertising raises cost
q.feedback: A change in buyers’ willingness to purchase at each price is a demand shift, not a movement along demand.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A loyalty campaign makes customers less willing to switch to rival brands after a price increase. The firm’s demand has become:
options: More elastic
Perfectly elastic
Perfectly inelastic in every case
Less elastic
q.feedback: Greater brand loyalty reduces responsiveness to the firm’s price, making demand less elastic.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A firm develops a distinctive new feature that rivals have not yet copied. What is the most immediate competitive effect?
options: Perfectly elastic firm demand
Automatic long-run zero profit immediately
Temporary product differentiation
Guaranteed permanent monopoly
q.feedback: A distinctive feature can temporarily strengthen differentiation until rivals respond or imitate it.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: Why can consumers value monopolistic competition even though firms may not produce at minimum ATC?
options: It guarantees the lowest possible price for every product
It eliminates all selling costs
It makes every firm a price taker
It offers product variety that can match different preferences
q.feedback: Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: In the standard long-run model, which condition signals allocative inefficiency for a monopolistically competitive firm?
options: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost
Economic profit equals zero
Price exceeds marginal cost
Price equals average total cost
q.feedback: Allocative efficiency requires P=MC. A positive markup means some mutually beneficial trades may not occur.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: A market has only three differentiated firms, and each changes strategy when a rival cuts price. Why may monopolistic competition be a poor model?
options: Price changes are impossible under monopolistic competition
Strategic interdependence points toward oligopoly
Differentiated products require perfect competition
Few firms automatically create a natural monopoly
q.feedback: The monopolistic-competition model assumes many firms whose individual strategic reactions are usually not central.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: Why is a larger number of brands not automatically socially better?
options: Additional variety can create benefits but also use resources and duplicate fixed costs
Every new brand necessarily lowers marginal cost
More brands guarantee P=MC for all firms
Product variety eliminates excess capacity
q.feedback: The welfare question compares the value of added variety with the resources used to create and sustain it.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: A market has 150 independently owned salons, each with a distinct location and reputation, and new salons can open without major legal barriers. Which model fits best?
options: Perfect competition with identical services and a horizontal demand curve for each salon
Pure monopoly
Monopolistic competition
Oligopoly
q.feedback: Many firms, differentiation, and entry fit monopolistic competition.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: A clothing store raises price and loses some, but not all, customers to nearby brands. What does this imply?

It is a price-taking commodity seller facing a horizontal demand curve at the market price
It has no substitutes
Its firm demand is downward sloping and relatively elastic
q.feedback: Differentiation gives market power, while close substitutes keep demand responsive.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: A new cluster of coffee shops opens near an established café. Which immediate effect is most likely for the café?

Its demand shifts right and becomes less elastic
Its MC curve shifts down automatically
Its ATC becomes zero
q.feedback: Entry creates more close substitutes.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: Several boutique gyms close after sustained losses. Which effect is most likely for a surviving gym?
options: Its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic because fewer alternatives remain available
Its demand shifts right and may become less elastic
Its MR becomes horizontal at zero
Its fixed cost disappears
q.feedback: Exit removes substitutes and can strengthen surviving demand.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

The firm earns zero economic profit but has an $11 markup
The firm must exit

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

options: It remains unchanged

It falls because fixed cost raises MC
It becomes the minimum-ATC output
q.feedback: A pure fixed cost changes ATC and profit, not MR or MC.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

MC, AVC, and ATC

Demand and MR only
q.feedback: A per-unit selling cost is a variable cost.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A brand campaign makes customers less willing to switch to rivals. What is the most direct demand effect?

Demand shifts only because the campaign lowers marginal cost and average variable cost
The firm’s demand becomes less elastic
MR equals price at every quantity
q.feedback: Greater loyalty reduces responsiveness to price.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A comparison website makes prices and features easier to compare across brands. What is the likely effect?
options: Firm demand becomes vertical
Every seller becomes a monopoly because buyers can now compare all products directly
Entry becomes impossible
Firm demand becomes more elastic
q.feedback: Lower search costs make switching easier.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

Many sellers make the restaurant demand curve perfectly elastic
The restaurant controls the entire market supply

options: It becomes less elastic because the market has more sellers
It becomes vertical because each shop is now smaller
It becomes perfectly inelastic because products remain differentiated
It becomes more elastic because customers have more close substitutes
q.feedback: More close substitutes make customers more responsive to one firm’s price.

q.q: A city has dozens of independently owned fitness studios. Each offers a somewhat different mix of classes, and new studios can enter without major legal barriers. Which model is the best starting point?

Oligopoly
Monopolistic competition
Perfect competition

Service differentiation
Resource ownership
Patent protection

A perfectly competitive price
A horizontal firm demand curve

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose the firm’s demand shifts outward while costs are unchanged. What is the immediate short-run effect?
options: The firm must earn zero profit immediately

Existing-firm demand shifts left immediately because entry occurs before the outward demand change

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which equality at Q1 establishes that the firm earns zero economic profit?
options: Price equals average total cost
Price equals marginal cost
Marginal revenue equals average total cost
Average total cost equals minimum average variable cost

q.q: Refer to the graph. After short-run profit induces entry, what happens to the demand curve facing an existing firm?
options: It shifts left until it is tangent to ATC
It shifts right until price equals marginal cost
It becomes horizontal at minimum ATC
It remains fixed while marginal cost shifts left
q.feedback: Entry provides more substitutes and shifts each existing firm’s demand left until tangency restores zero economic profit.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison at Q1 demonstrates allocative inefficiency?
options: Price exceeds marginal cost
Price equals marginal cost
Price is below average variable cost
Marginal revenue exceeds price

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Once entry restores long-run equilibrium, which combination can still persist?
options: Zero economic profit with a positive markup
Positive economic profit with price equal to marginal cost
A shutdown loss with minimum average total cost
Zero economic profit with no excess capacity
q.feedback: Tangency gives zero economic profit, while the downward-sloping demand curve leaves price above marginal cost.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Q2 marks minimum ATC while the firm produces Q1. What does Q2 − Q1 measure?

Economic profit
The price markup
The shutdown gap

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Why does entry stop at the long-run outcome shown?
options: Price equals average total cost, so economic profit is zero

Output equals efficient scale, so excess capacity is zero

q.feedback: Entry stops when the demand curve is tangent to ATC and price equals ATC, eliminating economic profit.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

Demand must be perfectly inelastic

q.q: A market has differentiated products but only three firms that react strategically to one another. Which model is the better starting point?

Perfect competition
Pure monopoly
Oligopoly

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: Why is a differentiated firm’s demand downward sloping?
options: Some customers prefer its variety, but they can switch when price rises
The firm is a price taker
The product has no close substitutes, so buyers cannot switch when the firm raises its price
Marginal cost creates demand
q.feedback: Differentiation gives limited market power.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: For a downward-sloping firm demand curve, why is MR below price?
options: ATC is U-shaped
Selling more requires a lower price, creating a price effect
Entry raises fixed cost and therefore pushes marginal revenue below the firm’s demand curve
Products are identical
q.feedback: Added revenue is reduced by the lower price on units sold.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: What is the correct sequence for short-run firm choice?
options: Choose P where demand equals MC, then read Q from MR
Choose minimum ATC, then set P=MC
Choose Q where MR=MC, then read P from demand
Choose the highest price on demand
q.feedback: Quantity comes from the marginal rule; demand supplies price.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: A table has no exact MR=MC equality. Which output should be selected?
options: No output can be chosen
The first unit whose MC exceeds price
The minimum-ATC output
The last unit whose MR is at least MC
q.feedback: The discrete marginal rule compares the added revenue and cost of each unit.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: A firm has P>MC but P<ATC. Which statement is correct?
options: It has a markup but an economic loss
It earns economic profit because P>MC
It must have zero profit
It is allocatively efficient
q.feedback: Profit depends on P versus ATC, not P versus MC.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: A firm has P<ATC but P>AVC. What should it do in the short run?
options: Shut down because P<ATC
Produce at MR=MC and minimize its loss
Exit immediately because any economic loss requires the firm to leave the market
Produce at minimum ATC
q.feedback: Covering AVC allows production to contribute toward fixed cost.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: Short-run profit attracts entry. What happens to an existing firm’s demand?
options: It shifts right because the market is larger
It becomes vertical
It shifts left as new substitutes appear
It remains fixed by assumption
q.feedback: New varieties divide customers among more firms.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: How does entry usually affect the elasticity of an existing firm’s demand?
options: It becomes less elastic
It becomes perfectly inelastic
Elasticity is determined by fixed cost
It becomes more elastic
q.feedback: More substitutes make switching easier.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: Persistent losses cause exit. What happens to a surviving firm’s demand?
options: It shifts right
It shifts left
It becomes horizontal at zero
It disappears
q.feedback: Fewer substitutes leave more customers for survivors.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: Why does exit help eliminate losses?
options: Exit raises every surviving firm’s fixed cost and directly reduces the quantity each firm supplies
Surviving firms face stronger demand and may charge a higher price
Exit makes products identical
Exit forces P below AVC
q.feedback: The demand recovery improves revenue opportunities for survivors.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: What does zero economic profit mean?
options: Accounting profit is zero
The owner receives no return for time, capital, or entrepreneurship once economic profit reaches zero
All explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered
Price equals marginal cost
q.feedback: Economic profit subtracts opportunity costs.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Where does long-run tangency occur in the standard model?
options: At minimum ATC
Where demand intersects marginal cost at the output that minimizes average total cost
At the shutdown point
On the downward-sloping portion of ATC before its minimum
q.feedback: The equilibrium output is below the minimum-ATC quantity.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Why can a firm have a markup with zero economic profit?
options: Price can equal ATC while exceeding MC
Markup equals economic profit by definition
MC must equal ATC
Entry sets price below demand
q.feedback: Markup and profit use different cost comparisons.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: What does excess capacity measure?
options: Price equals marginal cost at minimum average total cost, eliminating markup and excess capacity
Q at minimum ATC minus the firm’s equilibrium Q
Price minus marginal cost
ATC minus AVC
q.feedback: It is a cost-curve output gap.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: An ad shifts firm demand right. Is that a movement along demand?

Yes, because price changes
No, it is a demand shift
No, it is a supply shift

q.q: A fixed advertising bill rises. Which curve does not shift directly?

q.q: Why is product variety not automatically wasteful?

q.q: What does nonprice competition mean?
options: Price never matters
Firms compete through quality, service, location, branding, and other dimensions in addition to price
Firms coordinate prices
Products become identical
q.feedback: Nonprice dimensions supplement rather than eliminate price competition.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A market has many small sellers and easy entry, but every seller offers exactly the same product. What key condition for monopolistic competition is missing?
options: A large number of sellers
Freedom of entry and exit
Independent ownership
Product differentiation
q.feedback: Many sellers and easy entry are not enough. Monopolistic competition also requires differentiated products.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses its MR=MC output. At that output, price is below ATC but above AVC. What should the firm do in the short run?
options: Raise output until price equals ATC
Exit the industry immediately because price is below ATC
Continue producing and accept an economic loss
Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
q.feedback: If price covers AVC, producing helps pay some fixed cost even though the firm earns an economic loss.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: A fixed advertising bill increases but demand does not change. Why does the MR=MC output stay the same?
options: Advertising expenses never affect profit
The fixed cost does not directly shift MR or MC
The fixed cost lowers price by the same amount
The fixed cost raises MC at every unit
q.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change lowers profit but does not alter the marginal decision when demand is unchanged.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: An ad tells buyers the product price and where to buy it. Why is this informational rather than persuasive?
options: It supplies facts that reduce search costs
It guarantees buyers will prefer the brand
It changes the product’s physical quality
It prevents consumers from switching brands
q.feedback: Informational advertising communicates useful facts instead of mainly trying to reshape preferences.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: After a successful campaign, buyers purchase more at every possible price. Is this a movement along the firm’s demand curve?
options: Yes, because quantity demanded increased
Yes, because advertising changes the posted price
No, it is a leftward shift of supply
No, it is a rightward shift of demand
q.feedback: More demanded at every price is a demand shift. A movement along demand requires a change in the firm’s own price.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit in long-run equilibrium. Does that prove the outcome is fully efficient?
options: Yes. Entry forces price to equal MC and minimum ATC
No. Zero economic profit means the firm should shut down
No. Price can still exceed MC and output can remain below the minimum-ATC quantity
Yes. Zero economic profit guarantees both allocative and productive efficiency
q.feedback: Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: A differentiated firm uses MC, AVC, and ATC from cost analysis. Which curve chooses output?
options: ATC alone
AFC alone
MC together with MR
TFC alone
q.feedback: Output follows the marginal comparison.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: Which cost measure determines short-run shutdown?
options: ATC
AFC
Total fixed cost
AVC
q.feedback: The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: Which cost measure determines whether long-run economic profit is zero?
options: ATC including opportunity cost
AVC only
MC only
AFC only
q.feedback: P=ATC means all economic cost is covered.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Why does minimum ATC matter for excess capacity?
options: It identifies the price on demand
It identifies the output that minimizes unit cost
It determines MR
It eliminates entry
q.feedback: Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Which feature does monopolistic competition share with perfect competition?
options: Identical products
Horizontal firm demand
Relatively easy entry and exit
P=MC in long-run equilibrium
q.feedback: Entry and exit operate in both models.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: Which long-run result occurs in both models?
options: Price equals MC
Production at minimum ATC
Horizontal firm demand
Zero economic profit
q.feedback: Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Why does monopolistic competition retain a markup unlike perfect competition?
options: Differentiation leaves downward-sloping firm demand
Entry is impossible
Products are identical
MC is always falling
q.feedback: Limited market power keeps P above MC.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: Which model achieves productive efficiency in its standard long-run equilibrium?
options: Monopolistic competition
Perfect competition
Both models
Neither model
q.feedback: The competitive firm produces at minimum ATC.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: What decision rule is shared by monopoly and monopolistic competition?
options: Take price as given
Produce where demand equals MC
Choose output where MR=MC and read price from demand
Earn persistent profit automatically
q.feedback: Both firms face downward-sloping demand.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: Why is entry more important in monopolistic competition than monopoly?
options: Entry is prohibited in both
Entry makes demand vertical
Entry raises monopoly barriers
Entry shifts each existing firm’s demand and erodes profit
q.feedback: Relatively easy entry is a defining difference.

labels: Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.

q.q: Which structure generally has more close substitutes for each firm’s product?
options: Monopolistic competition
Pure monopoly
Both have none
The answer depends only on fixed cost
q.feedback: Many differentiated rivals supply close alternatives.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: Which model can sustain long-run economic profit because barriers block entry?
options: Monopolistic competition
Monopoly
Both by definition
Neither
q.feedback: Entry erodes profit in monopolistic competition.

labels: Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium, tangency, markup, and excess capacity.

q.q: More close substitutes make a firm’s demand:
options: Less elastic
Perfectly inelastic
More elastic
Unrelated to price
q.feedback: Substitution opportunities increase responsiveness.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: A successful loyalty program makes demand less elastic. What market-power effect follows?
options: MR becomes equal to price
Entry becomes illegal
ATC becomes horizontal
The firm may sustain a larger markup
q.feedback: Lower elasticity generally strengthens pricing power.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: Why can differentiation create consumer value?
options: It offers varieties better matched to heterogeneous preferences
It eliminates opportunity cost
It guarantees identical quality
It forces every buyer to pay the same willingness to pay
q.feedback: Different buyers may prefer different attributes.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: A brand changes perceived value without changing physical quality. Which concept is central?
options: Marginal product
Preference and perceived differentiation
Natural monopoly
Comparative advantage
q.feedback: Consumer perceptions can shape demand for a variety.

labels: Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.

q.q: Why can markup create lost trades?
options: Every unit becomes a fixed cost
Consumer surplus always becomes zero
Some units valued above MC are not sold because price exceeds MC
Entry eliminates demand
q.feedback: P>MC can exclude mutually beneficial units.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: How can informational advertising improve market performance?
options: It guarantees zero markup
It prevents entry
It makes products identical
It can reduce search costs
q.feedback: Useful information helps buyers compare alternatives.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: What separates monopolistic competition from oligopoly?
options: Many firms act without central strategic interdependence in the basic model
Products are never differentiated
Demand is always horizontal
Entry never occurs
q.feedback: Strategic few-firm interaction belongs to oligopoly.

labels: Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.

q.q: Why can successful product development create temporary economic profit?
options: It makes MC equal price forever
It shifts demand before imitation and entry erode the advantage
It eliminates all substitutes
It sets accounting profit to zero immediately
q.feedback: Innovation can temporarily strengthen demand.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: Cost analysis tells a differentiated firm its MC curve. Which additional curve is needed to apply the usual profit-maximizing output rule?
options: Market supply
Marginal revenue
Average fixed cost
Long-run average cost
q.feedback: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses output where MR equals MC, subject to the usual marginal condition.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: The shutdown rule from cost analysis carries directly into monopolistic competition. Which comparison determines whether the firm should produce in the short run?
options: Price compared with AVC at the chosen output
Price compared with AFC at the chosen output
Marginal revenue compared with ATC
Total revenue compared only with fixed cost
q.feedback: A firm should produce in the short run when price covers average variable cost at its profit-maximizing output.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: A firm has already selected output where MR=MC. Which comparison now determines whether it earns profit or loss?
options: Price compared with MC
MR compared with AVC
Demand compared with market supply
Price compared with ATC
q.feedback: At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.

labels: Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.

q.q: Elasticity analysis helps explain branding. If brand loyalty reduces the absolute value of price elasticity of demand, buyers become:
options: Completely unwilling to buy
Perfectly responsive at one market price
Less responsive to the firm’s price
More responsive to the firm’s price
q.feedback: Lower absolute elasticity means quantity demanded changes less for a given percentage price change.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: Cost analysis helps separate two advertising cases. Which selling expense acts most like variable cost?
options: A fixed monthly billboard lease
A fee charged on each unit sold
A flat annual sponsorship payment
A one-time logo redesign
q.feedback: A per-unit fee varies with output and therefore enters variable and marginal cost.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: A successful new product feature creates short-run profit in a market with easy entry. What long-run force can erode that profit?
options: Entry and imitation by rivals
A permanent legal ban on substitutes
Automatic shutdown of the innovating firm
A requirement that demand become perfectly inelastic
q.feedback: With relatively easy entry and close substitutes, successful differentiation can attract rivals and imitation over time.

labels: Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.

q.q: Which feature most directly distinguishes a monopoly from perfect competition?
options: A single seller is protected by substantial barriers to entry
Many sellers offer an identical product
Each firm faces a horizontal demand curve
Entry eliminates economic profit quickly
q.feedback: A monopoly is sustained by one seller and barriers that prevent competitive entry.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: A firm has market power when it can:
options: Choose any price and quantity without losing customers
Influence the price of its product within the limits imposed by demand
Eliminate all production costs
Force every consumer to buy the product
q.feedback: Market power permits price influence, but demand still constrains the firm.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: Which is a legal barrier to entry?
options: A downward-sloping market demand curve
A decline in marginal revenue
A patent that grants temporary exclusive production rights
A competitive firm earning normal profit
q.feedback: Patents are government-created, time-limited barriers.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: Control of the only commercially useful deposit of a critical mineral is an example of:
options: Perfectly elastic demand
Constant returns to scale
Price discrimination
Ownership of a key resource
q.feedback: Exclusive control of a necessary input can block entry.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: A network effect can strengthen monopoly power when:
options: The product becomes more valuable as more people use the same network
Average fixed cost rises with output
Consumers can resell the product freely
New firms face no coordination problem
q.feedback: Network value can make switching and entry difficult.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: A natural monopoly usually exists because:
options: Marginal revenue equals price at every output
Average total cost falls over the relevant range of market demand
The firm owns a patent forever
Demand is perfectly elastic
q.feedback: Large scale economies can make one supplier less costly than several.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: The demand curve facing a single-price monopolist is:
options: Horizontal at the market price
The marginal-cost curve
The market demand curve
Vertical at the competitive quantity
q.feedback: With one seller, firm demand and market demand are the same.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: For a monopolist, average revenue equals:
options: Marginal cost
Average total cost
Economic profit per unit
Price and therefore the demand curve
q.feedback: AR=TR/Q=P, so average revenue lies on demand.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: Why is marginal revenue below price for a single-price monopolist?
options: Selling another unit requires a lower price that also applies to earlier units
Marginal cost always exceeds average cost
The firm pays a tax on every unit
Fixed cost rises when output expands
q.feedback: The price effect on previous units makes MR less than the new price.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: The output effect of selling one more unit is:
options: Revenue lost because all earlier units sell for less
Revenue gained from selling the additional unit
The increase in fixed cost
The decline in average total cost
q.feedback: The added unit contributes its sale price to revenue.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: The price effect of selling one more unit is:
options: Revenue gained from the new unit
The increase in marginal cost
Revenue lost because the lower price applies to units already being sold
The elimination of fixed cost
q.feedback: A single-price monopolist must lower price on all units.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: When marginal revenue is positive, total revenue is:
options: Falling as output rises
Always equal to total cost
At its minimum
Increasing as output rises
q.feedback: Positive MR means another unit adds to total revenue.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: For a downward-sloping linear demand curve, the marginal-revenue curve has:
options: The same price intercept and twice the slope
The same slope and half the price intercept
A horizontal shape at market price
A higher quantity intercept than demand
q.feedback: Linear MR shares demand’s vertical intercept and is twice as steep.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: A single-price monopolist with nonnegative marginal cost will choose output on:
options: The inelastic portion of demand
The elastic portion of demand
The vertical portion of demand
Only the unit-elastic point regardless of cost
q.feedback: MR is positive on elastic demand; on inelastic demand, reducing output raises revenue and lowers cost.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: The standard monopoly output rule is to produce where:
options: Demand equals marginal cost
Price equals average total cost
Marginal revenue equals marginal cost on rising MC
Total revenue is highest regardless of cost
q.feedback: MR=MC identifies the profit-maximizing quantity.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: After finding the monopoly quantity, the monopolist determines price by:
options: Reading the marginal-revenue curve at that quantity
Using minimum average total cost
Setting price equal to marginal cost
Reading the demand curve at that quantity
q.feedback: Demand gives the highest price consumers will pay for the chosen quantity.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost for the next unit, the monopolist should:
options: Increase output
Reduce output
Raise fixed cost
Shut down immediately
q.feedback: That unit adds more revenue than cost.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: If marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue for the next unit, producing it would:
options: Increase profit
Reduce profit
Leave profit unchanged
Eliminate the barrier to entry
q.feedback: The unit adds more cost than revenue.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Monopoly profit per unit equals:
options: Price minus marginal cost
Marginal revenue minus average variable cost
Price minus average total cost
Total revenue minus quantity
q.feedback: ATC includes all economic cost per unit.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: A monopoly can earn an economic loss because:
options: A monopoly is required to charge marginal cost
Marginal revenue always equals zero
Barriers to entry force price below AVC
Its demand may be too weak relative to its costs
q.feedback: Market power does not guarantee profitable demand and cost conditions.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: A loss-making monopolist should shut down in the short run when:
options: Price at its best output is below average variable cost
Price is below average total cost but above AVC
Economic profit is zero
Marginal revenue is below price
q.feedback: The short-run shutdown rule still compares price with AVC.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: Why can monopoly economic profit persist in the long run?
options: The demand curve becomes horizontal
Barriers prevent entry from expanding supply and eroding profit
Fixed costs disappear
Marginal revenue rises above demand
q.feedback: Barriers block the entry mechanism that removes competitive profit.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: Compared with perfect competition, a single-price monopoly generally charges:
options: A lower price and produces a higher quantity
The same price and quantity
A higher price and produces a lower quantity
A price equal to minimum ATC
q.feedback: The monopoly restricts output where MR=MC rather than producing where P=MC.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: Monopoly deadweight loss represents:
options: The entire monopoly profit rectangle
All consumer surplus transferred to the firm
The monopolist’s fixed cost
Total surplus lost because mutually beneficial units are not produced
q.feedback: DWL is the value of trades between monopoly and efficient output that do not occur.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: Price above marginal cost signals:
options: Allocative inefficiency
Productive efficiency
Zero economic profit
Perfect price discrimination
q.feedback: Consumers value additional units above their marginal production cost.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: Rent seeking occurs when resources are used to:
options: Lower marginal cost through innovation
Obtain or protect monopoly privileges rather than produce valuable output
Expand output toward the efficient level
Calculate consumer surplus
q.feedback: Rent-seeking effort consumes resources to capture economic rents.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: Under marginal-cost pricing for a natural monopoly, the firm may require a subsidy because:
options: Marginal revenue exceeds demand
Output falls below monopoly output
Price can fall below average total cost
Fixed cost becomes variable cost
q.feedback: With declining ATC, MC lies below ATC, so P=MC may not cover total cost.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Average-cost pricing regulation sets price where:
options: Marginal revenue intersects marginal cost
Demand intersects marginal cost
Average variable cost is minimized
Demand intersects average total cost
q.feedback: P=ATC permits the regulated firm to cover economic cost.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Price discrimination requires the seller to:
options: Separate customers and prevent profitable resale
Face perfectly elastic demand
Charge every buyer the same price
Have zero fixed cost
q.feedback: Segmentation and limits on arbitrage are necessary.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A third-degree price-discriminating monopolist generally charges the higher price to the group with:
options: More elastic demand
Less elastic demand
The highest resale opportunity
The lowest willingness to pay at every quantity
q.feedback: The less responsive group receives the larger markup.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At what quantity does the monopolist maximize profit?
options: 36 units
24 units
42 units
60 units
q.feedback: Profit is maximized where MR intersects MC, which occurs at Q = 36.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing quantity, what price does the monopolist charge?
q.feedback: After choosing Q = 36 from MR = MC, move up to demand; the demand curve shows P = $42.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What marginal-revenue value is shown at Q = 36?
q.feedback: At Q = 36, the MR curve meets MC at $24.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What is average total cost at Q = 36?
q.feedback: The ATC guide at the monopoly quantity is $27.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What quantity is selected where MR = MC?
options: 40 units
20 units
60 units
67 units
q.feedback: MR and MC intersect at Q = 40.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 40, what price is read from the demand curve?
q.feedback: The demand curve shows P = $40 at Q = 40.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What is ATC at the monopoly quantity?
q.feedback: The ATC guide at Q = 40 is $45.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What output does the unregulated natural monopolist choose?
options: 45 units
20 units
60 units
90 units
q.feedback: The unregulated monopoly chooses Q where MR = MC, marked at Q = 45.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What price does demand indicate at the monopoly output?
q.feedback: At Q = 45, the demand curve shows a price of $47.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does demand intersect marginal cost?
options: 45 units
60 units
90 units
125 units
q.feedback: With MC at $20, demand reaches MC at Q = 90.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Approximately what output does the unregulated monopolist choose where MR = MC?
options: 45 units
116 units
70 units
140 units
q.feedback: The MR curve reaches the $10 MC line at about Q = 70.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What price does the demand curve show at the unregulated monopoly output?
q.feedback: At about Q = 70, demand indicates a price of about $27.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: For a single-price monopolist, which curve also shows average revenue at each quantity?
options: The marginal-cost curve
The average-total-cost curve
A horizontal line at marginal revenue
The demand curve
q.feedback: Because AR = TR/Q = P, average revenue lies on the monopolist’s demand curve.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: A monopolist charges $50, has ATC=$38, and sells 100 units. What is total economic profit?
q.feedback: Profit per unit is $12 and total profit is $12 × 100.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: A monopolist charges $24 while ATC is $30 at its chosen output. Which statement is correct?
options: The firm earns $6 economic profit per unit
The firm must shut down immediately
The firm is breaking even
The firm has an economic loss of $6 per unit
q.feedback: When P<ATC, the firm incurs a loss equal to ATC−P per unit.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: A monopolist has P=$18, AVC=$12, and ATC=$25 at its best operating output. In the short run it should generally:
options: Exit permanently because any accounting loss requires exit
Produce only if price equals MC at every unit
Produce because price covers variable cost and contributes toward fixed cost
Shut down because price is below ATC
q.feedback: A short-run loss does not imply shutdown when price remains above AVC.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: When a monopolist’s price equals ATC at its chosen output, economic profit is:
options: Positive because monopoly has market power
Zero
Equal to total revenue
Negative because MR is below price
q.feedback: P=ATC means revenue exactly covers explicit and implicit economic costs.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: Compared with an otherwise similar competitive market, a single-price monopoly typically produces:
options: Less output at a lower price
Less output at a higher price
More output at a lower price
The same output at the same price
q.feedback: Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: Why is P>MC at the monopoly quantity evidence of allocative inefficiency?
options: Some buyers value additional units more than the marginal cost of producing them
The monopolist must be earning zero profit
Marginal revenue must equal price
Average total cost must be at its minimum
q.feedback: When willingness to pay exceeds MC for foregone units, mutually beneficial trades are left unrealized.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: What does monopoly deadweight loss represent?
options: All profit earned by the monopolist
All consumer surplus transferred to the monopolist
The firm’s fixed cost
Gains from trade lost because output is restricted below the efficient quantity
q.feedback: Deadweight loss is surplus that disappears rather than being transferred between buyers and sellers.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: If firms spend resources lobbying for an exclusive monopoly privilege, those expenditures are an example of:
options: Price discrimination
Marginal-cost pricing
Rent seeking
Productive efficiency
q.feedback: Resources used to obtain or protect economic rents can create additional social cost.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: A monopoly price increase transfers some surplus from consumers to the firm. Is that entire transfer deadweight loss?
options: No; because monopoly never changes total surplus
No; transferred surplus changes who receives the surplus, while deadweight loss is surplus that disappears
Yes; every dollar of monopoly profit is deadweight loss
Yes; consumer surplus and total surplus are identical
q.feedback: Distributional transfers and efficiency losses are different pieces of monopoly welfare analysis.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: A natural monopoly is most likely when average total cost:
options: Is unrelated to scale
Falls over the relevant range of market demand
Rises at every output
Equals price at every output
q.feedback: Large scale economies over market demand can make one producer less costly than several.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Under marginal-cost regulation, the regulator sets price equal to:
options: Marginal cost
Average total cost
Marginal revenue
The unregulated monopoly price
q.feedback: P=MC targets allocative efficiency.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Average-cost regulation generally targets a price equal to:
options: Marginal revenue
The monopoly demand intercept
Zero
Average total cost
q.feedback: P=ATC allows the regulated firm to cover economic cost including normal return.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Why can P=MC create a financial problem for a natural monopoly?
options: Demand becomes perfectly elastic
The firm necessarily earns monopoly profit
When ATC exceeds MC, revenue may be insufficient to cover total cost
MR must become negative
q.feedback: Declining ATC often implies MC below ATC, so marginal-cost pricing can produce losses.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A binding price cap below the unregulated monopoly price is intended primarily to:
options: Make the firm a price taker in an unregulated market
Limit the price the regulated monopolist may charge
Guarantee monopoly profit
Eliminate all fixed cost
q.feedback: A price cap constrains the allowable price and can alter incentives and output.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: If a regulator sets P=ATC rather than P=MC, the main efficiency compromise is that:
options: Price may remain above marginal cost even though the firm can cover total cost
The firm must shut down immediately
Demand becomes horizontal
The firm earns unlimited economic profit
q.feedback: Average-cost pricing addresses financial viability but usually does not attain allocative efficiency.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: If a regulator requires P=MC and the firm would otherwise incur a loss, one possible policy response is:
options: Raise the price back to the unregulated monopoly level
Require output to fall until MR=0
Eliminate the demand curve
Provide a subsidy financed outside the firm’s price revenue
q.feedback: A subsidy can cover the gap between total cost and revenue under marginal-cost pricing.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Which example best fits natural monopoly rather than a legal monopoly created only by statute?
options: A license limits taxi entry even though many firms could operate efficiently
A copyright protects a particular book
A single water network has lower ATC than duplicating pipes across several firms
A patent gives one pharmaceutical producer exclusive rights for a fixed term
q.feedback: Natural monopoly is rooted in cost structure and economies of scale rather than legal exclusion alone.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: For price discrimination to be profitable, the seller generally needs:
options: Perfectly competitive pricing and free entry
Identical demand elasticity in every group
A requirement that price equal marginal cost
Market power and some ability to separate buyers by willingness to pay or demand responsiveness
q.feedback: Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Why must a price-discriminating seller often prevent resale between customer groups?
options: Resale guarantees the high-price group becomes less elastic
Resale forces average cost to zero
Low-price buyers could otherwise resell to high-price buyers and undermine the price difference
Resale would make marginal cost negative
q.feedback: Arbitrage erodes segmented prices.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A museum charges local students one price and tourists another based on verifiable group status. This is closest to:
options: A natural monopoly
Third-degree price discrimination
Perfect competition
Marginal-cost regulation
q.feedback: Third-degree discrimination separates identifiable groups and charges them different prices.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: All else equal, which customer group usually receives the higher markup under third-degree price discrimination?
options: The group with less elastic demand
The group with more elastic demand
The group with the lowest fixed cost
The group with the easiest resale opportunities
q.feedback: Less responsive buyers support a larger markup over marginal cost.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Under perfect first-degree price discrimination, the seller attempts to charge each buyer:
options: The same single monopoly price
Marginal cost for every unit and nothing more
Average total cost regardless of willingness to pay
That buyer’s maximum willingness to pay for each unit
q.feedback: Perfect first-degree discrimination extracts each unit’s willingness to pay.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A theater can identify student status but students can freely transfer discounted tickets to anyone. Which requirement is missing?
options: A downward-sloping market demand curve
Positive marginal cost
Effective prevention of arbitrage or resale
Market power
q.feedback: Identification alone is not enough if buyers can defeat segmentation through resale.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A seller faces two separated groups with the same MC. Group A has more elastic demand than Group B. Which pricing pattern is generally expected?
options: Zero price in the more elastic group
A lower price in Group A and a higher price in Group B
A higher price in Group A and a lower price in Group B
The same price because MC is the same
q.feedback: The more elastic group receives the smaller markup.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Can price discrimination ever increase output relative to single-price monopoly?
options: Yes; serving additional low-value or elastic-market buyers can expand output in some cases
No; discrimination always leaves output unchanged
No; discrimination always eliminates all consumer purchases
Yes, but only if marginal cost is zero
q.feedback: The welfare effect depends partly on whether discrimination expands or contracts total output.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $75, $70, $65, $60, $55, $50. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
q.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

Earn economic profit of $100
Produce where demand equals MC
Produce and incur an economic loss of $100
q.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 22.5 units at $56.25; ATC is $58.03 and AVC is $20.25. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $40
Shut down solely because P<ATC
Earn economic profit of $40
Produce where demand equals MC
q.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

options: Economic loss of $191

Profit of $784.93
Economic profit of $191

Units that cost more than buyers value
The monopoly profit rectangle

Monopoly transfers some surplus and destroys additional surplus
Monopoly profit equals deadweight loss
Total surplus is unchanged
q.feedback: Some consumer surplus is transferred; the output restriction creates DWL.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: A single-price monopolist produces 22.73 units, while the competitive benchmark is 41.67 units. What does the output gap represent?
options: Units that cost more than buyers value
The monopoly profit rectangle
Mutually beneficial units not produced by the monopoly
Government tax revenue
q.feedback: Between Qm and Qc, demand exceeds MC, so those units would create surplus.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: For a market with monopoly price $74.33 and competitive price $32.04 under the stated linear demand and MC, which statement is correct?
options: All consumer loss becomes monopoly profit
Monopoly profit equals deadweight loss
Total surplus is unchanged

q.feedback: Some consumer surplus is transferred; the output restriction creates DWL.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

options: The firm needs a subsidy or another way to cover its loss
The firm earns monopoly profit automatically
Output must be reduced below monopoly output
Entry will immediately create competition
q.feedback: P=MC can be efficient but fail to cover fixed cost.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Compared with marginal-cost pricing, average-cost pricing for a natural monopoly generally produces:
options: A lower price and higher output with larger losses
A higher price and lower output but avoids an operating subsidy
The unregulated monopoly price and output
Perfect competition with free entry
q.feedback: P=ATC covers cost but leaves P above MC.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A theater charges students less than adults for the same seat. Which condition is essential for the pricing strategy to work?
options: Students must have less elastic demand
Marginal cost must differ by buyer

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Two customer groups have the same marginal cost, but Group A has less elastic demand than Group B. A profit-maximizing discriminator will usually:

Charge both groups marginal cost
Charge both groups the same price regardless of elasticity
Charge Group A a higher price
q.feedback: The less elastic market supports a larger markup.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.
