q.q: A town currently has one ambulance provider, but licenses are readily available and several firms can enter with ordinary equipment. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The current one-seller market does not by itself establish durable monopoly power
The provider is a natural monopoly because only one firm operates today
The provider must have a patent protecting ambulance service
The provider can charge any price because entry has not happened yet
q.feedback: A monopoly requires meaningful barriers to entry, not merely one seller at a moment in time.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: A patented medical device is profitable while the patent remains in force. What is the patent doing economically?
options: Making the firm’s demand curve horizontal
Forcing marginal revenue to equal price
Guaranteeing that average total cost will fall forever
Restricting entry and helping preserve the incumbent’s market power
q.feedback: A patent is a legal barrier that can prevent rivals from copying the protected product.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: A messaging platform becomes more useful as more friends and businesses join it. Why can this discourage entry by a rival platform?
options: The rival automatically faces perfectly inelastic demand
Network effects remove the need for consumer choice
Users may prefer the established network because its large user base raises its value
The incumbent’s marginal cost must be zero
q.feedback: Network effects can create a demand-side barrier because users value access to the existing network.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: A firm owns the only economically viable source of a rare input required to make a specialized product. Which mechanism protects its market position most directly?
options: Its customers cannot respond to price changes
Control of an essential resource blocks rivals from obtaining a necessary input
Its price must equal marginal cost
Its fixed costs disappear as output rises
q.feedback: Exclusive control of a critical resource can prevent otherwise capable rivals from entering.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: A regional water network requires an enormous pipe system, and duplicating the network would raise average cost. Which fact best supports natural-monopoly status?
options: One firm can serve market demand at lower average cost than multiple duplicative networks
The provider has the legal right to discriminate among all buyers
Marginal revenue is always positive
The firm earns accounting profit in the current year
q.feedback: Natural monopoly comes from scale economies over the relevant range of market demand.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: A monopolist cuts price to sell one additional unit. Why can marginal revenue be far below the new price?
options: Average revenue becomes zero when price falls
The demand curve becomes horizontal after the price cut
The extra unit adds revenue, but the lower price also reduces revenue collected on earlier units
Marginal cost is automatically subtracted from marginal revenue
q.feedback: Marginal revenue reflects both the output effect and the price effect on units already sold.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: At 40 units a monopolist has MR=$28 and MC=$22; at 41 units MR=$24 and MC=$25. Which output is the better marginal choice?
options: 40 units, because the 41st unit costs more at the margin than it adds to revenue
41 units, because price must still exceed marginal revenue
41 units, because a monopolist always produces until price equals MC
40 units only if average total cost is minimized there
q.feedback: Produce units for which MR covers MC and stop before the next unit has MC greater than MR.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: A monopolist has already found its profit-maximizing quantity using MR=MC. What is the next step for determining the monopoly price?
options: Use the MR curve value as the price
Set price equal to average total cost
Choose the lowest price on the demand curve
Move up to the demand curve at that quantity
q.feedback: MR determines the quantity condition; demand gives the price buyers will pay for that quantity.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Suppose competition would produce 100 units at $20, while monopoly produces 70 units at $35. Which change is the clearest source of efficiency loss?
options: The 30 units between 70 and 100 that would have generated gains from trade are not produced
The monopolist receives revenue on the 70 units it sells
The market price is written in dollars rather than units
Consumers buy positive quantities under monopoly
q.feedback: The efficiency loss comes from mutually beneficial transactions forgone because of restricted output.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: If a monopolist reduces output farther below the competitive quantity while demand and cost curves are unchanged, what generally happens to deadweight loss?
options: It necessarily falls because the firm earns more profit
It becomes zero when price rises
It is unchanged because transfers do not matter
It increases because more mutually beneficial units are forgone
q.feedback: Greater output restriction usually widens the range of lost gains from trade.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: A natural monopoly has MC=$12 and ATC=$20 at the allocatively efficient quantity. If regulation sets P=$12, which outcome is most likely without a subsidy?
options: The firm must reduce output to zero by definition
The firm incurs an economic loss because price is below ATC
The firm earns $8 profit per unit
The firm breaks even because P=MC
q.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A regulator sets price where demand intersects ATC for a natural monopoly. Which combination best describes the result?
options: The firm can cover total economic cost, but price generally remains above MC
The firm earns maximum monopoly profit and output falls to zero
Price equals MC and allocative efficiency is guaranteed
The firm necessarily faces a horizontal demand curve
q.feedback: Average-cost pricing aims for financial viability, not full P=MC efficiency.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A price cap is set above the price the monopolist would charge without regulation. What is the immediate effect?
options: The firm must charge the cap even if it prefers a lower price
The firm becomes perfectly competitive
The firm’s fixed cost becomes zero
The cap is nonbinding and does not constrain the firm’s chosen price
q.feedback: A ceiling above the unregulated price does not bind.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A regulator wants lower prices but also wants the utility to maintain infrastructure and innovate. Which concern best captures the tradeoff?
options: Investment incentives are unrelated to expected returns
Any regulation automatically produces the competitive quantity
Aggressive price limits can improve consumer terms while weakening incentives or revenue for cost recovery and investment
Lower prices always increase monopoly profit
q.feedback: Regulation balances static consumer/efficiency goals against financial and dynamic incentives.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Demand for a utility expands enough that the relevant output range moves beyond the region where ATC is falling. What does that suggest about the natural-monopoly argument?
options: It guarantees marginal cost is zero
It may weaken because one firm may no longer have a cost advantage over multiple firms across the new relevant range
It becomes stronger automatically because demand increased
It proves that price discrimination is efficient
q.feedback: Natural-monopoly status depends on cost conditions over the relevant market-demand range.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A firm has market power and observes two groups with different demand elasticities, but buyers can costlessly resell the product. What happens to the proposed two-price strategy?
options: The firm can preserve both prices indefinitely
The high-price group automatically becomes less elastic
Marginal cost becomes different across groups
Arbitrage tends to collapse the price difference
q.feedback: Segmentation must be enforceable; costless resale undermines differentiated prices.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Why does a third-degree discriminator compare MR from each market with the common MC?
options: Average revenue must equal average cost in every market
MC determines demand elasticity directly
Profit is increased by allocating another unit to a market whenever that market’s MR exceeds MC
The firm must make prices identical across markets
q.feedback: The firm allocates output across separated markets using marginal revenue relative to marginal cost.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Two groups have identical MC. Seniors have less elastic demand than students. What happens to the optimal markup?
options: Both prices must equal ATC
The senior markup is larger
The student markup is larger
Both markups must be zero
q.feedback: A less elastic market supports a larger markup over common marginal cost.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Compared with a single-price monopoly, perfect first-degree price discrimination can eliminate the standard output deadweight loss when:
options: The firm sells every unit for which willingness to pay is at least MC
The firm charges one common price above MC
Buyers can freely resell units
The firm ignores willingness to pay
q.feedback: Perfect discrimination can expand output to the efficient quantity while transferring surplus to the seller.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A discriminatory pricing plan raises total output by serving a new low-price market. What is the most defensible welfare conclusion?
options: Total surplus must fall because prices differ
Consumer surplus must rise in every group
Deadweight loss is necessarily unchanged
Total surplus may rise because additional mutually beneficial trades occur, though distribution also changes
q.feedback: Welfare effects depend on output as well as how surplus is redistributed.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: An airline sells a discounted ticket that cannot be transferred and imposes restrictions that separate leisure from business travelers. What economic purpose do the restrictions serve?
options: They force the same elasticity in both groups
They eliminate the airline’s fixed costs
They help prevent arbitrage and maintain market segmentation
They make the airline a price taker
q.feedback: Restrictions can help keep low-price buyers from reselling or masquerading as high-value segments.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A firm can separate buyers perfectly but faces a perfectly competitive market with many identical sellers. Why is discrimination difficult to sustain?
options: Buyer groups necessarily have identical elasticities
The firm lacks enough market power to set different markups without losing customers
Resale prevention becomes irrelevant only because MC is zero
Competitive firms have no costs

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: What distinguishes monopoly profit from monopoly deadweight loss?
options: Both are identical rectangles
Profit is consumer surplus and DWL is fixed cost
Profit includes surplus transferred to the seller; DWL is surplus that disappears
DWL is tax revenue
q.feedback: Transfers remain in total surplus; unrealized trades do not.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: Why does reducing monopoly output below the competitive quantity create DWL?
options: All producer surplus disappears
ATC necessarily rises
Demand becomes perfectly elastic
Some buyers value omitted units above their marginal cost
q.feedback: The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: Under perfect first-degree discrimination, what happens to the competitive gains from trade in the benchmark model?
options: They are realized, but the seller captures nearly all of the surplus
They disappear because output is zero
They are divided equally
Consumer surplus rises above total surplus
q.feedback: Personalized prices can restore output while changing distribution.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: What marginal comparison determines monopoly output?
options: Price compared with ATC
MR compared with MC
TR compared with fixed cost only
Demand compared with AVC
q.feedback: Produce units whose marginal revenue covers marginal cost.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: If the next unit has MR greater than MC, what does marginal analysis imply?
options: Reject the unit because it lowers price
Shut down immediately
Produce the unit because it increases profit
Raise fixed cost
q.feedback: The incremental benefit exceeds the incremental cost.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: A patent can create monopoly pricing while encouraging research. What tradeoff should policy evaluate?
options: Accounting profit versus total revenue
Fixed cost versus sunk cost only
Market demand versus firm demand
Static output loss versus dynamic innovation incentives
q.feedback: Patent policy can sacrifice static efficiency to encourage innovation.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: A domestic monopolist gains access to a larger export market. Which monopoly tool still determines total output?
options: Compare marginal revenue from available markets with marginal cost
Set price equal to world price in every case
Use average fixed cost alone
Produce where domestic demand equals MC only
q.feedback: Market expansion changes demand opportunities, but marginal analysis remains central.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Why is monopoly classified as a market-failure source in the standard model?
options: Every monopoly has negative profit
Market power can keep price above MC and block beneficial trades
One seller eliminates demand
Fixed cost is always socially wasteful
q.feedback: The output restriction prevents allocatively efficient exchange.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: How do barriers to entry connect monopoly structure to persistent economic profit?
options: They make total cost independent of output
They guarantee that the monopolist chooses the efficient quantity
They prevent new rivals from entering quickly when profit appears
They force demand to become perfectly elastic
q.feedback: Barriers can keep profit from triggering the entry response that erodes profit in competitive markets.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: Why does natural-monopoly cost structure often lead directly to a regulation question?
options: Regulation is needed only when a patent expires
Efficient scale may favor one supplier, yet that supplier still has market power over price and output
Natural monopolies always produce where price equals marginal cost without policy
Scale economies make demand perfectly elastic
q.feedback: Natural monopoly can make one-firm production cost-efficient while still creating a market-power problem.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: What happens to a patent-based barrier when the patent expires, holding other barriers constant?
options: Legal protection weakens and potential entry becomes easier
The firm’s marginal revenue becomes equal to price automatically
Demand shifts to zero
Average total cost must rise above price
q.feedback: Removing a legal barrier increases contestability even if the incumbent remains large.

labels: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.

q.q: How does the monopolist’s downward-sloping demand curve create the MR curve used for output choice?
options: Demand forces MR to equal MC at every quantity
The demand curve makes ATC horizontal
MR is simply the vertical distance between demand and MC
Selling more generally requires a lower price, so MR falls below price
q.feedback: The price effect from expanding sales makes marginal revenue lower than the price on demand.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: What does positive marginal revenue tell you about the portion of a monopolist’s demand curve?
options: Demand is perfectly inelastic at that output
Demand must have unit elasticity at every output
Demand is elastic at that output
Demand is inelastic at that output
q.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: Why does P = MR hold for a competitive firm but not for a single-price monopolist?
options: The monopolist’s average revenue is unrelated to price
The competitive firm can sell another unit at the unchanged market price, while the monopolist generally must lower price to expand sales
The monopolist has no demand curve
The competitive firm always has zero marginal cost
q.feedback: Price taking removes the price effect that drives monopoly MR below price.

labels: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.

q.q: How do monopoly revenue analysis and marginal cost combine into the output decision?
options: ATC determines quantity before revenue is considered
Price is chosen first and forces MR to equal MC
Demand generates MR, and the firm compares that MR with MC to choose quantity
Demand sets MC directly, so MR is unnecessary
q.feedback: The monopolist’s demand conditions determine MR; costs determine MC; their marginal comparison selects output.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: Why is monopoly price determined only after the profit-maximizing quantity is chosen?
options: Average total cost sets price before marginal analysis begins
The firm first uses MR and MC to choose output, then demand reveals the highest single price consistent with that output
Price is unrelated to demand until output is produced
The monopolist has no control over quantity
q.feedback: Monopoly analysis is a two-step decision: marginal output choice first, demand-based price second.

labels: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.

q.q: How does the MR = MC output rule connect to the firm’s profit-or-loss calculation?
options: Profit is known before quantity is chosen
The shutdown rule replaces MR=MC whenever the firm has market power
MR=MC identifies the best quantity; price from demand and ATC at that quantity determine profit or loss
ATC determines output first and MR then determines price
q.feedback: Output optimization and profit measurement are separate steps in monopoly analysis.

labels: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.

q.q: How does the monopolist’s MR=MC output choice create the welfare result P>MC?
options: Average total cost replaces demand in setting price
Market power makes willingness to pay irrelevant
MR lies below demand, so choosing Q where MR=MC typically leaves price on demand above MC
The firm sets price equal to MC and then raises output
q.feedback: The gap between demand price and MC at monopoly output is the link between firm optimization and allocative inefficiency.

labels: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.

q.q: How does declining ATC connect the natural-monopoly cost story to the case for one network rather than duplicated networks?
options: Serving the market through one larger network can avoid duplicative fixed infrastructure and lower average cost
Declining ATC makes price equal MR
It guarantees one firm will choose the efficient quantity without oversight
It eliminates fixed cost
q.feedback: Scale economies explain why breaking the firm into many duplicative networks may raise production cost.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: How does marginal-cost regulation connect monopoly policy to the competitive efficiency benchmark?
options: Both require P=ATC at every output
Both maximize monopoly profit
Both eliminate the need for demand
Both target P=MC so the last unit’s willingness to pay matches its marginal production cost
q.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing tries to reproduce the allocative condition associated with competitive equilibrium.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Why might a subsidy accompany marginal-cost pricing for a natural monopoly?
options: The subsidy makes demand horizontal
A subsidy prevents all entry barriers
P=MC can leave revenue below total cost when ATC exceeds MC
A subsidy is required because MR always exceeds price
q.feedback: The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: How does average-cost regulation trade some allocative efficiency for financial sustainability?
options: P=ATC makes marginal revenue equal price
P=ATC covers total cost, but price can remain above MC and output below the P=MC level
P=ATC forces the firm to price below MC
P=ATC eliminates all monopoly power
q.feedback: Average-cost pricing is a compromise between cost recovery and the P=MC efficiency benchmark.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: How can a well-designed price cap change a regulated monopolist’s cost incentives compared with simply reimbursing whatever costs it reports?
options: If the firm can keep some gains from lowering cost below the cap, it may have stronger cost-reduction incentives
A cap guarantees the firm will never invest
A cap automatically sets P=MC regardless of its level
A cap makes fixed costs irrelevant
q.feedback: Price-cap design can affect incentives to control cost, not just the allowed price.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: How does elasticity connect directly to third-degree discriminatory pricing?
options: Elasticity determines fixed cost rather than price
Elasticity matters only under perfect competition
Groups with less elastic demand can sustain larger markups over marginal cost
More elastic groups always pay more
q.feedback: Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: How does resale connect segmented pricing back toward a single price?
options: Resale guarantees first-degree discrimination
Arbitrage lets low-price buyers supply high-price buyers, eroding the price gap
Resale makes demand perfectly inelastic
Resale raises marginal cost only in the low-price market
q.feedback: Preventing resale is what allows separated prices to persist.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: How should welfare analysis of price discrimination differ from simply asking whether some buyers pay more?
options: Track how total output and total surplus change as well as how surplus is redistributed among buyers and the seller
Any price difference is automatically deadweight loss
Only monopoly profit matters for welfare
Consumer surplus alone always equals total surplus
q.feedback: Distribution and efficiency are separate questions; output changes can alter total surplus.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: How does perfect first-degree discrimination connect willingness to pay to the efficient-output condition?
options: The firm must stop where one common price equals MR
The firm ignores willingness to pay and charges ATC
The firm produces only where demand is unit elastic
The firm can sell units until the next buyer’s willingness to pay falls below MC
q.feedback: Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.

labels: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

q.q: Which characteristic most clearly distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition?
options: Firms must account for likely rival responses
Products are always identical
Firms can enter and exit the market freely.
Each firm is a price taker
q.feedback: Strategic interdependence is the defining behavioral feature of oligopoly.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: A duopoly is:
options: A monopoly with two products
An oligopoly with two firms
A market with two buyers
A perfectly competitive market
q.feedback: Duopoly is the two-firm special case of oligopoly.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: Products in an oligopoly may be:
options: Only standardized
Only differentiated products.
Standardized or differentiated
Always public goods
q.feedback: Oligopoly describes market structure, not a single product type.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: Why do barriers to entry matter in oligopoly?
options: They make incumbent firms price takers.
They eliminate strategic behavior
They guarantee identical costs
They help a few incumbent firms retain large market shares
q.feedback: Entry barriers help sustain concentration.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: A four-firm concentration ratio is calculated by:
options: Adding the market shares of the four largest firms
Squaring every firm’s market share
Averaging the four smallest firms
The sum of squared shares for every firm and competitive fringe participant
q.feedback: A concentration ratio sums selected leading shares.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: The HHI is calculated by:
options: Adding the four largest shares only
Summing squared market shares
Dividing market demand by firm count
Squaring the concentration ratio
q.feedback: HHI weights larger firms more heavily through squaring.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: Why does market definition matter when measuring concentration?
options: It fixes the number of firms that must be included at four.
It determines the legal price ceiling
Changing product or geographic boundaries changes which firms and sales are included
It makes strategic behavior disappear
q.feedback: Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: In game theory, a strategy is:
options: The payoff received by every player
The payoff a player receives after all firms choose.
The market concentration ratio
A possible action or plan available to a player
q.feedback: Strategies are the choices available to players.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: In a payoff pair written (8, 5), the first number usually belongs to:
options: The row player
The column player
Both players combined
The government
q.feedback: The standard stated order is row player first, column player second.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A best response is:
options: The strategy that maximizes the firms’ combined payoff.
The strategy producing the highest payoff given the rival’s action
Any strategy chosen first
The strategy with the lowest fixed cost
q.feedback: A best response is conditional on what the other player does.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A dominant strategy is one that:
options: The action associated with the highest payoff in one isolated cell only
Always gives both firms equal payoffs
Produces a higher payoff than the player’s alternatives for every rival action
Requires a written agreement
q.feedback: Dominance is a comparison across every possible rival action.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A Nash equilibrium occurs when:
options: The firms maximize joint profit
Both players receive equal payoffs
The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
Each player is choosing a best response to the other
q.feedback: No player can improve by changing alone.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: Why can a Nash equilibrium be inefficient?
options: Mutual best responses need not maximize joint payoff
Equilibrium requires zero profit
The government sets every payoff
The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
q.feedback: Individual incentives can lead to a jointly inferior outcome.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A prisoner’s dilemma describes a situation in which:
options: Cooperation is always stable
Individually attractive choices can make all players worse off
There is only one player
The jointly best outcome is always a Nash equilibrium.
q.feedback: The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: Collusion occurs when firms:
options: Independently choose the same price after a common cost shock.
Take price as given
Coordinate rather than compete independently
Sell only differentiated products
q.feedback: Collusion involves coordinated conduct.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: A cartel is:
options: A group of firms that happen to charge similar prices without coordinating.
A single price-taking firm
A market with free entry
A group of firms coordinating output or price
q.feedback: A cartel attempts to act collectively like a monopoly.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: A profit-maximizing cartel chooses total output where:
options: Industry marginal revenue equals industry marginal cost
Price equals average total cost
Market price equals industry marginal cost.
Each member’s price equals zero
q.feedback: The cartel uses the monopoly marginal rule for joint output.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: Why does a cartel member often want to cheat?
options: Cheating always raises joint profit
Selling extra output at the cartel price can raise its own profit
Cheating guarantees that other members keep cooperating forever.
Entry is impossible
q.feedback: Private incentives can conflict with the cartel’s collective restriction.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: Which factor makes cartel cheating harder?
options: More secret discounts
More substitute products
Reliable monitoring of member prices and output
A shorter expected relationship among cartel members.
q.feedback: Monitoring increases the chance that cheating is detected.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: Repeated interaction may support cooperation because:
options: Future punishment guarantees cooperation regardless of observability or credibility
It makes all threats credible
It removes entry barriers
Current cheating can trigger costly future punishment
q.feedback: Future consequences can change current incentives.

labels: Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

q.q: A threat is credible when:
options: Carrying it out remains in the threatening firm’s interest later
It is announced loudly
It would hurt only the rival
The announced response is credible because it sounds severe and harms the entrant
q.feedback: Credibility requires sequential rationality.

labels: Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

q.q: A price war is most likely to:
options: Guarantee higher profit for every firm
Reduce margins for several rival firms
Eliminate strategic interdependence
Create a monopoly immediately
q.feedback: Aggressive price cutting can damage all firms’ profits.

labels: Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

q.q: Tacit coordination differs from explicit collusion because tacit coordination:
options: Always involves a written contract
Occurs only when every firm charges exactly the same price.
Can occur without an explicit agreement
Requires identical products
q.feedback: Tacit coordination can arise through expectations and repeated conduct.

labels: Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

q.q: Price leadership occurs when:
options: The largest firm has legal authority to set every rival’s price.
The government guarantees the price
All firms become price takers
Other firms follow a price announced by a leading firm
q.feedback: Following can occur without formal control.

labels: Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

q.q: Nonprice competition includes competition through:
options: Quality, service, design, or advertising
Coordinating output quotas with rival firms.
Only lower posted prices
Only government licenses
q.feedback: Oligopolists often compete on several dimensions.

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

q.q: Limit pricing refers to:
options: Setting the monopoly price after entry occurs.
Keeping price low partly to discourage entry
A legal maximum price
Matching every rival’s advertising
q.feedback: The incumbent may sacrifice current profit to affect entry.

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

q.q: What does the kinked-demand model primarily attempt to explain?
options: How firms determine the original market price.
Why every oligopoly colludes
Price rigidity around an existing price
Why demand becomes vertical
q.feedback: The model explains rigidity, not the initial price.

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

q.q: Compared with competition, an effective cartel typically produces:
options: More output at a lower price
The same output at minimum ATC
Zero producer surplus
Less output at a higher price
q.feedback: A successful cartel mimics monopoly restriction.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: Why is high concentration not enough by itself to prove harmful conduct?
options: Entry conditions, efficiencies, imports, and actual behavior also matter
A high HHI guarantees high economic profit.
HHI measures only product quality
Every concentrated market is regulated
q.feedback: Concentration is evidence, not a complete conclusion.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: Which statement best captures oligopoly outcomes?
options: They always reproduce the monopoly outcome.
They can range from intense rivalry to substantial coordination
They always equal perfect competition
They are determined only by firm count
q.feedback: Rules, payoffs, timing, and repetition shape outcomes.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: Why does an oligopoly firm pay unusually close attention to a rival’s likely response before changing price?
options: Because a few large rivals can materially change the payoff from the firm’s decision
Because oligopoly firms are required to match every rival price change in order to remain in the market
Because oligopoly firms sell only identical products
Because market demand is perfectly elastic for each firm
q.feedback: With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: Which condition most helps a few established firms remain dominant in an oligopoly?
options: Perfectly free entry by many small firms
A requirement that every product be identical
A horizontal demand curve for each individual firm
Significant barriers that make entry difficult
q.feedback: Entry barriers help preserve a market in which a small number of firms account for much of total sales.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: A four-firm concentration ratio of 82% means that:
options: The HHI must equal 8200
Eighty-two firms control the market
The four largest firms together account for 82% of market sales
Each of the four largest firms individually controls 82% of total market sales
q.feedback: A concentration ratio adds the market shares of the specified number of largest firms.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: In a two-firm game, what does a payoff represent?
options: The slope of the industry demand curve
The outcome value a player receives from a particular combination of strategies
The maximum number of firms that regulators permit to enter the market under the industry’s legal rules
The market concentration ratio
q.feedback: A payoff records how well a player does under a particular combination of actions.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A payoff cell is written (14, 9), with Row’s payoff listed first. What is Column’s payoff?
q.feedback: With payoff order (Row, Column), the second number belongs to Column.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A best response is the action that:
options: Maximizes the two firms’ combined payoff regardless of incentives
Is chosen by every rival in the market
Always remains best no matter what the rival does
Gives a player the highest payoff given the rival’s chosen action
q.feedback: A best response is conditional on what the other player does; it need not be a dominant strategy.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: Which statement describes a Nash equilibrium?
options: Both players must have dominant strategies
No player earns positive profit
Each player is choosing a best response to the other player’s action
The two players necessarily choose the outcome that maximizes their combined payoff even if one could gain by deviating alone
q.feedback: At a Nash equilibrium, neither player can improve by changing action alone while the other action stays fixed.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A cartel that successfully coordinates output tries to behave most like:
options: A single profit-maximizing monopolist for the industry
A group of independent price-taking firms
A perfectly contestable market with free entry
A regulator that sets the market price equal to marginal cost and assigns output to each participating firm
q.feedback: A successful cartel restricts joint output and chooses the industry outcome that maximizes combined profit.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: Why can a cartel agreement be unstable even when all members gain from the agreement?
options: Every member must legally charge a different price
Cartels require marginal cost to equal zero
Joint profit is always lower under collusion than under competition because restricting output reduces total sales
An individual member may gain by secretly expanding sales while others keep output restricted
q.feedback: The group can prefer restriction while each member has a private incentive to capture extra sales.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: What does monitoring do for a cartel?
options: It makes each firm a price taker
It eliminates the need to restrict output
It helps members detect whether other members are cheating on the agreement
It guarantees that barriers to entry disappear once all cartel members can observe one another’s sales
q.feedback: Monitoring makes hidden deviations easier to discover and therefore easier to punish.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: In a one-shot prisoner’s-dilemma-style pricing game, why might both firms cut price even though both would prefer that neither cut?
options: Both firms face perfectly inelastic demand
Each firm has an individual incentive to cut given the rival’s possible action
The firms are maximizing total industry profit because the individually attractive price cut also maximizes their joint payoff
Price cuts are legally required
q.feedback: Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: Why can the expectation of future competition sometimes make cooperation easier to sustain?
options: Future interaction makes current payoffs irrelevant
Repeated games eliminate every incentive to cheat
Firms become price takers when they meet repeatedly
A firm that cheats today may lose future cooperative gains
q.feedback: When future interaction matters, the short-run gain from cheating can be weighed against future losses after retaliation.

labels: Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

q.q: What makes a strategic threat credible?
options: The threat was announced publicly
The threat would be costly to both firms
Carrying it out would be in the threatening firm’s interest if the situation actually occurred
The threat sounds severe to the rival
q.feedback: Credibility depends on whether the threatened response would actually be rational when the time comes to act.

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

q.q: Compared with a competitive outcome, an effective cartel usually chooses:
options: Lower output and a higher price
Higher output and a lower price
The same output with zero profit
Price equal to minimum average total cost
q.feedback: A cartel acts like a joint monopolist, restricting output to raise price and combined profit.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: Why is a high HHI not enough by itself to prove consumers are being harmed?
options: HHI directly measures consumer surplus
A high HHI guarantees prices equal marginal cost
HHI is unrelated to market shares
Concentration measures structure, while welfare also depends on conduct, entry conditions, efficiencies, and rivalry
q.feedback: Concentration is evidence about market structure, not a complete welfare verdict.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: If two firms merge and all other market shares remain unchanged, what happens to market concentration?
options: It cannot change unless market demand shifts
It becomes zero if the merged firm cuts price
It generally increases because two separate shares become one larger share
It must fall because there is one fewer firm
q.feedback: Combining shares raises concentration measures such as HHI, all else equal.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: A concentrated industry charges high markups but also spends heavily on research. What is the soundest conclusion?
options: Concentration always increases total surplus
There may be a tradeoff between market-power costs and innovation benefits that requires evidence
High research spending proves the market is efficient
High markups prove innovation has no value
q.feedback: Oligopoly welfare can involve competing effects rather than a one-variable verdict.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: What is the basic economic concern behind antitrust scrutiny of collusion?
options: Coordinated restriction of competition can raise price and reduce output below competitive levels
Collusion makes every firm a price taker
Collusion necessarily creates free entry
Collusion guarantees maximum consumer surplus
q.feedback: The core welfare concern is reduced rivalry that raises prices, restricts output, and can create deadweight loss.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: Why should an economist be cautious about predicting one outcome for every oligopoly market?
options: Every oligopoly has the same payoff matrix
Oligopoly theory assumes firms never respond to rivals
Market concentration fully determines every price
Different numbers of firms, products, information, costs, and strategic settings can produce different behavior
q.feedback: Oligopoly is a strategic family of models, not a guarantee that every few-firm market behaves identically.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: Which statement best summarizes why oligopoly welfare analysis can be complicated?
options: Only the number of firms matters for welfare
Oligopoly always produces the monopoly outcome
Few firms may create market power, but rivalry, innovation, efficiencies, and entry conditions also matter
Any market with four firms is automatically inefficient
q.feedback: A sound evaluation combines structure, strategic conduct, efficiency claims, and market responses.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: Four firms have market shares of 35%, 25%, 20%, and 10%, with the remaining firms holding 10%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
q.feedback: Add the shares of the four largest firms.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: A market has shares of 50%, 25%, 15%, and 10%. Which measure gives especially heavy weight to the 50% firm?

Average market share
Total revenue
HHI

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

35 points

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: A national market appears unconcentrated, but each rural town has only two local suppliers. What is the main lesson?

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: Two airlines choose whether to cut fares. Each earns more from cutting when the rival holds fares, but both earn less when both cut. This structure is closest to:

A natural monopoly

q.q: Row’s payoff is higher with strategy B whether Column chooses X or Y. What does Row have?

q.q: A cell is a Nash equilibrium when:

The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
It contains equal payoffs
Both firms chose the same letter
q.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A game has two outcomes in which both players are best responding. What does the game have?
options: No equilibrium
Two pure-strategy Nash equilibria
Two dominant strategies for each player
A unique prisoner’s dilemma
q.feedback: Games can have multiple equilibria.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

Free entry
Strategic interdependence
Accounting profit
q.feedback: The firm’s best action depends on the expected response.

q.q: A punishment strategy requires a rival to start a costly price war after cheating. When is the threat credible?

Whenever firms have identical products
When starting the price war is still the rival’s best response after cheating occurs
q.feedback: A threat must be rational when its decision node is reached.

Collusion becomes legal
q.feedback: A short horizon weakens the future cost of cheating.

labels: Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

Price leadership

A binding legal price floor
q.feedback: A leader’s announced price can become a focal point.

q.feedback: Common conditions can produce parallel conduct without agreement.

Automatically profitable

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

q.q: A firm maintains a lower price today to reduce expected entrant profit. What is the strategic cost?

It sacrifices some current profit
It eliminates marginal cost
It guarantees no future rivalry
q.feedback: Limit pricing trades current profit for possible entry deterrence.

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

q.q: In the kinked-demand model, rivals are assumed to match:

Every advertising campaign
Price cuts more readily than price increases
All capacity expansions

The demand kink disappears
The market becomes competitive
Price and output may remain unchanged

q.q: An effective cartel raises price and reduces output. Which part of lost consumer surplus is not transferred to producers?

Cartel profit
Fixed cost
Accounting revenue

Both increased market power and efficiencies must be evaluated
The merger must be blocked
HHI becomes irrelevant
q.feedback: Concentration and efficiency evidence both matter.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: A merger lowers marginal cost, but the merged firm keeps price high because rivalry weakens. What does this show?
options: Every efficiency improves consumer surplus
Lower cost removes market power
Cost savings need not be passed fully to consumers
Merger concentration cannot matter
q.feedback: Pass-through depends on competitive pressure.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

Foreign firms never affect price
HHI measures only domestic costs
Imports may provide substitutes that constrain domestic firms
q.feedback: Relevant competitors may include foreign suppliers.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price. This is:

Tacit collusion automatically
A concentration-ratio calculation
A shutdown decision
q.feedback: Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions.

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

Price competition may soften because firm demand becomes less elastic
Entry barriers disappear
Marginal revenue equals price
q.feedback: Loyalty can reduce substitution among brands.

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

q.q: A market has six firms, but two control 78% of sales and rivals closely watch one another. Which structure is most plausible?

Pure monopoly
Oligopoly
A nonmarket allocation
q.feedback: Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

options: Game theory assumes identical markets
Every oligopoly has one dominant strategy
Firm costs never matter
Payoffs, information, timing, and repetition differ
q.feedback: Strategic settings differ across industries.

labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: A grocery chain has only 8% of national grocery sales but 55% of sales in one isolated county. What does this example show about concentration measures?
options: They measure profit rather than market share
They depend on how the relevant market is defined
They are valid only for national markets
They ignore geographic differences and therefore always produce the same concentration result nationwide
q.feedback: The same firm can appear small or dominant depending on the economically relevant geographic and product market.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: Two markets each have a four-firm concentration ratio of 80%. In Market A the four firms have nearly equal shares; in Market B one firm is much larger than the other three. Which statement is most accurate?

Both markets must have the same HHI because an equal CR4 guarantees identical concentration among the leading firms
Market A must have the higher HHI because equal shares are squared
HHI cannot distinguish markets with the same CR4
q.feedback: Squaring market shares makes HHI more sensitive to a very large firm even when CR4 is unchanged.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: Three national wireless carriers dominate a market. Before one carrier cuts price, its managers estimate how the other two are likely to respond. Which feature of oligopoly is being illustrated?
options: Perfect information with no rivalry
Automatic collusion
Zero barriers to entry
Strategic interdependence
q.feedback: The payoff from one firm’s choice depends partly on how a small number of major rivals react.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: An industry’s HHI rises after two sizable firms merge. What can the HHI increase tell an analyst directly?

Market concentration increased under the chosen market definition
Consumer welfare necessarily fell
q.feedback: HHI measures concentration; welfare and policy conclusions require additional evidence about competition and efficiencies.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

Choose the low price
Choose the high price
Randomize because the payoffs differ

q.feedback: A dominant strategy gives the player a higher payoff for every action the rival might take.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

The first strategy is not dominant for A
q.feedback: Dominance requires the same strategy to be best against every rival action.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

The game has no strategic interdependence

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

A Nash equilibrium need not maximize combined payoff
Every Nash equilibrium is efficient
Coordination eliminates strategic incentives
q.feedback: Mutual best responses can lead to a stable outcome with lower total payoff than a cooperative alternative.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

Compare Column’s second-number payoffs across every column, regardless of which action Column has already chosen
Add both payoffs in every cell and choose the largest sum
Compare only the diagonal cells
q.feedback: A best-response calculation holds the rival action fixed and compares the player’s own payoff across its alternatives.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

Make price independent of demand

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
