labels: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

q.q: How can foreign suppliers weaken a domestic cartel?
options: Tariffs always lower cartel price
Imports provide alternative sources and can expand outside supply
World price eliminates strategic behavior
Foreign firms cannot enter
q.feedback: Outside supply can destabilize domestic coordination.

labels: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.

q.q: A market has four dominant firms. Which feature would most strongly distinguish oligopoly from monopoly or perfect competition?
options: Assume four dominant firms automatically mean monopolistic competition because any market with multiple sellers and differentiated products fits that model
Classify the market only by whether products are identical
Treat every concentrated market as a legal monopoly
Focus on few-firm strategic interdependence rather than requiring one firm or many tiny price takers
q.feedback: Oligopoly sits between monopoly and atomistic competition because a few large firms interact strategically.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: A student already understands market shares. What extra step turns those shares into an HHI?
options: Average the two largest shares
Multiply each firm's market share by the market price and add the resulting dollar values across firms
Square each firm’s percentage share and add the squared shares
Add only the four largest shares
q.feedback: HHI builds on market shares by squaring each percentage share and summing across firms.

labels: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.

q.q: Before trying to find a Nash equilibrium in a payoff matrix, what should a student verify first?
options: Whether the market’s concentration measure is high enough to imply that strategic behavior must be present
Whether both players earn equal payoffs
Which payoff belongs to each player and which actions define the rows and columns
Which cell has the highest combined payoff
q.feedback: Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A student keeps searching for one action that is always best, but the player’s preferred action changes with the rival’s move. What concept should the student use?
options: A guaranteed dominant strategy
Conditional best responses
Market concentration
Joint-profit maximization only
q.feedback: Best responses can vary with the rival’s action even when no dominant strategy exists.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A student has correctly found a player’s best response in each column. How should the student check for a dominant strategy?
options: See whether the same action is the best response in every column
Add the two players’ payoffs in each cell
Choose the action with the highest single payoff anywhere in the matrix
Look only at the rival’s payoffs
q.feedback: A dominant strategy must remain the player’s best response to every rival action.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: After marking each player’s best responses in a matrix, what identifies a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
options: The cell with the largest total payoff even if someone wants to deviate
Any cell where the payoffs are equal
The first cell in which one player has a dominant strategy
A cell where both players’ best-response markings coincide
q.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses in the same outcome cell.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A student found the cell with the largest combined payoff and calls it the Nash equilibrium. What must still be checked?
options: Whether the firms have equal market shares
Whether the cell lies on the main diagonal
Whether each player would choose to stay there given the other player’s action
Whether the two payoffs are both positive and add to more than the payoffs in every neighboring cell
q.feedback: Joint-payoff maximization and Nash stability are separate questions.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: How does a noncooperative game differ from an assumed cartel solution?
options: The government chooses each firm’s strategy
Each firm follows its own incentives rather than committing to maximize joint profit
The firms necessarily choose identical actions because noncooperative behavior rules out different strategies
The firms ignore rivals completely
q.feedback: Noncooperative analysis asks what individually rational strategies imply without assuming binding joint-profit coordination.

labels: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.

q.q: A student understands a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma. What new consideration enters when the firms expect to interact again?
options: Market concentration falls with each round
Today’s action can change future responses and future payoffs
The payoff matrix no longer matters at all
Every cooperative promise becomes binding
q.feedback: Repeated interaction links current choices to future rewards or punishments, which can alter incentives.

labels: Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

q.q: A student knows that talk alone may not deter entry. What can make an incumbent’s announced response more believable?
options: A costly action taken in advance that changes the incumbent’s future incentives
A vague promise that entry will be punished somehow
A larger concentration ratio by itself
A public statement with no change in capacity or costs
q.feedback: A commitment can make future behavior credible by changing what the incumbent will find profitable after entry.

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

q.q: A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes. What is the next step when firms compete through quality or advertising instead?
options: Ignore rivals because only prices create interdependence
Apply the same strategic logic to nonprice actions because rivals may respond there too
Assume nonprice choices have no effect on demand
Treat advertising as proof of collusion
q.feedback: Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price.

labels: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.

q.q: Which condition is most consistent with perfect competition?
options: Many small firms sell an identical product
One firm controls a unique product
A few firms coordinate prices
Each seller offers a heavily differentiated brand
q.feedback: Perfect competition has many small sellers and a standardized product.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: A perfectly competitive firm is called a price taker because:
options: It is legally forbidden to change output
Its individual output is too small to affect the market price
It sets the price for all firms
It faces no production costs
q.feedback: The market determines price; one small firm cannot move it.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: Which decision remains for a price-taking firm?
options: What market price to impose
How to block all entry
How much output to produce
Which rival to acquire
q.feedback: The firm accepts price but chooses quantity.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: The demand curve facing an individual competitive firm is:
options: The same downward-sloping curve as market demand
Vertical at the market quantity
Upward sloping because cost rises
Horizontal at the market price
q.feedback: The firm can sell its feasible output at the given price.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: Market demand differs from the individual firm’s demand because market demand is:
options: Downward sloping while firm demand is horizontal
Horizontal while firm demand slopes downward
Vertical while firm demand is horizontal
Identical to firm demand
q.feedback: The market determines price; the small firm takes it.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: For a competitive firm, average revenue equals:
options: Average total cost
The market price
Marginal cost
Economic profit
q.feedback: AR=TR/Q=P.

labels: Calculate and interpret total, average, and marginal revenue for a competitive firm.

q.q: For a competitive firm, marginal revenue equals:
options: Average fixed cost
Total revenue
The market price
Accounting profit
q.feedback: Each additional unit sells at the constant market price.

labels: Calculate and interpret total, average, and marginal revenue for a competitive firm.

q.q: If price is $12 and the firm sells 20 units, total revenue is:
q.feedback: TR=P×Q.

labels: Calculate and interpret total, average, and marginal revenue for a competitive firm.

q.q: Which relationship holds for a price-taking firm?
options: P = AR = MR
P = ATC = AFC at every output
MR falls below price as output rises
AR equals total cost
q.feedback: Constant price makes average and marginal revenue equal to price.

labels: Calculate and interpret total, average, and marginal revenue for a competitive firm.

q.q: For a competitive firm, economic profit is calculated as:
options: Price minus marginal cost
Total revenue minus total economic cost
Total revenue minus variable cost only
Average revenue minus quantity
q.feedback: Economic profit subtracts all explicit and implicit costs.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost for the next unit, the firm should:
options: Decrease output
Shut down immediately
Increase output
Raise the market price
q.feedback: The unit adds more revenue than cost.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: For the next unit of output, marginal cost is greater than marginal revenue. Producing that unit would:
options: Increase profit
Leave profit unchanged
Set the market price
Reduce profit
q.feedback: The unit adds more cost than revenue.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: The standard output rule for a competitive firm is to produce where:
options: MR equals MC on the rising portion of MC
Price equals ATC at every output
AFC is minimized
Total revenue is zero
q.feedback: The relevant MR=MC crossing lies on rising MC.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Why is the rising-MC condition important?
options: It guarantees zero fixed cost
A falling-MC crossing need not be a profit maximum
It makes demand slope downward
It causes market entry
q.feedback: Profit is maximized at the crossing where MC rises through MR.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: If price exceeds ATC at the chosen output, the firm earns:
options: Zero economic profit
A shutdown loss
Positive economic profit
Negative total revenue
q.feedback: P>ATC creates positive profit per unit.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: If price equals ATC at the chosen output, the firm earns:
options: Zero accounting revenue
A loss equal to fixed cost
Maximum monopoly profit
Zero economic profit
q.feedback: P=ATC is the break-even condition.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: If price is below ATC but above AVC at the chosen output, the firm should generally:
options: Produce in the short run while earning a loss
Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
Exit immediately and erase fixed cost
Raise price above the market
q.feedback: Covering AVC and some fixed cost reduces the short-run loss.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: The short-run shutdown rule compares price with:
options: Average total cost
Average variable cost
Average fixed cost
Total revenue
q.feedback: Variable cost is avoidable in the short run.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: The shutdown price is the minimum of:
options: ATC
AFC
AVC
MR
q.feedback: The minimum AVC is the threshold for short-run operation.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: If a firm shuts down in the short run, its fixed cost:
options: Falls to zero
Becomes marginal revenue
Turns into variable cost
Still remains
q.feedback: Short-run fixed cost is unavoidable even at zero output.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Short-run shutdown differs from long-run exit because exit:
options: Removes the firm from the industry and avoids all future costs
Leaves all fixed costs forever
Occurs whenever P is below ATC for one day
Means the firm produces at minimum AVC
q.feedback: Exit is the long-run industry decision.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: The competitive firm’s short-run supply curve is:
options: The entire ATC curve
The portion of MC at or above AVC
The horizontal demand curve
The portion of MC below AVC
q.feedback: Below AVC the firm shuts down rather than supplies along MC.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: Market supply in a competitive industry is found by:
options: Vertically summing firms’ prices
Using one firm’s ATC curve
Horizontally summing firms’ quantities supplied at each price
Adding total revenues
q.feedback: At each price, add quantities across firms.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: Short-run economic profit tends to attract:
options: Immediate shutdown
A fall in market supply
A permanent increase in profit
Entry in the long run
q.feedback: Entry expands market supply and erodes profit.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Persistent economic losses tend to cause:
options: Exit in the long run
Entry
A permanent fall in supply price with more firms
Zero fixed cost immediately
q.feedback: Exit contracts market supply and helps remove losses.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: In long-run competitive equilibrium, firms earn:
options: Zero accounting profit necessarily
Zero economic profit
A permanent positive economic profit
A loss equal to fixed cost
q.feedback: Entry and exit eliminate economic profit and loss.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Zero economic profit means the firm covers:
options: Only variable costs
No owner compensation
All explicit and implicit opportunity costs
Only fixed cost
q.feedback: Normal profit is included among implicit costs.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Productive efficiency occurs when a firm produces at:
options: P = MC regardless of ATC
Minimum AVC only
Maximum total revenue
Minimum ATC
q.feedback: Minimum ATC is the lowest feasible per-unit cost.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Allocative efficiency occurs when:
options: Price equals marginal cost
Price equals average fixed cost
Economic profit is positive
Market demand is horizontal
q.feedback: P reflects marginal benefit and MC reflects marginal cost.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Perfect competition is best understood as:
options: A literal description of every farm or stock market
A benchmark model for studying price taking and efficiency
A model in which firms never choose output
A guarantee of equal incomes
q.feedback: The model is an analytical benchmark with strong assumptions.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What market price does the competitive firm take as given?
q.feedback: The horizontal P = MR = AR line is at $30.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Where does the $30 MR line meet rising MC, identifying the profit-maximizing quantity?
options: 20 units
50 units
30 units
70 units
q.feedback: The relevant rising MC curve meets P = MR at Q = 50.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing output, what is average total cost?
q.feedback: At Q = 50, the ATC guide is $20.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does the firm operate?
options: 50 units
25 units
75 units
100 units
q.feedback: P = MR intersects rising MC at Q = 50.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 50, what relationship holds between price and ATC?
options: P = $15 and ATC = $25
P = ATC = $25
P = $25 and ATC = $15
P exceeds ATC by $10
q.feedback: The price line passes through ATC at $25.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Where does the $30 MR line meet rising MC, identifying the firm’s output in the loss-but-operate case?
options: 20 units
40 units
30 units
60 units
q.feedback: The horizontal price line meets rising MC at Q = 30.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What market price does the firm face?
q.feedback: The P = MR = AR line is at $30.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What price is shown by the horizontal P = MR = AR line?
q.feedback: The horizontal price line is at $10.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which labeled point marks the minimum of AVC?
options: Point B
Point C
Point D
Point A
q.feedback: MC crosses AVC at its minimum at point A.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Given the price, what is the firm’s short-run output?
options: 0 units
22 units
44 units
50 units
q.feedback: The $10 price lies below minimum AVC, so the firm shuts down and supplies zero.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What market-clearing price is determined by the intersection of market supply and demand?
q.feedback: Market supply and demand intersect at a price of $40.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The market panel settles at $40. Reading across to the firm panel, which quantity is selected where MR meets rising MC?
options: 40 units
75 units
100 units
90 units
q.feedback: On the firm panel, P = MR = $40 meets rising MC at Q = 90.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. In the paired loss case, what price is transmitted from the market equilibrium to the representative firm?
q.feedback: Market supply and demand intersect at $15.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. With the market equilibrium price at $15, where does the firm panel place the MR–MC output choice?
options: 15 units
50 units
75 units
100 units
q.feedback: The firm’s P = MR line meets rising MC at Q = 50.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. In the market panel where equilibrium quantity is 100, what equilibrium price is shown?
q.feedback: Market supply and demand intersect at $25.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the long-run market price of $25, which firm quantity lies at the rising-MC intersection?
options: 25 units
75 units
100 units
50 units
q.feedback: The firm’s horizontal MR line meets MC at Q = 50.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: A competitive firm has price $18 and ATC $15 at its chosen output. Economic profit per unit is:
q.feedback: Profit per unit equals price minus average total cost.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A firm sells 40 units at $12 and has ATC of $9. Total economic profit is:
q.feedback: Total profit equals (P − ATC) × Q = $3 × 40.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: At a competitive firm’s chosen output, price equals ATC. The firm is:
options: Earning a loss equal to fixed cost
Breaking even with zero economic profit
Earning positive economic profit
Required to shut down
q.feedback: When P = ATC, total revenue equals total economic cost.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A firm has price $14 and ATC $17 at its chosen output. Its economic loss per unit is:
q.feedback: Loss per unit is ATC minus price when ATC exceeds price.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A firm produces 25 units, receives $10 per unit, and has ATC of $12. Total economic loss is:

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Which statement is true when a competitive firm earns zero economic profit?
options: Accounting profit must also be zero because economic and accounting costs are identical in competition
The firm must leave the industry immediately
Economic cost already includes normal profit to owner-supplied resources
The owner receives no return of any kind
q.feedback: Zero economic profit means revenues cover explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A competitive firm should shut down in the short run when price is:
options: Below minimum AVC
Below minimum ATC but above AVC
Above marginal cost
Equal to average fixed cost
q.feedback: If price cannot cover variable cost, producing makes the short-run loss larger than shutting down.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A firm has P = $14, AVC = $10, and ATC = $18 at its best positive output. In the short run it should:
options: Shut down because P is below ATC
Exit the industry immediately
Raise price to $18
Produce even though it has an economic loss
q.feedback: Price covers variable cost and contributes toward fixed cost, so producing minimizes the short-run loss.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Which statement best distinguishes shutdown from exit?
options: Shutdown occurs only when economic profit is positive
Exit refers only to reducing one unit of output
Shutdown is a short-run zero-output decision; exit is a long-run decision to leave the industry
Shutdown and exit are identical because both set output to zero and permanently remove the firm from the market
q.feedback: A firm can temporarily shut down while fixed commitments remain, whereas exit changes long-run industry participation.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: For a competitive firm, the short-run supply curve is the portion of:
options: ATC at and above minimum AVC
AVC below minimum ATC
AFC above minimum MC
MC at and above minimum AVC
q.feedback: The firm follows rising MC when operating and supplies zero below the shutdown price.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: If market price rises and the competitive firm remains open, the firm typically moves:
options: Along a horizontal MC curve by assumption
To zero output because price changed
Up along its rising MC curve to a larger quantity
Down its ATC curve with no output change
q.feedback: Since P = MR, a higher price intersects rising MC at a larger output.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: A rise in a firm’s fixed property tax, with variable costs unchanged, does what to its short-run supply curve?
options: Makes it vertical
Leaves it unchanged
Shifts it left because MC rises
Shifts it right because AVC falls
q.feedback: Fixed cost does not change MC or AVC, so the firm’s short-run supply schedule is unchanged.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: A wage increase raises the variable cost of producing each unit. Other things equal, the firm’s short-run supply tends to:
options: Shift left/up as MC rises
Shift right because fixed cost is spread out
Stay unchanged because wages are not marginal costs
Become perfectly elastic
q.feedback: Higher variable input costs raise MC and reduce quantity supplied at each price.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: To construct market supply from individual competitive firms, economists:
options: Vertically adding each firm’s prices at one quantity
Using the output of the largest firm only
Adding market demand to one firm’s MC curve
Add the quantities each firm supplies at the same price
q.feedback: Industry quantity supplied is the sum of firm quantities at the same market price.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: Below the firm’s shutdown price, its short-run quantity supplied is:
options: The quantity where P = ATC
Always one unit
Zero
The quantity at minimum ATC
q.feedback: Below minimum AVC, the firm minimizes loss by shutting down.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: At a price of $20, each of 50 identical firms supplies 8 units. Market quantity supplied is:
options: 8 units
400 units
58 units
160 units
q.feedback: Market supply adds the 8 units supplied by each of 50 firms: 50 × 8 = 400.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: Which change is most likely to leave a competitive firm’s short-run supply unchanged?
options: A higher fixed annual permit fee
A higher hourly wage
A higher price for raw materials
A per-unit production tax
q.feedback: Fixed-cost changes do not alter the firm’s MC or AVC schedule.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: Persistent positive economic profit in a competitive industry tends to encourage:
options: Entry of new firms
Exit of existing firms
A permanent price increase with no supply response
Government price setting
q.feedback: Positive economic profit attracts resources and firms when entry is available.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Persistent economic losses in a competitive industry tend to encourage:
options: Entry of new firms
Permanent expansion of industry supply
Higher fixed cost by itself
Exit of firms
q.feedback: Long-run losses push resources toward better alternatives.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: In the standard long-run competitive equilibrium, economic profit is:
options: Always equal to accounting profit
Equal to total revenue
Zero
Always positive
q.feedback: Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Zero economic profit means the firm is earning:
options: A monopoly rent
A normal return included in economic cost
No accounting profit and no return to the owner
A loss equal to fixed cost
q.feedback: Normal profit compensates owner resources for their opportunity cost and is included in economic cost.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: When firms enter a competitive industry, market supply generally:
options: Increases
Decreases
Becomes vertical
Equals market demand at every price
q.feedback: More firms contribute output at each price, shifting market supply right.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Several firms permanently leave a competitive industry. Holding the remaining firms’ cost schedules fixed, market supply:
options: Increases
Becomes perfectly elastic automatically
Stops responding to price
Decreases
q.feedback: Fewer firms supply the market, shifting industry supply left.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: In a constant-cost competitive industry, industry expansion leaves input prices and firms’ cost curves essentially unchanged. The long-run industry supply curve is typically:
options: Downward sloping
Vertical
Horizontal
Upward sloping
q.feedback: If expansion does not change input costs, the long-run equilibrium price can return to the original cost level.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: If industry expansion bids up specialized input prices, the industry is best described as:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Increasing-cost
Constant-cost
Decreasing-cost
q.feedback: Higher input prices raise firms’ costs as the industry expands.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: If industry expansion leads to cheaper specialized suppliers and lower unit costs, the industry may be:
options: Decreasing-cost
Increasing-cost
Constant-cost by definition
Unable to have entry
q.feedback: Industry growth can lower firm costs when external economies develop.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A permanent demand increase in a competitive industry usually creates what first?
options: Immediate zero economic profit with no price change
Immediate exit of firms
A permanent shutdown of incumbents
A short-run price and profit increase before entry completes
q.feedback: Demand changes first affect the existing set of firms; entry is a long-run response.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Which condition best supports a constant-cost industry?
options: Industry growth creates supplier efficiencies that lower costs
Firms are legally prevented from entering
The industry can expand without materially changing the prices of its inputs
Every new firm makes a key input scarcer and more expensive
q.feedback: Constant-cost means industry size does not materially shift representative firms’ cost curves.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Allocative efficiency in the competitive benchmark is associated with:
options: P = MC
P = AVC
P = AFC
TR = fixed cost
q.feedback: Price reflects marginal willingness to pay while MC reflects marginal opportunity cost.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Productive efficiency for a competitive firm is associated with producing at:
options: Minimum AVC regardless of price
Maximum total cost
The highest possible output
Minimum ATC
q.feedback: Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A competitive firm faces price $18. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $6, $9, $12, $16, $20, $25. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
options: 3 units
5 units
4 units

Only total fixed cost

Its ATC becomes the market supply curve
q.feedback: The market price change is transmitted to the firm as a change in MR, producing movement along its supply curve.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

Exit raises supply and lowers price
q.feedback: Long-run exit contracts industry supply and raises the market price relative to the loss-making situation.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A firm has positive accounting profit but zero economic profit in long-run competitive equilibrium. How can both be true?

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Demand for an industry rises permanently. As firms enter, specialized suppliers expand and input costs fall. What long-run outcome is consistent with a decreasing-cost industry?

q.feedback: External cost reductions can shift firms’ costs down as the industry grows.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Why is P = MC important for competitive allocative efficiency?
options: It means every firm earns positive economic profit
It makes all fixed costs disappear
The value buyers place on the last unit matches the opportunity cost of producing it
It guarantees equal incomes across consumers
q.feedback: At P = MC, the marginal benefit reflected by price equals marginal resource cost.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A representative competitive firm is in long-run equilibrium at the minimum point of ATC. What efficiency idea does that condition illustrate most directly?

Income equality

q.feedback: Producing at minimum ATC uses the least-cost scale available to the firm in the benchmark.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Which observation is a limitation of using perfect competition as a literal description of many real markets?

Consumers never care about product differences
q.feedback: The competitive model is a benchmark; many real markets relax one or more of its assumptions.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A competitive allocation maximizes total surplus under the benchmark assumptions, but one household receives very little income. What does this illustrate?

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A firm graph shows the price line above ATC at the rising-MC intersection. Which sequence is correct?

Produce in the short run and incur a loss
Earn positive profit because price exceeds AVC

Exit with zero fixed cost immediately
Shut down and bear fixed cost
Raise price to ATC

q.q: On a competitive firm graph, price is tangent to minimum ATC and intersects rising MC there. The firm earns:

An economic loss while producing above the minimum point of average total cost
Zero accounting profit while producing where price exceeds marginal cost
Zero economic profit and produces productively efficiently

q.q: Refer to the paired market and firm graph and compare the firm’s price line with ATC at the rising-MC intersection. Suppose the displayed position followed a rise in buyer demand from an initial zero-profit equilibrium, before any entry and with firm cost curves unchanged. Which transmission from the market explains the displayed firm outcome?
options: Its horizontal MR line rises, it expands output along MC, and economic profit increases
Its MC shifts down, so it can expand while its MR line stays fixed
Its horizontal MR line falls because more buyers enter the market
Its output stays fixed because a price taker cannot respond to price
q.feedback: Market demand raises the equilibrium price. The firm takes that price as P = MR, so the higher horizontal line intersects rising MC at more output. With unchanged costs and initial zero profit, it can earn positive short-run profit before entry responds.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: A competitive firm’s MC curve crosses the price line twice. Which crossing is relevant?
options: The crossing on falling MC
The crossing on rising MC
Both crossings create identical maxima
Neither because output is chosen at minimum ATC
q.feedback: The second-order condition requires MC to rise through MR.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: A graph shows MC below AVC for low quantities. Why is that MC segment not part of short-run supply?
options: Prices on that segment exceed the profit-maximizing threshold for every firm
Prices on that segment equal average total cost but remain below marginal cost
Prices on that segment are below the shutdown threshold
Prices on that segment allow production because they exceed average variable cost
q.feedback: The firm shuts down when price is below minimum AVC.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: After entry, the market supply curve shifts right and the firm price line falls. Why does entry stop?

All firms shut down
Marginal revenue becomes downward sloping
Economic profit is driven to zero

q.q: After exit, market supply shifts left and the remaining firm’s price line rises. Why does exit stop?

q.q: A competitive firm initially faces a market price of $30 and sells 80 units. A market-wide demand decrease lowers the price to $26. Holding the firm’s output at 80 units only for comparison, which statement is correct?

AR stays at $30 because the firm is a price taker
The firm can keep charging $30 if its costs have not changed
The firm’s AR and MR both fall by $4, and total revenue falls by $320

q.q: A competitive firm is currently producing where its own cost conditions make 50 units optimal. Industry entry then lowers the market price. Which change occurs before the firm chooses a new output?

The firm’s horizontal demand and MR lines shift downward to the new market price
The firm rotates its demand curve downward while MR stays fixed

q.q: A competitive industry has 40 identical firms. At a price of $25, each initially supplies 12 units. Higher energy costs reduce each firm’s supply at that price to 9 units. With unchanged market demand and no entry, equilibrium price then rises to $28. At its new MR = MC quantity of 10 units, a firm has ATC $30 and AVC $21. Which assessment is correct?

Market supply shifted right; the firm earns $70 economic profit
Market supply shifted left; the firm shuts down because P is below ATC
Market supply stayed fixed; the firm earns $30 economic profit

At the new optimum, profit is (28 - 30) × 10 = -$20; price still exceeds AVC, so the firm operates. A cost shock can raise market price while reducing profit; the profit result requires the stated cost comparison.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: A learner chooses the output with the lowest ATC as the profit-maximizing quantity. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Choose output where AFC is minimized
Choose output where total revenue is smallest
Choose output using MR and MC; minimum ATC answers a different question
Choose the largest feasible output instead because spreading fixed cost always maximizes profit
q.feedback: Productive efficiency and profit maximization are distinct decisions.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: A learner computes profit per unit as ATC − P when P exceeds ATC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Use MC − MR
Use P − ATC for profit per unit
Use P − AVC for economic profit per unit
Use TR − TC without dividing by quantity and call it per-unit profit
q.feedback: When price exceeds ATC, the vertical gap P − ATC is profit per unit.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A learner reports $5 of total profit because P − ATC = $5 and the firm sells 60 units. What is missing?
options: Multiply the $5 per-unit profit by 60 units
Subtract fixed cost a second time
Multiply price by ATC
Use only the last unit’s marginal cost
q.feedback: The price-ATC gap is per unit; total profit requires multiplying by quantity.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A learner says P = ATC means the firm has no accounting profit and no return to the owner. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: P = ATC means the firm is shutting down because covering total cost leaves no reason to produce
P = ATC means marginal revenue is zero
P = ATC guarantees an accounting loss
P = ATC means zero economic profit; normal profit is included in economic cost
q.feedback: Economic cost includes implicit opportunity costs, including the normal return needed to keep owner resources in the firm.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A learner sees P < ATC and concludes the firm must shut down. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Shutdown depends on P versus AFC
Losses matter only in the long run
P < ATC establishes an economic loss, but shutdown depends on P versus AVC
Any economic loss requires immediate shutdown even when the market price still covers variable cost
q.feedback: Profit/loss measurement and the short-run shutdown decision use different comparisons.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A learner uses P < ATC as the shutdown rule. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Compare MR with total fixed cost
Any loss means shutdown
Compare price with AVC for shutdown; ATC determines profit or loss
Compare price with AFC for shutdown
q.feedback: The firm may rationally produce at a loss if price covers variable cost.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A learner says producing at a loss is irrational under any circumstances. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Fixed cost is avoidable whenever profit is negative
In the short run, producing can reduce the loss when price covers AVC and contributes to fixed cost
A firm should produce whenever price is positive
Losses disappear if output rises enough
q.feedback: The relevant comparison is the loss from producing versus the fixed-cost loss from shutting down.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A learner says shutting down eliminates all costs immediately. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Short-run fixed costs remain even when output is zero
Shutdown makes fixed cost become variable
The firm earns zero economic profit when shut down
Shutdown raises average fixed cost to zero
q.feedback: Shutdown avoids variable production cost but does not erase fixed commitments in the short run.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A learner treats a one-month shutdown as permanent industry exit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Exit is the short-run version of shutdown
A shut-down firm has no fixed cost
Only profitable firms can exit
Shutdown can be temporary; exit means leaving the industry in the long run
q.feedback: Time horizon separates the temporary operating decision from long-run participation.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A learner labels the entire MC curve as the firm’s short-run supply curve. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Use MC only below minimum AVC
Use average fixed cost above its minimum
Use only the rising MC portion at and above minimum AVC
Use the entire ATC curve instead
q.feedback: Below minimum AVC the firm shuts down rather than supplying the MC-indicated positive quantity.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: A learner shifts short-run supply left after a fixed-cost increase. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Supply shifts right because firms spread the cost
Fixed cost changes ATC and profit, not MC or AVC, so short-run supply does not shift
Any cost increase must shift MC
Fixed cost lowers market demand
q.feedback: The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: A learner adds firms’ supply prices vertically to build market supply. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: At each price, add the quantities supplied across firms horizontally
At each quantity, add firms’ fixed costs
Use only the median firm’s output
Add market demand to firm supply
q.feedback: Market supply sums how much all firms supply at a common market price.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: A learner says a higher wage cannot shift supply because the firm is a price taker. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Price-taking means the market price is given, so input-cost changes affect profit but not the firm's marginal cost curve
A higher wage changes average fixed cost because labor payments become fixed after the firm hires its workers
A wage increase changes the firm's demand curve by raising the price required to cover its labor costs
Price taking fixes the output price, not the firm’s costs; a wage increase can raise MC and shift supply
q.feedback: Competitive firms take price as given but still respond to changes in production costs.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: A learner says positive economic profit causes existing firms to raise the market price. What is the long-run repair?
options: Profit causes exit, which raises price
Each firm can raise price independently because profit is positive
Economic profit has no effect on industry size
Profit attracts entry, which increases market supply and tends to lower price
q.feedback: In competition, the adjustment occurs through entry and market supply, not unilateral price setting.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A learner says loss-making competitive firms can remain forever with no industry adjustment. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Losses shift demand right automatically
Long-run fixed costs prevent any firm from leaving
Persistent losses encourage exit when firms can leave in the long run
Losses guarantee new entry
q.feedback: Long-run mobility lets resources leave industries that do not cover opportunity cost.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A learner says every competitive industry has a horizontal long-run supply curve. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Long-run supply depends only on market demand
A horizontal curve requires monopoly power
Horizontal long-run supply is the constant-cost case; other cost conditions can slope up or down
Competition always makes long-run supply vertical
q.feedback: The slope depends on how industry expansion affects input costs and firms’ cost curves.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A learner says entry can never raise production costs because each firm is a price taker. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Competitive firms do not buy inputs
Industry expansion can bid up shared input prices even though firms take output price as given
Price-taking firms also take every input price as permanently fixed
Entry always creates economies that lower cost
q.feedback: Output-market price taking does not prevent industry growth from affecting input markets.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A learner interprets a downward-sloping long-run industry supply curve as a violation of competition. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: It can arise when industry expansion lowers firms’ costs through external economies
It proves firms are colluding
It means demand is perfectly elastic
It means firms are operating below AVC
q.feedback: A decreasing-cost industry can remain competitive while industry growth reduces input or supplier costs.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A learner says productive efficiency and allocative efficiency are the same condition. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Productive efficiency requires monopoly pricing
Allocative efficiency means every firm earns positive profit
Productive efficiency concerns minimum ATC; allocative efficiency concerns P = MC
Both require only P = AVC
q.feedback: The two efficiency concepts answer different questions: least-cost production versus whether marginal value equals marginal cost.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A competitive firm uses which cost curve to decide whether another unit should be produced?
options: Average fixed cost
Total fixed cost
Marginal cost
Accounting profit
q.feedback: The incremental output decision compares MR with MC.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Which average cost determines profit per unit after output is chosen?
options: Average variable cost
Average fixed cost
Marginal revenue
Average total cost
q.feedback: Profit per unit=P−ATC.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Which average cost determines the short-run shutdown threshold?
options: Average variable cost
Average total cost
Average fixed cost
Long-run average cost
q.feedback: AVC represents avoidable cost in the short run.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Why does a fixed-cost increase not change short-run competitive output?
options: It lowers MR
It does not change MC or AVC
It changes market demand
It eliminates ATC
q.feedback: Output and shutdown depend on marginal and variable costs.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Zero economic profit includes which owner return?
options: No return at all
Only accounting depreciation
Normal profit
Consumer surplus
q.feedback: Normal profit covers entrepreneurial opportunity cost.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: How is a competitive firm’s supply response connected to cost?
options: It follows ATC below AVC
It equals horizontal demand
It follows AFC
It follows rising MC above AVC
q.feedback: MC gives the additional cost of supply.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: What converts individual competitive firm supplies into market supply?
options: Horizontal summation at each price
Vertical summation of prices
Averaging ATC curves
Adding market demands
q.feedback: Add firm quantities supplied at each price.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: Entry affects market supply by:
options: Moving upward along the same supply curve
Shifting it to the right
Shifting demand right
Making it horizontal by definition
q.feedback: More firms supply more total output at each price.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: Exit affects market supply by:
options: Shifting demand left
Moving down firm ATC
Shifting it to the left
Raising every firm’s fixed cost
q.feedback: Fewer firms reduce total quantity supplied.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A competitive firm should expand output while:
options: ATC exceeds AVC
Price exceeds total revenue
AFC is falling
MR exceeds MC
q.feedback: Marginal benefit to the firm exceeds marginal cost.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: The last profitable unit in a discrete table is the last unit with:
options: MR at least as large as MC
ATC equal to AVC
TR equal to fixed cost
Price below AVC
q.feedback: The next unit would reduce profit once MC exceeds MR.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Why is the rising-MC crossing used?
options: It minimizes AFC
It is the crossing where moving beyond the output makes MC exceed MR
It sets market demand
It eliminates fixed cost
q.feedback: The local profit maximum occurs where MC rises through MR.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: Why is P=MC associated with allocative efficiency?
options: Profit is always zero
ATC is necessarily minimized
The marginal buyer’s value equals the marginal unit’s cost
Consumer surplus equals producer surplus
q.feedback: The last unit’s marginal benefit equals marginal cost.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: What does entry after profit tend to do to consumer surplus?
options: Raise price and lower consumer surplus
Eliminate all producer surplus
Make demand vertical
Lower price tends to increase consumer surplus
q.feedback: Entry expands supply and lowers price.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A per-unit tax on competitive output directly raises:
options: Marginal and average variable cost
Only fixed cost
Only market demand
Only accounting profit
q.feedback: The tax is tied to each unit produced.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: A lump-sum annual tax on a competitive firm directly raises:
options: Marginal revenue
Average total cost but not marginal cost
Average variable cost and MC
Market demand
q.feedback: A lump-sum tax acts like fixed cost.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: A higher wage shifts a competitive firm’s cost curves because labor is:
options: Always a fixed input
The firm’s product price
A variable input in the standard short-run model
A source of marginal revenue
q.feedback: Higher variable input cost raises AVC and MC.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: Compared with a price-taking firm, a firm with market power generally faces:
options: A horizontal demand curve at all outputs
No marginal cost
Zero fixed cost
A downward-sloping demand curve
q.feedback: Market power changes the firm’s revenue conditions; the competitive firm takes price.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: Why can a perfectly competitive outcome fail to maximize social surplus?
options: Private marginal cost may omit external costs
Firms cease being price takers
MC cannot be calculated
Entry always creates monopoly
q.feedback: The benchmark requires private and social marginal costs to align.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A small competitive firm selling a traded good takes which price as given in the open-market model?
options: Its own chosen monopoly price
The relevant market or world price
Average fixed cost
The tariff revenue per unit
q.feedback: Competitive firms respond to the price established in the wider market.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: How does the competitive firm’s price-taking assumption connect market equilibrium to the firm’s decision problem?
options: Market demand determines the firm’s fixed cost
Market supply and demand determine price; the firm then chooses quantity at that price
The firm chooses price first from its cost curves and then the market determines how much buyers take
The firm’s ATC determines the market equilibrium price directly
q.feedback: The market establishes the price signal, and the individual firm responds by selecting output.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: How does P = AR = MR connect the competitive revenue model to marginal analysis?
options: The market price is both revenue per unit and the added revenue from one more unit
Average revenue equals fixed cost while marginal revenue equals price
Marginal revenue falls below price because selling more requires the firm to cut price on all earlier units
Price equals marginal cost at every possible output
q.feedback: With price fixed, each additional unit adds the same amount to total revenue, so marginal revenue equals price. The firm then compares that marginal revenue with marginal cost when choosing output.

labels: Calculate and interpret total, average, and marginal revenue for a competitive firm.

q.q: How does a horizontal firm demand curve connect to the shape of the competitive firm’s total-revenue function?
options: A horizontal demand curve makes total revenue constant even when the firm sells additional units
A constant price makes total revenue fall as quantity rises
The total-revenue function must be U-shaped
A constant price makes total revenue rise proportionally with quantity
q.feedback: With price fixed, TR = P × Q rises by the same dollar amount for each additional unit.

labels: Calculate and interpret total, average, and marginal revenue for a competitive firm.

q.q: What prior market concept helps explain why the individual competitive firm can face a horizontal demand line even though market demand slopes downward?
options: The firm owns the market supply curve
The firm faces no scarcity in its inputs
The firm is a tiny participant taking the equilibrium price generated by the whole market
The law of demand stops applying at the firm level because competitive sellers can choose any price they want
q.feedback: Firm-level price taking is consistent with a downward-sloping market demand curve because the individual seller is negligible relative to the market.

labels: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.

q.q: How does the competitive firm’s MR = MC rule connect to the broader marginal-analysis principle?
options: Maximize output whenever average benefit is positive
Expand an activity while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost and stop near equality
Choose the activity with the largest total cost because total cost identifies the strongest marginal gain
Ignore incremental effects once fixed cost exists
q.feedback: For the firm, marginal revenue is the marginal benefit of another unit and MC is its marginal cost.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: How does a market-price increase reach a competitive firm’s profit-maximizing output decision?
options: The higher price raises the firm’s MR line, so the firm moves along rising MC to a larger output
The higher price shifts the firm’s MC curve left automatically while leaving its marginal revenue line unchanged
The higher price lowers MR and therefore output
The firm ignores market price once its plant is built
q.feedback: Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice.

labels: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.

q.q: How does the price-versus-ATC comparison connect a cost curve to the firm’s profit status?
options: ATC is irrelevant once output is chosen
The vertical gap P − ATC measures profit per unit when positive and loss per unit when negative
ATC determines marginal revenue directly
The gap P − AVC always equals total profit because fixed cost is irrelevant once the firm chooses output
q.feedback: Average total cost converts the firm’s chosen price and quantity into a per-unit economic-profit measure.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: How does total economic profit connect the revenue and cost frameworks?
options: Profit equals total revenue minus total economic cost
Profit equals total revenue minus variable cost only
Profit equals price minus marginal cost on the last unit only
Profit equals accounting revenue plus implicit cost
q.feedback: The firm combines its revenue from price and quantity with all economic costs to measure profit.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: Why can a firm remain in long-run competitive equilibrium when economic profit is zero?
options: The firm has no opportunity costs
Zero economic profit means total revenue is zero
The government reimburses fixed costs
Revenue covers explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
q.feedback: Normal profit is part of economic cost, so zero economic profit can still keep resources in their current use.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: How does break-even connect the firm’s revenue line to its average-cost curve?
options: MR equals zero at minimum ATC
Market demand becomes perfectly inelastic
At the chosen output, price equals ATC so total revenue equals total cost
Price equals AVC so fixed cost disappears
q.feedback: Break-even is the point where the per-unit revenue and total-cost averages match.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: How should a measured short-run economic loss connect to the next decision?
options: The firm should compare price with AFC instead
After measuring the loss, separately compare price with AVC to decide produce versus shut down
Any loss automatically implies exit today because a competitive firm should never operate while ATC exceeds price
A loss means the firm should maximize quantity
q.feedback: Loss measurement uses ATC; the short-run operating decision uses AVC.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: How does the shutdown rule connect to the distinction between fixed and variable costs?
options: Variable cost is sunk in the short run
Fixed cost determines marginal revenue
Price must cover variable cost because fixed cost is unavoidable in the short run
Price must cover fixed cost before variable cost matters
q.feedback: The shutdown test asks whether operating revenue covers the costs that can be avoided by not producing.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: How does producing at a loss connect to incremental decision making?
options: Use average fixed cost as the marginal benefit of output
Produce if operating adds more revenue than avoidable variable cost, even if total profit is negative
Produce only if accounting profit is positive
Ignore revenue because fixed cost is already paid
q.feedback: Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: How does the shutdown-versus-exit distinction connect to the short-run/long-run distinction in cost theory?
options: Some inputs and costs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs are adjustable in the long run
All costs are variable in the short run and fixed in the long run
Exit changes only marginal cost, not industry participation
Shutdown requires the firm to sell all fixed inputs immediately
q.feedback: Temporary shutdown occurs with short-run fixed commitments; exit becomes possible when those commitments can be changed.

labels: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.

q.q: How does the firm’s short-run supply curve connect the MR = MC rule to market supply?
options: The firm supplies where ATC equals AFC
The firm’s supply is its horizontal demand curve
At each price above shutdown, P = MR identifies the quantity on rising MC that the firm supplies
Market supply is unrelated to the firm’s marginal choice
q.feedback: The output rule becomes a price-to-quantity supply schedule when repeated across possible market prices.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: How does individual-firm supply become the competitive industry supply curve?
options: Use the market demand curve instead
Add firms’ quantities supplied at each common price
Add firms’ prices at each quantity
Average the firms’ fixed costs
q.feedback: Horizontal aggregation connects firm-level marginal-cost decisions to the market supply schedule.

labels: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.

q.q: How does entry connect firm-level profit to a market-level supply response?
options: Entry guarantees higher long-run price
Positive economic profit attracts firms, and additional firms increase industry supply
Positive profit shifts market demand left
Entry makes each incumbent’s MC automatically fall
q.feedback: The profit signal changes the number of firms, linking firm outcomes to market supply.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: How does exit connect economic loss to long-run resource allocation?
options: Resources leave uses that fail to cover opportunity cost and move toward better alternatives
Losses make resources permanently immobile
Exit increases the number of firms in the industry
Economic loss means variable cost is always zero
q.feedback: Long-run exit is an opportunity-cost response: resources seek higher-valued uses.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: How does normal profit connect long-run competitive equilibrium to economic cost?
options: Normal profit is a monopoly markup above economic cost
Normal profit is excluded from economic cost
Normal profit exists only when P exceeds ATC
Normal profit is the implicit return required to keep owner resources in the industry
q.feedback: Zero economic profit can be sustainable because normal profit is already included among opportunity costs.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: How does a constant-cost industry connect entry/exit to the long-run supply curve?
options: Entry permanently raises every firm’s ATC
Exit makes long-run supply vertical
The number of firms cannot change
Entry changes industry quantity without permanently shifting representative firms’ cost curves, producing horizontal long-run supply
q.feedback: Stable input costs let entry absorb demand changes while long-run price returns to the original cost level.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: How does an increasing-cost industry connect output-market expansion to input markets?
options: Input prices cannot matter in perfect competition
Higher input prices shift market demand rather than supply
Industry growth raises demand for scarce inputs, which can raise input prices and firm costs
Industry growth reduces input demand automatically
q.feedback: The long-run industry response can feed back through shared input markets.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: How does a demand increase connect short-run profit to the eventual long-run industry response?
options: Long-run price is always the short-run peak price
Higher short-run price can create profit, attracting entry; final price depends on the industry’s cost condition
Demand changes cause immediate exit before price changes
Profit has no connection to entry
q.feedback: Short-run market adjustment creates the profit signal; entry and cost conditions determine the long-run destination.

labels: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

q.q: A transit study predicts that a lower fare will increase ridership. Why is this positive?
options: Evidence could test the predicted change
The prediction must be socially desirable
The result is guaranteed to be true
Transit policy contains no value judgment
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A council member says parks should receive more funding because access is fair. Why is this normative?
options: It includes a government budget
It ranks outcomes using a value judgment
It predicts a measurable funding change
It must be supported by all voters
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: Which statement is positive?
options: The city should make rent cheaper.
Rent control is unfair.
A binding rent ceiling reduces apartment supply
The best policy is always lower rent.
q.feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about what the policy will do.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A library reports that Sunday hours increased visits. What makes this positive?
options: The increase in visits is a desirable outcome
Library officials support Sunday hours
The report is written confidently, so the claim must be true.
Visit records could test the claimed increase
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: “The library should stay open Sundays because access matters.” Why is this normative?
options: It recommends a choice using a value judgment
Sunday visits can be counted
The statement concerns a public institution
Evidence could show whether Sunday hours increase attendance.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A forecast that later proves false can still be positive when:
options: The forecast was made by an expert
Evidence could in principle have tested it
The forecast described an outcome people wanted
The forecast was stated with certainty.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: Which claim is normative in a school debate?
options: Average class size fell by two students last year
Smaller classes increased per-student spending
The district ought to favor smaller classes despite higher costs
Enrollment is projected to rise next year.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: Which claim is positive in a transit debate?
options: The city should make transit more affordable
Lower fares are fairer to low-income riders
Expanding transit access is more important than balancing the transit budget.
A lower fare increased weekday ridership
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: An economist says, 'A higher minimum wage will reduce employment among low-skill workers.' What kind of statement is this?
options: Positive
Normative
A price floor
A circular-flow claim
q.feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about cause and effect.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer. What makes this normative?
options: The ability to measure travel time
The ranking of safety against travel time
The prediction that streets can change
The reference to a city decision
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A report says a fee reduced waste and therefore is fair. What is normative?
options: The claim that the fee reduced waste
The measured amount of waste reduction
The judgment that the fee is fair
The fact that a fee was imposed.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: A weakly supported prediction later fails. What classification remains possible?
options: Normative, because the prediction turned out to be false
Normative, because the evidence supporting it was weak
Neither positive nor normative until the prediction is confirmed.
Positive, because testability does not require truth
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: “Costs rose 8%, so the city should respond.” What is present?
options: A positive measurement plus a normative recommendation
A purely positive statement because it includes a measured percentage
A purely normative statement because it recommends action
Two positive claims because both parts refer to economic conditions.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: A program “works,” but no outcome is named. What is missing?
options: A statement that the program is desirable
A measurable claim that evidence could contradict
A recommendation about whether the program should continue
A larger sample of people who support the program.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: “Equal access matters more than maximum output.” What is this?
options: A positive claim because access and output can both be measured
A positive claim because it compares two economic outcomes
A normative ranking of competing values
Neither positive nor normative because no policy is named.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A tax study uses the word efficient for a measurable revenue criterion. Is it necessarily normative?
options: Yes; the word efficient always expresses a value judgment
Yes; any claim about taxes is normative
Yes; a policy criterion cannot be evaluated with evidence.
No; the stated criterion can be tested with evidence
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: Which statement is positive rather than normative?
options: A binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied
The city should cap rents to protect tenants
Housing is too important to leave to markets
Fair rents matter more than landlord profits
q.feedback: The claim that a binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied is a testable prediction. The other claims prescribe what the city should do or express judgments about fairness and priorities.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: An economist says, 'The city should accept some efficiency loss to make housing more affordable.' What makes this normative?
options: It can be tested with rental data alone
It uses a value judgment about what policy should do
It describes only current prices
It states the law of demand
q.feedback: The statement recommends what policy should do, so it is normative.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A report predicts that extending library hours will increase weekly visits. Another recommends the extension because access is worth the staffing cost. Which assessment is correct?
options: The visit prediction is testable; the recommendation adds a value judgment
Both claims are normative because a public agency is involved
The recommendation is positive because staffing costs can be measured
The visit prediction is normative until the extension occurs
q.feedback: Evidence can test the predicted visit change. Calling improved access worth its cost also ranks outcomes; future predictions can be positive before observation.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A subsidy is predicted to raise enrollment and is therefore recommended. Which split is correct?
options: Both parts are positive because enrollment can be measured
Both parts are normative because a subsidy is a policy
The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative
The forecast is normative; the recommendation is positive.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: “The policy benefits most residents, so it is just.” Where is the normative step?
options: The claim that most residents benefit
The number of residents affected by the policy
The measured size of the benefits.
Calling the distribution just
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: What could test the claim that a road fee reduces congestion?
options: Traffic counts around comparable fee changes
A survey asking whether drivers think the fee is fair
A city council vote on the fee
A statement from officials that the fee will work.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: When can “the project has positive net benefits” be positive?
options: Always, because net benefits are measured in dollars
When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable
Never, because the word benefits is inherently normative
Only when everyone agrees the project is desirable.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: “The only acceptable policy is universal access.” Why is this normative?
options: Universal access can be measured
The statement refers to a policy outcome
It embeds a value standard despite objective wording
The sentence does not include a numerical prediction.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A rule lowers costs but is called morally wrong. What can evidence settle?
options: Both the cost effect and whether the rule is morally wrong
Only whether the rule is morally wrong
