Neither claim, because the rule is a policy.
The cost effect, but not the moral conclusion by itself
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: An economist says, 'A rent ceiling below equilibrium will reduce housing quality over time.' Another says, 'The city should accept that cost to help low-income renters.' Which pairing is correct?
options: First is positive; second is normative
First is normative; second is positive
Both are positive
Both are normative
q.feedback: The first is testable. The second recommends what policy should do, so it is normative.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A report defines success only as maximum total surplus. What choice is normative?
options: Calculating total surplus from observed prices and quantities
Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
Measuring how total surplus changes after the policy
Estimating the policy’s effect on output.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: Two analysts agree that an archive plan preserves more records but delays public access. One recommends it; the other rejects it. What additional finding would show a factual disagreement as well as a value disagreement?
options: They agree on the delay but differ on whether it is acceptable
They use the same probabilities but prefer different distributions of access
They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative
They give different ethical priority to immediate public access
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Probabilities of record loss are empirical assessments. The other differences concern how agreed consequences should be valued.

q.q: An evaluator says, "Option A saves more staff time, so it is the best policy." Which reply separates the testable component from the hidden value premise?
options: Measure the time savings, then ask why that objective should outrank other consequences
Treat the entire sentence as positive because staff time is measurable
Treat the time-saving estimate as normative because it supports a recommendation
Conclude more accurate timing data will uniquely determine the preferred policy
q.feedback: Time savings can be tested. Moving from that estimate to "best" requires a criterion for weighing time against other outcomes.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A board ranks plans only by the number of people served and selects A. New evidence shows B serves more people but offers less privacy. Which conclusion distinguishes logic from values?
options: Choosing A would necessarily show the new service count is false
Its stated rule now favors B; preferring A would require changing or qualifying that rule
The privacy difference makes the service-count evidence normative
More people served proves B is morally superior under every criterion
q.feedback: A fixed criterion has implications that evidence can change. Preferring privacy can justify a different criterion, but does not refute the service-count evidence.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A forecast says a digitization plan will reduce waiting. A recommendation says it should be adopted only if access for people without internet is protected. Waiting falls but offline access worsens. Which inference is sound?
options: Observed waiting reductions prove the plan satisfies the value criterion
The forecast becomes normative because implementation affected access
The forecast is supported, while the recommendation's stated condition is unmet
The failed access condition refutes the waiting-time forecast
q.feedback: The observed waiting result bears on the positive claim. Protecting offline access is a separate condition in the recommendation; success on one outcome does not satisfy it.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A report states that volunteers prefer evening shifts and therefore evening-only service is fair. A representative survey confirms the preference. What remains unresolved?
options: Whether a confirmed preference statement can count as positive
Whether using a survey converts the fairness conclusion into a measured fact
Whether the fairness judgment proves daytime users have no unmet needs
Whether fairness should be judged by volunteer preferences rather than users' access
q.feedback: A preference claim is empirically testable. The move from measured volunteer preferences to fairness requires a value premise about whose interests count.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A rule gives priority to people facing the greatest hardship. New data show that a different group meets that description. What change is consistent with keeping the same normative principle?
options: Change the priority group because the evidence changed who satisfies the criterion
Keep the old group because normative principles cannot use evidence
Declare hardship measurement normative solely because it informs policy
Treat the data as proof that greatest-hardship priority is the only fair principle
q.feedback: A stable value criterion can lead to a different recommendation when facts change. Evidence identifies its beneficiaries without uniquely establishing the criterion itself.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A researcher predicts that simplifying an application raises completion when eligibility is unchanged. A trial simplifies the form and broadens eligibility; completion rises. Which statement is justified?
options: Only recommendations can be evaluated when two policies change together
The prediction is positive, but the joint change does not isolate the form's effect
The rise proves the form alone caused every added completion
The extra eligibility change makes the original claim normative
q.feedback: The conditional causal prediction is testable. Because eligibility changed too, the observation does not by itself identify the effect of form simplification.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A report finds that a shuttle saves travelers time but increases neighborhood noise. It recommends adoption using travelers' gains alone. Which critique is precise?
options: Time savings become normative when expressed in money
Adding more precise effect estimates removes the need to decide whose welfare counts
The effects are testable; excluding neighbors from the recommendation embeds a value choice
Noise estimates are normative because neighbors dislike the outcome
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Time and noise effects can be measured. Counting only travelers when recommending a policy assigns standing to one group and excludes another, which is a value choice.

q.q: Two forecasts disagree about whether a new scheduling rule will shorten next year's queues. Both specify measurable waiting times and comparable staffing. What would change their status as positive claims?
options: The forecast with the larger benefit is positive; the other is normative
Both become normative until next year's data exist
Agreement by the forecasters is required before evidence can test them
Neither disagreement nor the future date changes their testable status
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: Positive status depends on empirical testability, not agreement, truth, desirability or whether the outcome has occurred. Later evidence can support one forecast over the other.

q.q: An analyst rejects a delivery plan because predicted delays exceed her stated acceptable limit. Better evidence places delays below that limit, but she still rejects it on privacy grounds. Which interpretation fits?
options: The factual case changed, and the rejection now requires an additional value criterion
The original delay forecast was normative because it supported rejection
The unchanged decision proves the new delay estimate is irrelevant to the original argument
Privacy concerns establish that the revised forecast is false
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: The delay objection no longer follows from the updated evidence and original threshold. A privacy objection can support rejection, but it is a separate normative premise.

q.q: A planner defines "optimal" as maximizing visits, then claims the chosen schedule is objectively best. Another schedule serves fewer visitors but reaches people with greater need. Which statement is most defensible?
options: A numerical criterion cannot contain a value judgment
Visit maximization identifies an optimum under one criterion, not a uniquely justified social ranking
Calling a result optimal makes its criterion empirically true
The need difference disproves the measured visit counts
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: Optimization can be objective conditional on a criterion. Choosing visits rather than need as the social objective remains a normative judgment.

q.q: What is a positive statement?
options: A testable claim about how the world is
A claim about how the world should be
A statement that is always morally good
A policy recommendation
q.feedback: A positive statement describes or predicts how the world is.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: An instructor presents this claim: 'A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage.' What kind of statement is this?
options: Normative
Positive
A value judgment
A policy recommendation
q.feedback: This is positive because it is a testable cause-and-effect claim.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: An instructor gives two claims. Claim 1: 'Rent control reduces housing supply.' Claim 2: 'The city should use rent control anyway.' Which pairing is correct?
options: Claim 1 is normative; Claim 2 is positive
Both claims are positive
Claim 1 is positive; Claim 2 is normative
Both claims are normative
q.feedback: The first claim is testable. The second claim recommends what should happen, so it is normative.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A report predicts gains and calls them worth unequal losses. What is normative?
options: The judgment that gains justify the losses
The prediction that the policy creates gains
The estimated size of the gains
The measured distribution of gains and losses.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: What best tests “a fee reduces congestion”?
options: A survey asking whether residents support the fee
Traffic counts before and after comparable changes
A council vote to adopt the fee
A statement from officials that congestion will fall.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: Why is “Policy A is responsible” not automatically positive?
options: The statement mentions a policy
The word responsible refers to a measurable outcome
Responsible may hide an unstated value standard
Any sentence about policy performance is positive.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: “A bus lane reduced travel time.” What kind of claim is this?
options: Positive and empirically testable
Normative because reduced travel time is desirable
Normative because the statement concerns transportation policy
Neither, because one observed result cannot be tested.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: “The city ought to accept higher costs for cleaner air.” What kind?
options: Positive because costs and air quality can be measured
Normative because it ranks a tradeoff
Positive because the statement describes a policy tradeoff
Neither, because the statement contains no numerical estimate.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: When does a false forecast remain positive?
options: Only when the forecast describes a desirable outcome
Only when an expert made the forecast
When evidence could have tested the forecast
Never; a false claim cannot be positive.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: An adviser predicts a wage rule raises employed teenagers’ annual income by $8 million but reduces teenage employment by 3%. She recommends it because the income gain is worth the employment loss. A pilot instead finds a 1% job loss. Which conclusion separates evidence from values?
options: The pilot makes the original employment prediction normative because a positive statement cannot be contradicted by data.
The pilot challenges the size of the positive employment prediction; it does not by itself establish the adviser’s tradeoff criterion.
The smaller loss proves the recommendation objectively correct, regardless of how the affected teenagers value work and income.
The recommendation makes both numerical predictions normative, so neither can be evaluated using pilot evidence.
q.feedback: Predictions about income and employment are testable positive claims even when inaccurate. Calling one outcome worth another introduces a value judgment. New evidence informs the tradeoff but cannot supply the normative weighting by itself.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A report states: (1) a tax reduces cigarette purchases; (2) the tax burden falls heavily on low-income smokers; (3) therefore the tax is unjust. Which classification is correct?
options: All three are positive, because technical wording removes every value judgment
Only statement 1 is positive
Statements 1 and 2 are positive; statement 3 is normative
Statements 2 and 3 are normative
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: The first two claims can be tested empirically. The conclusion that the policy is unjust is normative.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: School plan A is predicted to raise scores by 6 points and reduce free time by 4 hours weekly. Plan B raises scores by 4 points and reduces free time by 1 hour. A board declares A preferable because each extra score point is worth at least 2 hours of free time. Which assessment is exact?
options: The outcome predictions are normative; the board’s numerical weighting is positive, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours.
All claims are positive because they contain numbers; A dominates B on both scores and free time.
The weighting is normative, so the score and time predictions cannot be tested against observed outcomes.
The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Comparative predictions imply A adds 2 score points while costing 3 more hours, or 1.5 hours per extra point. Whether that is worthwhile depends on the board’s stated value criterion, not merely on the accuracy of the predictions.

q.q: A positive statement is best described as:
options: A testable claim about how the world is
A claim about how the world should be
A statement that is always good
A policy recommendation
q.feedback: Positive statements describe or predict how the world is.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: A statement using 'should' is usually:
options: Positive
Normative
A demand shifter
A supply schedule
q.feedback: Normative statements make value judgments about what should happen.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: Does positive mean good or favorable?
options: Yes; positive means the outcome is desirable
Yes; positive claims support the policy being discussed
No; it means testable in principle
Yes; positive claims are facts that must be true.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: Does false automatically mean normative?
options: Yes; normative claims are the claims that turn out to be false
Yes; positive claims must be factually correct
Yes; a claim becomes normative once evidence rejects it.
No; a false claim can still be testable
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: Is every policy statement normative?
options: No; policy predictions can be positive
Yes; any statement about government policy is normative
Yes; policy effects cannot be tested with evidence
Yes; mentioning a recommendation makes every related claim normative.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: Does technical tone guarantee a positive claim?
options: Yes; technical language makes a statement factual
No; technical wording can conceal a value judgment
Yes; numerical language removes value judgments
Yes; professional wording means the claim can be tested.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A price-support study predicts more output, then recommends the policy as fair. How should these two claims be evaluated?
options: Test the output prediction separately from the fairness judgment
Ignore the prediction once advice appears
Treat both parts as positive because evidence exists
Treat both parts as normative because policy is involved
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: An analyst writes: "A congestion charge will reduce downtown car trips by 10%. That reduction is worth the added financial burden on commuters." How are the two claims classified?
options: First normative; second positive.
Both positive.
First positive; second normative.
Both normative.
q.feedback: The 10% traffic prediction can be tested against evidence, whether or not it proves true. Saying the reduction is worth the burden ranks competing outcomes; that judgment needs a value premise that traffic data alone cannot establish.

labels: LO2.4

q.q: An economist predicts job losses and recommends against a rule. What additional judgment turns the prediction into policy advice?
options: The existence of a measurable employment effect
The fact that the rule is a government policy
The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost
The use of an economic forecast.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: A model predicts a tax effect under stated assumptions. Why is it positive?
options: Because the prediction supports the tax
Because the model is written in technical language
Because the prediction must be true if the assumptions are stated.
Evidence could test the conditional prediction
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: Prices help allocate scarce resources by:
options: Sending signals to buyers and sellers
Eliminating scarcity
Preventing all shortages forever
Making opportunity cost disappear
q.feedback: Prices send signals that help buyers and sellers adjust behavior.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: When a good becomes scarce and its price rises, buyers are encouraged to:
options: Buy less or look for substitutes
Demand more because price is higher
Ignore the price signal
Shift supply left
q.feedback: Higher prices encourage buyers to buy less or look for substitutes.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: When a good's price rises, sellers are generally encouraged to:
options: Produce more of the good
Buy less of the good
Shift demand left
Create a price ceiling
q.feedback: Higher prices encourage sellers to supply more.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A rising market price typically signals producers that:
options: Demand must have fallen.
Resources should leave the market immediately.
No adjustment is needed.
The good has become relatively more valuable to buyers or scarcer to supply.
q.commonError: Reading a higher price as a signal to reduce supply in all cases.
q.feedback: A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A drought raises the price of water-intensive crops. How does the price signal help coordinate adjustment?
options: Consumers conserve and producers seek ways to expand or redirect supply.
Consumers buy more solely because price rose.
Producers reduce output because revenue is higher.
The price prevents scarcity from existing.
q.commonError: Reversing buyer and seller responses to a higher price.
q.feedback: Higher prices discourage some consumption and reward additional supply.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: The price of a product falls after a new production technology spreads. What information does the lower price convey?
options: Demand must have increased.
The product can be supplied at lower cost or has become less scarce.
Every producer should enter immediately.
The product has become a public good.
q.commonError: Treating any lower price as evidence of lower demand.
q.feedback: A supply improvement can lower price by reducing the good’s relative scarcity.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A shortage persists because a legal ceiling prevents price from rising. Which coordinating signal is muted?
options: The signal to increase quantity demanded and reduce quantity supplied.
The signal that opportunity costs are zero.
The signal to conserve consumption and expand supply.
The signal that all buyers value the good equally.
q.commonError: Ignoring the coordinating information contained in an allowed price increase.
q.feedback: A rising price would normally ration demand and attract additional supply.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: High profits in a market can function as a signal that:
options: Consumers should stop valuing the product.
Entry must be legally prohibited.
Production costs are irrelevant.
Resources may earn more by moving into that activity.
q.commonError: Treating profit only as a reward rather than an allocation signal.
q.feedback: Profit attracts resources toward uses where buyers value output above cost.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A high price reflects both strong demand and a temporary supply disruption. Why can the price alone be insufficient for policy diagnosis?
options: The same price movement can arise from different underlying shifts.
Prices contain no information.
Demand and supply never change together.
A high price always proves monopoly power.
q.commonError: Inferring a unique cause from the direction of price alone.
q.feedback: Price summarizes pressure but does not by itself identify which curve shifted.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A subsidy lowers the buyer’s out-of-pocket price while paying sellers an additional amount. How can the subsidy distort the price signal buyers receive?
options: The resource cost disappears.
The social resource cost can be hidden from buyers by the subsidized price.
Sellers receive no incentive to expand.
Quantity demanded must fall.
q.commonError: Equating the consumer price with the full social cost.
q.feedback: A subsidy changes who pays but does not erase resource cost.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A congested road has no toll. What price-signal problem is present?
options: The road has no opportunity cost.
Demand for travel must be zero.
Drivers do not face the full marginal congestion cost they impose.
A market price is unnecessary because congestion is beneficial.
q.feedback: Without a congestion price, drivers receive too weak a signal to account for delays imposed on others.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A sudden price spike attracts rapid entry, but the shock disappears before new capacity arrives. What does this show?
options: The original price contained no information.
Supply never responds to incentives.
Entry always stabilizes price immediately.
Price signals can be accurate yet responses may arrive with lags.
q.feedback: Prices signal opportunities, but investment and production take time.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A price rises while quantity sold also rises. Which inference is safest?
options: Demand likely increased, but additional evidence is needed if several forces changed.
Supply must have decreased and nothing else changed.
The higher price caused quantity demanded to rise.
Price signals cannot coordinate markets.
q.commonError: Confusing an equilibrium movement with movement along one curve.
q.feedback: A higher price and quantity are consistent with a demand increase, though simultaneous shifts can complicate diagnosis.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A firm earns losses despite producing a product consumers value. What allocation signal do losses send?
options: Consumers place no value on the product.
Resources may create more value in alternative uses.
The firm should expand regardless of cost.
Losses prove the market is competitive.
q.commonError: Treating value to consumers as sufficient without comparing cost.
q.feedback: Losses indicate that costs exceed revenue and resources may be worth more elsewhere.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: An electricity supplier charges more during evening peaks and less overnight. Some households can delay appliance use, while others need electricity immediately. Which response shows how the price signal can coordinate scarce capacity?
options: Flexible users shift use into the evening, reducing peak pressure because peak prices are higher.
Inflexible users must stop consuming before the price difference can affect peak demand.
Flexible users shift some use overnight, reducing peak pressure without requiring every household to shift.
All households must use less electricity over the full day for timing prices to reduce peak demand.
q.feedback: Higher peak prices encourage users with flexible timing to move consumption. Daily consumption need not fall, and users with urgent needs need not shift for this coordinating effect to occur.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A government caps a medicine price and separately rations access through waiting lists. What has occurred?
options: Scarcity has been eliminated.
The ceiling increased the legal market-clearing price.
Waiting time has no opportunity cost.
Nonprice rationing has replaced part of the suppressed price signal.
q.commonError: Ignoring rationing mechanisms that emerge when prices cannot adjust.
q.feedback: When price is constrained, queues, eligibility rules, or quality changes may allocate the scarce good.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A carbon price raises energy prices. What information is the policy trying to add to the market signal?
options: The external climate cost associated with emissions.
A guarantee that all energy use ends.
The producer’s accounting profit only.
A fixed quantity demanded at every price.
q.commonError: Treating corrective pricing as arbitrary punishment.
q.feedback: The policy attempts to make private prices reflect a social cost previously omitted.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: “Prices speak when no one gives orders.” What role do prices play in a market economy?
options: They signal scarcity and help allocate resources
They eliminate scarcity completely
They prevent all shortages forever
They remove opportunity cost
q.feedback: Prices send signals to buyers and sellers about scarcity, value, and incentives.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A resource becomes scarce, and its price rises. How do buyers and sellers usually respond?
options: Buyers buy less while sellers try to supply more
Buyers buy more while sellers supply less
Both buyers and sellers ignore the signal
Demand and supply both disappear
q.feedback: Higher prices encourage buyers to conserve and sellers to produce more.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A student claims that a high price by itself means the market has failed. What is wrong with that claim?
options: A high price can be a scarcity signal, not automatically a market failure
High prices always prove demand disappeared
High prices always mean a price ceiling is binding
High prices eliminate the need for supply
q.feedback: A high price may simply signal scarcity and guide buyers and sellers. It is not automatically a market failure.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A rising price and rising quantity most strongly suggest which change, other things equal?
options: A decrease in demand.
An increase in demand.
An increase in supply.
A binding price floor becoming lower.
q.commonError: Misreading what prices, profits, or losses communicate.
q.feedback: An increase in demand raises both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity, other things equal.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A market loss most directly encourages resources to:
options: Remain permanently in the same activity.
Ignore production costs.
Move toward alternative uses with higher expected value.
Increase quantity demanded.
q.commonError: Misreading what prices, profits, or losses communicate.
q.feedback: Persistent losses signal that the resources used in this activity may create greater value elsewhere, encouraging them to move toward alternative uses.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A congestion toll is intended to communicate:
options: That road space is unlimited.
That every trip has equal value.
That supply of roads rises instantly.
The additional delay cost created by using the road at busy times.
q.commonError: Misreading what prices, profits, or losses communicate.
q.feedback: A congestion toll makes drivers face more of the additional delay cost their trip imposes on others during busy periods.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: When a price rises, buyers generally receive a signal to:
options: Conserve or seek substitutes.
Demand more because the price is higher.
Ignore scarcity.
Expand market supply themselves.
q.commonError: Reversing the buyer response to a higher price.
q.feedback: A higher price raises the cost of consuming the good and encourages substitution or conservation.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: What response does a higher market price normally encourage from sellers?
options: Reduce output because revenue rises.
Expand quantity supplied when feasible.
Increase quantity demanded.
Treat costs as zero.
q.commonError: Reversing the seller response to a higher price.
q.feedback: A higher price can make additional production worthwhile.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A higher market price normally signals producers to:
options: Increase quantity supplied
Decrease quantity supplied
Demand less automatically
Ignore the market
q.feedback: Higher prices communicate greater relative value and encourage producers to supply more.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: A hospital posts the real-time wait at each clinic, and patients shift toward shorter waits. The wait-time information acts like:
options: A price floor.
A guarantee of unlimited capacity.
A nonmonetary signal coordinating demand across locations.
A supply curve shift caused by income.
q.commonError: Failing to recognize nonmoney signals that coordinate scarce capacity.
q.feedback: Information about waiting costs can redirect users much like a price signal.

labels: LO4.5

q.q: The circular-flow model shows how dollars, goods and services, and resources move between:
options: Households and firms
Banks and foreign governments
Workers and tax agencies
Retailers and central banks
q.feedback: The circular-flow model shows flows between households and firms.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: In the simple circular-flow model, households usually supply:
options: Finished goods and services
Factors of production
Price ceilings
Tax wedges
q.feedback: Households supply factors of production such as labor, land, and capital.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: In the simple circular-flow model, firms usually supply:
options: Labor services to households
Household income to product markets
Goods and services
Tax revenue to resource markets
q.feedback: Firms produce and sell goods and services.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A production possibilities frontier shows:
options: The exact market price of each good
Government’s preferred production mix
The economy’s current unemployment rate
Currently feasible combinations of two goods
q.feedback: A PPF shows possible production combinations with current resources and technology.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A point inside the PPF usually means:
options: Resources are not being used efficiently
The point is unattainable
The economy has no tradeoffs
The economy is beyond its resources
q.feedback: A point inside the PPF is attainable but inefficient.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A point outside the PPF is:
options: Efficient but always chosen
Unattainable with current resources and technology
A price floor
A market surplus
q.feedback: A point outside the PPF cannot be reached with current resources and technology.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Moving along a PPF usually means:
options: Producing more of every good without cost
Creating a tax wedge
Producing more of one good and less of another
Changing only the price level
q.feedback: Moving along the PPF shows a tradeoff between two goods.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: An outward shift of the PPF usually represents:
options: A shortage
A binding price ceiling
A decrease in demand
Economic growth
q.feedback: An outward shift means the economy can produce more than before.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A circular-flow model shows households supplying labor to firms and receiving wages. Which market is being described?
options: The market for factors of production
The market for final goods and services
The market for price ceilings
The market for tax revenue
q.feedback: Households provide factors of production such as labor in factor markets and receive income.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A PPF is bowed outward. Moving from low production of Good X to high production of Good X requires giving up larger and larger amounts of Good Y. What principle does this show?
options: Increasing opportunity cost
Constant opportunity cost
A binding price floor
A tax wedge
q.feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: An economist uses a PPF to show how producing more military goods requires producing fewer consumer goods. What is the model showing?
options: Tradeoffs and opportunity cost
Tax incidence
A binding price ceiling
A market surplus
q.feedback: The PPF shows tradeoffs because producing more of one good requires giving up some of another.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: An economy moves from a point inside its PPF to a point on the PPF. What happened?
options: It reached an unattainable point
It used idle resources more efficiently
It created a tax wedge
It shifted demand left
q.feedback: Moving from inside the PPF to the frontier means resources are being used more efficiently.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: An economy gets better technology for producing both goods. What happens to its PPF?
options: It shifts inward
It becomes a price ceiling
It shifts outward
It creates a shortage
q.feedback: Better technology increases productive capacity, shifting the PPF outward.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A point is outside the PPF today but becomes attainable after an increase in capital and technology. What changed?
options: The market price was fixed
Demand decreased
The economy moved inside the PPF
The economy's productive capacity increased
q.feedback: More capital and better technology increase what the economy can produce.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Which points are efficient production points?
options: A, B, C, D, and E
F, because it is attainable inside the frontier
G, because it represents greater output
B, C, and D, because only interior points on the frontier are efficient.
q.feedback: Points on the PPF are efficient because the economy is using its available resources fully.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is attainable but inefficient?
options: G
F
C
E
q.feedback: Point F is inside the PPF, so it is attainable but inefficient.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is currently unattainable?
options: F
A
G
D
q.feedback: Point G is outside the PPF, so it is unattainable with current resources and technology.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. What does the bowed-out shape of the PPF suggest?
options: Opportunity cost remains constant along the frontier
Opportunity cost falls as more Good X is produced
The economy has idle resources at each frontier point
Opportunity cost rises as more Good X is produced
q.feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward producing more of one good.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy moves from F to C, what has happened?
options: The economy has moved from inefficient production to efficient production
The economy has moved from unattainable production to attainable production
The economy has reduced both goods
The economy has moved outside the PPF
q.feedback: Point F is inside the PPF and point C is on the PPF, so the economy moved from inefficient to efficient production.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from A to B, what is the opportunity cost per additional pizza?
options: 1 robot
2 robots
0.5 robot
40 robots
q.imageAlt: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.
q.feedback: The move gains 40 pizzas and gives up 40 robots, so each pizza costs 1 robot.
q.graphDescription: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A household buys groceries in the product market and sells labor in the factor market. In the circular-flow model, which flow goes from firms to households in factor markets?
options: Income such as wages, rent, and profit
Goods and services
Consumer spending from households to firms.
Price ceilings
q.feedback: Households provide factors of production, and firms pay income for those factors.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A storm destroys factories and equipment. What happens to the economy's PPF?
options: It shifts outward
The economy moves along the same PPF only
It shifts inward
The PPF becomes a demand curve
q.feedback: A loss of productive resources reduces what the economy can produce, shifting the PPF inward.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A student says, 'This point is inside the PPF, so it is impossible.' What is the correction?
options: Inside the PPF is unattainable
Inside the PPF is efficient
Inside the PPF means economic growth
Inside the PPF is attainable but inefficient
q.feedback: A point inside the PPF can be produced, but it wastes or underuses resources.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A student says, 'This point is outside the PPF, so it is efficient.' What is the correction?
options: Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology
Outside the PPF is inefficient but possible
Outside the PPF means unemployment and underused resources.
Outside the PPF means a binding ceiling
q.feedback: Outside the PPF means the economy cannot reach that point with current resources and technology.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Worker training improves human capital and shifts the PPF outward for both goods. Which economic relationship does this illustrate?
options: A price ceiling creates a shortage
Human capital raises productive capacity
A tax wedge reduces market size
A positive statement becomes normative
q.feedback: Better worker training improves human capital and can shift the PPF outward.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A student says, “A point outside the PPF is inefficient because the economy is not producing there.” What is wrong with that statement?
options: A point outside the PPF is always efficient
A point outside the PPF shows idle resources
It is unattainable with current resources, not merely inefficient.
A point outside the PPF means opportunity cost is zero
q.feedback: Inside the PPF is inefficient. Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which proposed change would require greater productive capacity rather than reallocation along PPF0?
options: Moving from A to B along PPF0
Moving from B toward A along PPF0
Producing at a point beyond PPF0
Choosing another point located on PPF0
q.imageAlt: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.
q.feedback: Points on PPF0 are attainable now; sustaining a point outside requires an outward capacity shift.
q.graphDescription: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: An economy is producing inside its PPF because some labor and capital are idle. Which change moves it toward the frontier without shifting the frontier?
options: Discovering a new technology
Putting unemployed resources back to work
Increasing the capital stock
Expanding the labor force permanently
q.feedback: Using idle resources moves the economy toward the existing PPF. New technology or more resources shift the PPF outward.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A new technology improves only the production of Good X, not Good Y. What happens to the PPF?
options: It shifts inward equally for both goods
It creates a shortage of Good Y
It becomes a price ceiling
It rotates outward on the Good X axis
q.feedback: Technology that helps only one good expands production possibilities for that good, rotating the PPF outward on that axis.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Which move has the highest opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X?
options: A to B
D to E
B to C
C to D
q.feedback: The move from D to E gives up 20 units of Good Y to gain only 4 units of Good X, the highest cost per unit among the listed moves.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Compare the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X from A to B with the cost from D to E. Which calculation and conclusion are supported?
options: A to B costs 0.625 Y per X, while D to E costs 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises
A to B costs 5 Y per X, while D to E costs 0.625 Y per X; opportunity cost falls
Both moves cost 1 Y per X; opportunity cost remains constant
A to B costs 8 Y per X, while D to E costs 4 Y per X; opportunity cost falls
q.feedback: The graph shows A to B gives up 5 Y for 8 X, or 0.625 Y per X. D to E gives up 20 Y for 4 X, or 5 Y per X, demonstrating increasing opportunity cost.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy is at F and moves to B, what happens?
options: It produces more Good X and less Good Y
It moves outside the PPF
It becomes unattainable
It produces the same amount of Good X but more Good Y
q.feedback: F and B both have about 8 units of Good X, but B has more Good Y and lies on the PPF.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy moves from F to C, what best describes the change?
options: It gains both Good X and Good Y by using resources more efficiently
It gives up Good Y to gain Good X
It moves from efficient to inefficient production
It moves beyond current resources
q.feedback: F is inside the PPF and C is on the PPF. Moving from F to C increases both goods by using idle or misallocated resources.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. As production moves farther right along bowed PPF0, what happens to the opportunity cost of additional pizzas?
options: It falls as fewer robots are sacrificed per pizza
It rises as more robots are sacrificed per pizza
It stays constant at one robot for each pizza
It becomes zero after production reaches B
q.imageAlt: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.
q.feedback: The frontier becomes steeper as pizza production rises, showing increasing robot cost per pizza.
q.graphDescription: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. On PPF0, moving from A to B gains 20 burgers. What is the opportunity cost per additional burger?
options: 0.5 order of fries
20 orders of fries
40 orders of fries
2 orders of fries
q.imageAlt: Burgers are on the horizontal axis and fries on the vertical axis. Bowed PPF0 includes A at 10 burgers and 120 fries and B at 30 burgers and 80 fries. Dashed PPF1 lies outside PPF0, reaching about 150 fries at zero burgers and 60 burgers at zero fries.
q.feedback: The move gives up 40 fries for 20 burgers, or 2 fries per burger.
q.graphDescription: Burgers are on the horizontal axis and fries on the vertical axis. Bowed PPF0 includes A at 10 burgers and 120 fries and B at 30 burgers and 80 fries. Dashed PPF1 lies outside PPF0, reaching about 150 fries at zero burgers and 60 burgers at zero fries.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A country invests more in capital goods today, sacrificing consumer goods. In a PPF framework, what is the likely long-run implication?
options: More future growth because capital accumulation can expand productive capacity
No future effect because PPF choices never matter
Immediate elimination of scarcity because future productive capacity will be larger.
A binding price floor in the capital market
q.feedback: Choosing more capital goods today can increase future productive capacity and shift the PPF outward later.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: An economy moves from inside its PPF to a point on the PPF and then later shifts the PPF outward. What sequence is correct?
options: First scarcity disappears, then opportunity cost disappears
First efficiency improves, then productive capacity grows
First demand shifts, then price controls bind
First the economy becomes unattainable, then efficient
q.feedback: Moving from inside to the frontier is improved efficiency. Shifting the frontier outward is growth.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A new technology improves only production of medical devices, not food. Which PPF interpretation is best?
options: The entire frontier must shift inward
The economy moves inside the PPF
The frontier rotates outward on the medical-device axis
The law of demand no longer applies
q.feedback: Technology that improves only one good expands capacity for that good, rotating the PPF outward along that axis.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Why does the opportunity cost of Good X rise as production moves from A toward E?
options: Resources become perfectly adaptable between X and Y
Resources are increasingly less suited to producing additional X
The economy has escaped scarcity by moving along the curve
The money price of X must fall as X production rises
q.feedback: A bowed-out PPF reflects increasing opportunity cost because resources are not equally suited to both goods.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement correctly distinguishes moving from A to B from shifting PPF0 to PPF1?
options: A to B reallocates; PPF1 expands capacity
Both changes expand productive capacity
A to B expands capacity; PPF1 shows unemployment
Both changes only reallocate current production
q.imageAlt: Burgers are on the horizontal axis and fries on the vertical axis. Bowed PPF0 includes A at 10 burgers and 120 fries and B at 30 burgers and 80 fries. Dashed PPF1 lies outside PPF0, reaching about 150 fries at zero burgers and 60 burgers at zero fries.
q.feedback: A and B share one frontier; the outward PPF1 expands feasible production.
q.graphDescription: Burgers are on the horizontal axis and fries on the vertical axis. Bowed PPF0 includes A at 10 burgers and 120 fries and B at 30 burgers and 80 fries. Dashed PPF1 lies outside PPF0, reaching about 150 fries at zero burgers and 60 burgers at zero fries.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. A proposal values each extra unit of X at 2 units of Y. Comparing the average tradeoff over A to B and D to E, which movement passes that benefit-cost test?
options: A to B passes; D to E fails
Both pass because each ends on the frontier
D to E passes; A to B fails
Neither passes because every frontier movement sacrifices Y
q.feedback: A to B forgoes 5 Y for 8 X, or 0.625 Y per X; D to E forgoes 20 Y for 4 X, or 5 Y per X. A benefit of 2 Y per X exceeds only the first average cost.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Starting at B, a planner must choose among labeled frontier points while keeping at least 30 units of Y. What is the greatest attainable X among those choices, and what Y is sacrificed?
options: 25 X at E, sacrificing 45 Y
15 X at C, sacrificing 10 Y
21 X at D, sacrificing 25 Y
8 X at B, sacrificing no Y
q.feedback: A, B and C meet the Y floor. C has the most X of those labeled points: 15. Relative to B, Y falls from 45 to 35, a cost of 10.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. An economy at F considers B as an immediate target and G as a longer-run target. Which diagnosis fits both?
options: Reaching B expands the frontier; reaching G merely removes unemployment
Both targets are currently efficient choices because each is desirable
Better resource use can reach B; reaching G requires an expansion of feasible production
Both targets require new technology because both are above F
q.feedback: F is inside the existing frontier, B lies on it and G lies outside. Removing inefficiency can reach B with current capacity; G requires a changed production possibility set.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF. Moving from point C to point D increases production of X but reduces production of Y. Suppose each additional unit of X generates a benefit equivalent to 3 units of Y. What is the net benefit, measured in units of Y, from moving from C to D?
options: 3 Y
q.feedback: The move gains 6 X and forgoes 15 Y. Its benefit is 6 times 3 = 18 Y; deducting the 15 Y opportunity cost leaves 3 Y.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Production first moves from F to C and then from C to D, with resources and technology unchanged. Why does only the second move clearly sacrifice Y for more X?
options: The first uses slack to raise both outputs; the second reallocates along the frontier
The first creates growth; growth eliminates opportunity cost on the second
F is unattainable, so its output cannot be compared with C
D lies inside the frontier and therefore wastes Y
q.feedback: F to C raises both outputs by improving use of existing capacity. C to D moves between efficient frontier points, gaining X at the expense of Y.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: The first ten generators cost two forgone repairs; the next ten cost six more. A buyer offers four repairs in exchange for each ten-generator block. Blocks must be produced in order. Which production choice yields the most net repairs?
options: Produce only the second block because its opportunity cost is higher
Produce neither because any generator production sacrifices repairs
Produce one block, gaining two net repairs
Produce both blocks because their average cost equals the offer
q.feedback: The first block gains 4 - 2 = 2 repairs; the second loses 4 - 6 = -2. Producing both yields zero net gain, so one block is better.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: From an efficient starting point, reallocating crews to the first four school reopenings forgoes 12 bridge repairs; the next four forgo 20 more. A planner uses the first block's cost to estimate all eight. What is the error?
options: The estimate is correct because equal numbers of schools must cost equal repairs
The estimate is 12 repairs too high because the first block is already planned
The estimate is 20 repairs too low because the first block has no opportunity cost
The estimate is 8 repairs too low because the later marginal tradeoff is steeper
q.feedback: Extrapolating the first block gives 24 repairs for eight schools. Actual cost is 12 + 20 = 32, eight more. The second block has the higher opportunity cost.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A factory raises both outputs after reorganizing idle workers. Later, training expands the maximum output possible even when all workers are occupied. Which evidence separates the two improvements?
options: The first can occur within existing capacity; the second changes the efficient production boundary
Any simultaneous output increase proves the frontier shifted
Any training program moves production along an unchanged frontier
Both improvements establish that the original output was outside the frontier
q.feedback: Using idle resources can raise both outputs without changing capacity. A higher maximum under full efficient use establishes a frontier expansion.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A straight-line PPF trades one turbine for three pumps. An observed move gains two turbines while pumps stay unchanged, with technology and resources fixed. Which explanation is consistent with both facts?
options: The straight frontier proves every observed move must lose six pumps
The turbine gain by itself proves the PPF shifted outward
The observation establishes zero opportunity cost everywhere on the frontier
The starting point was inside the frontier, so the move could use idle capacity
q.feedback: The three-pump tradeoff describes efficient frontier reallocations. An interior starting point can permit output gains without sacrificing the other good; the observation does not erase frontier opportunity cost.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the graph. After the shift from PPF0 to PPF1, production remains at B. Which statement combines the capacity change with the observed production choice?
options: Capacity expanded, and PPF1 identifies the preferred output combination; unchanged production at B therefore establishes that welfare has increased.
Capacity expanded, but unchanged B is now inside the new frontier; higher welfare is not established by the shift alone
Capacity expanded, but unchanged B remains on the efficient frontier; its earlier efficiency establishes that resources are still fully employed.
Capacity stayed unchanged because production remains at B; the shift to PPF1 changes the selected output mix rather than the feasible set.
q.imageAlt: Burgers are on the horizontal axis and fries on the vertical axis. Bowed PPF0 includes A at 10 burgers and 120 fries and B at 30 burgers and 80 fries. Dashed PPF1 lies outside PPF0, reaching about 150 fries at zero burgers and 60 burgers at zero fries.
q.feedback: The outward frontier makes more output feasible and places the old B inside the new boundary. A capacity change alone does not show that production adjusted or establish a welfare ranking.
q.graphDescription: Burgers are on the horizontal axis and fries on the vertical axis. Bowed PPF0 includes A at 10 burgers and 120 fries and B at 30 burgers and 80 fries. Dashed PPF1 lies outside PPF0, reaching about 150 fries at zero burgers and 60 burgers at zero fries.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: If moving from point A to point B on a PPF gives up 6 units of corn to gain 3 units of wheat, the opportunity cost per wheat is:
options: 2 units of corn
3 units of corn
6 units of corn
18 units of corn
q.feedback: Opportunity cost per wheat is corn given up divided by wheat gained: 6 / 3 = 2.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: With a constant production tradeoff, a country can produce either 80 units of food or 40 units of machinery. What is the opportunity cost of one unit of machinery?
options: 0.5 unit of machinery per unit of food
2 units of food per unit of machinery
2 units of machinery per unit of food
80 units of food per unit of machinery
q.feedback: Divide the 80 units of food forgone by the 40 units of machinery gained: 80 / 40 = 2 units of food per unit of machinery. The inverse ratio, 0.5 unit of machinery per unit of food, answers the opposite question; 80 is the total endpoint sacrifice, not the cost per machinery unit.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A PPF table shows that moving from Bundle B to Bundle C increases wheat from 40 to 55 but reduces corn from 90 to 60. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of wheat?
options: 15 units of corn
30 units of corn
2 units of corn
0.5 units of corn
q.feedback: Wheat rises by 15 and corn falls by 30. Opportunity cost per wheat is 30 / 15 = 2 corn.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when production moves from A to B?
options: 1.6 units of Good Y
5 units of Good Y
8 units of Good Y
0.625 units of Good Y
q.feedback: Moving from A to B gains 8 units of Good X and gives up 5 units of Good Y, so opportunity cost per Good X is 5 / 8 = 0.625.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when production moves from B to C?
options: About 1.43 units of Good Y
0.7 units of Good Y
7 units of Good Y
10 units of Good Y
q.feedback: Moving from B to C gains 7 units of Good X and gives up 10 units of Good Y, so 10 / 7 is about 1.43.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when production moves from D to E?
options: 4 units of Good Y
5 units of Good Y
0.2 units of Good Y
20 units of Good Y
q.feedback: Moving from D to E gains 4 units of Good X and gives up 20 units of Good Y, so 20 / 4 = 5.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good Y when production moves from E to D?
options: 5 units of Good X
4 units of Good X
0.2 units of Good X
20 units of Good X
q.feedback: Moving from E to D gives up 4 units of Good X to gain 20 units of Good Y, so 4 / 20 = 0.2 units of Good X per Good Y.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C increases production of Good X by how many units?
q.feedback: Point B has 8 units of Good X and point C has 15, so Good X increases by 7 units.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C requires giving up how many units of Good Y?
q.feedback: Good Y falls from 45 at B to 35 at C, so the economy gives up 10 units of Good Y.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost of moving from C to D?
options: 6 units of Good X
15 units of Good Y
20 units of Good Y
21 units of Good X
q.feedback: Moving from C to D raises Good X from 15 to 21, but Good Y falls from 35 to 20. The opportunity cost is 15 units of Good Y.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when moving from C to D?
options: 6 units of Good Y
15 units of Good Y
2.5 units of Good Y
0.4 units of Good Y
q.feedback: Moving from C to D gains 6 units of Good X and gives up 15 units of Good Y, so 15 / 6 = 2.5 units of Good Y per Good X.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: What does a production possibilities frontier show?
options: The legal maximum price in a market
Currently feasible combinations of two goods
The amount of tax paid by buyers
The demand curve for one product
q.feedback: A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: What does a point inside the PPF indicate?
options: Unattainable
Efficient
Attainable but inefficient
A binding price ceiling
q.feedback: A point inside the PPF is attainable, but resources are not being used efficiently.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A PPF move gives up 12 units of Good Y to gain 4 units of Good X. What is the opportunity cost per Good X?
options: 3 units of Good Y
4 units of Good Y
12 units of Good Y
48 units of Good Y
q.feedback: Opportunity cost per Good X is what is given up divided by what is gained: 12 / 4 = 3.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A country puts unemployed workers and idle factories back to work without gaining new technology. How does this appear on its PPF?
options: Production moves to the existing frontier, showing greater efficiency but no growth.
The frontier shifts outward, showing growth in productive capacity.
Production moves outside the frontier, becoming unattainable.
The frontier shifts inward because idle resources were used.
q.commonError: Calling movement to the existing frontier economic growth.
q.feedback: Using existing resources more fully moves production to the frontier; growth requires the frontier itself to shift outward.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A technological improvement affects only the production of medical equipment, not food. How does the PPF change?
options: The entire frontier shifts inward by the same amount.
The medical-equipment intercept moves outward; food stays fixed.
The frontier pivots outward toward the food axis only.
The economy moves along an unchanged frontier toward more food.
q.commonError: Treating a one-sector technology gain as an equal shift for both goods.
q.feedback: A productivity gain limited to one good expands the maximum attainable quantity of that good without changing the other intercept.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Why is a typical PPF bowed outward from the origin?
options: All resources are equally productive in every use.
Opportunity cost falls as specialization increases.
Specialized resources cause rising opportunity cost.
The economy is producing inside the frontier.
q.commonError: Attributing the bowed shape to equal resource adaptability or inefficiency.
q.feedback: As production shifts, resources increasingly unsuited to the expanding good must be reassigned, raising opportunity cost.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Moving from bundle A to B gains 5 machines and sacrifices 10 tons of food. Moving from B to C gains another 5 machines and sacrifices 20 tons of food. What does the pattern show?
options: The opportunity cost of machines rises from 2 to 4 tons of food per machine.
The opportunity cost of machines falls from 4 to 2 tons per machine.
The opportunity cost remains constant at 3 tons per machine.
Bundle C must lie inside the PPF because its food output is lower.
q.commonError: Comparing total sacrifices without converting each move to cost per additional unit.
q.feedback: The first move costs 10/5 = 2 tons per machine; the second costs 20/5 = 4, showing increasing opportunity cost.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Country A chooses more capital goods and fewer consumer goods today than Country B, with otherwise similar resources. What is the likely long-run implication?
options: Country A must have a lower future PPF because current consumption is smaller.
Country A may gain more future capacity because it produces more capital goods now.
Country B necessarily grows faster because consumption creates capital automatically.
Neither choice can affect future production possibilities.
q.commonError: Ignoring the link between current investment and future productive capacity.
q.feedback: Greater current production of capital goods can expand future capacity, though it requires sacrificing current consumption.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A disaster destroys equipment used only to produce electric power, while agricultural capacity is unchanged. What happens to the PPF?
options: It shifts outward equally for both goods.
It pivots inward toward the agricultural axis only.
Only the electric-power intercept moves inward.
It remains fixed because the economy can move along the frontier.
q.commonError: Treating a sector-specific loss as an equal inward shift or a movement along the same frontier.
q.feedback: Losing capacity in one sector reduces the maximum output of that good and rotates the frontier inward on that axis.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: On an unchanged efficient frontier, moving from 50 drones and 80 scanners to 65 drones and 50 scanners costs 2 scanners per added drone. The next 10 drones would reduce scanners from 50 to 20. A planner claims a constant cost of 2 and wants 10 more drones only if each is worth at least 2.5 scanners. Which evaluation is correct?
options: The next block costs 3 scanners per drone, so it fails the 2.5 threshold and indicates rising opportunity cost.
The next block costs 2 scanners per drone, so it passes the threshold because the previous average applies to every move.
The next block costs 0.33 scanner per drone, so it passes the threshold after inverting the ratio.
The next block costs 30 scanners per drone, so the frontier must have shifted inward rather than displaying changing tradeoffs.
q.feedback: The first cost is (80-50)/(65-50)=2. The next is (50-20)/10=3. At a value of 2.5 scanners per drone, the extra block loses 0.5 scanner-equivalent per drone. Changing slopes can occur along one unchanged bowed frontier.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A country starts inside its PPF with idle workers. Hiring them raises both outputs until the old frontier is reached. Later, technology improves only scanner production and the country can produce more scanners at the same drone output. Which diagnosis distinguishes the two changes?
options: Both changes shift the frontier outward equally because any rise in both observed outputs proves general capacity growth.
The first improves resource utilization; the second expands productive capacity asymmetrically, rather than merely moving along the old frontier.
The first is growth and the second is improved utilization because scanner output rises without reducing drones.
Neither changes productive capacity because every increase in one output must reduce the other under scarcity.
q.feedback: Using idle resources can move production to the existing frontier without changing capacity. Sector-specific technology expands feasible production toward scanners, so the later improvement cannot be attributed solely to more efficient use of the old technology.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: On one efficient frontier, the first 20 solar units sacrifice 5 food units and the next 20 sacrifice 14. A storage innovation then halves the food sacrifice required for each of those solar blocks, leaving maximum food output unchanged. Which conclusion separates the original tradeoff from the innovation?
options: Original marginal cost falls from 4 to about 1.43 food per solar unit; the innovation merely moves production along the same frontier.
Original marginal cost is constant at 0.475 food per solar unit; the innovation eliminates increasing opportunity cost because both blocks improve.
Original marginal cost rises from 0.25 to 0.70 food per solar unit; the innovation expands solar capacity, with the two costs falling to 0.125 and 0.35.
Original marginal cost rises from 5 to 14 food per solar unit; unchanged maximum food means productive capacity cannot expand.
q.feedback: Divide each food sacrifice by 20 solar units: 0.25 and 0.70. Halving sacrifices produces 0.125 and 0.35, still increasing across blocks. The new technology changes the feasible set, unlike movement along the original frontier.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: With full resource use and constant tradeoffs, an economy can make 100 food units or 50 medical units. Medical-only technology doubles maximum medical output, leaving maximum food unchanged. At 60 food, compare feasible medical output before and after; then assess an observed rise from an interior point to the old frontier.
options: Medical capacity rises from 20 to 50; every output increase from an interior point proves the whole frontier shifted equally.
Medical capacity stays 20 because food technology is unchanged; only a move to a new point on the old line is possible.
Medical capacity rises from 40 to 80; an interior-to-frontier move reduces efficiency because fewer resources remain idle.
Medical capacity at 60 food rises from 20 to 40; the separate interior-to-old-frontier move is improved utilization, not evidence of that technology shift.
q.commonError: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
q.feedback: The old linear frontier is M=50(1-F/100), giving 20 at F=60. The new one is M=100(1-F/100), giving 40. An interior-to-frontier move under old technology improves utilization without identifying a capacity change.

q.q: An economy initially produces 60 units of each good inside a frontier that permits 80 of each together. Reemploying idle labor reaches 80 of each. New machinery then permits 100 of each together. A planner attributes the entire increase to growth in productive capacity. Which counterfactual best exposes the error?
options: Without new machinery, reemployment could still reach 80 of each; only the later extension beyond the old feasible set demonstrates added capacity.
Without reemployment, machinery could not affect the frontier, because a frontier is defined by actual rather than possible output.
Without new machinery, output must remain at 60 of each, because any increase in both goods requires an outward frontier shift.
Without reemployment, the old frontier would automatically move inward to the observed 60-unit bundle.
q.commonError: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
q.feedback: Initial unused resources explain movement from 60 to 80 under the old feasible set. Machinery changes what can be produced, permitting 100 of each. Observed output growth combines utilization and capacity changes; it cannot all be labeled a frontier shift.

q.q: On a PPF, opportunity cost is measured by:
options: What must be given up to gain more of the other good
The money price of the good only
The legal maximum price
The tax paid by buyers
q.feedback: Opportunity cost on a PPF is what must be given up to get more of another good.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: An economy moves from inside its PPF to the frontier without new resources. What changed?
options: Productive capacity necessarily expanded
Unused resources were employed more efficiently
The frontier shifted outward
Opportunity cost disappeared
q.commonError: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
q.feedback: Moving from inside the PPF to its frontier uses idle or misallocated resources more fully; productive capacity and the frontier remain unchanged.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A production point lies inside the PPF. How should it be classified?
options: It is unattainable with current resources and technology.
It is efficient because it uses fewer resources.
It is attainable but inefficient because resources are underused.
It proves the economy has experienced long-run growth.
q.commonError: Treating an inside point as impossible or fully efficient.
q.feedback: A point inside the frontier is feasible, but the economy could produce more of at least one good with existing resources.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Is a point inside the PPF unattainable?
options: Yes; any point not on the frontier is unattainable
Yes; only points on the PPF are feasible
Yes; producing inside the frontier requires more resources than the economy has.
No; it is attainable but inefficient
q.feedback: A point inside the PPF is attainable with current resources but productively inefficient because some capacity is unused.

q.q: Does moving along a PPF represent economic growth?
options: No; it reallocates production on the same frontier
Yes; any movement to a different production mix is economic growth
Yes; producing more of one good means productive capacity has increased
Yes; moving along the frontier shifts it outward.
q.commonError: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
q.feedback: Movement along one PPF reallocates production between goods; economic growth requires an outward shift of the frontier.

q.q: What shifts a PPF outward?
options: Moving from one point to another on the existing frontier
More resources, better technology, or improved productive capacity
Reallocating idle resources without changing productive capacity
Producing more of one good by giving up some of the other.
q.commonError: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
q.feedback: More resources, improved technology, or better institutions can expand productive capacity and shift the PPF outward.

q.q: Why can opportunity cost rise along a bowed-out PPF?
options: Because the money price of the expanding good rises
Because the economy becomes less efficient as it moves along the frontier
Resources differ in suitability across uses
Because scarcity disappears for the good produced in larger quantities.
q.feedback: Specialized resources are less adaptable as production shifts toward one good, so each additional unit can require a larger sacrifice.

q.q: A bowed-out PPF shows that as more Good X is produced:
options: The opportunity cost of Good X rises
The opportunity cost of Good X falls to zero
The economy escapes scarcity
The PPF becomes a price floor
q.feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Why does opportunity cost usually rise along a bowed-out PPF?
options: Resources are perfectly identical in every use
Resources are not equally well suited to producing both goods
Scarcity disappears at high output levels
Prices are fixed by government
q.feedback: Opportunity cost rises because resources are specialized and become less well suited as they are shifted into the other good.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: An economy is producing inside its PPF. What is the best interpretation?
options: The point is unattainable
The point is efficient
The point is attainable but inefficient
The point eliminates scarcity
q.feedback: A point inside the PPF can be produced, but resources are not being used efficiently.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A workshop makes chairs and desks. Better scheduling lets previously idle machines produce more of both until no further increase in either is possible without reducing the other. Labor, machines and technology are unchanged. How does this appear on its PPF?
options: An outward shift of the frontier.
A move from one frontier point to another.
A move beyond the unchanged frontier.
A move from inside to the unchanged frontier.
q.feedback: Idle machines initially put production inside the PPF. Using existing capacity fully moves production to the frontier. The unchanged resources and technology mean capacity has not expanded, so the frontier does not shift.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: An economy gains more capital and better technology. What happens to its PPF?
options: It shifts outward
It shifts inward
It becomes a demand curve
It creates a binding price floor
q.feedback: More resources or better technology increase productive capacity, shifting the PPF outward.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A natural disaster destroys factories and equipment. What happens to the PPF?
options: It shifts outward
It shifts inward
The economy moves to a different point on the same PPF.
Opportunity cost disappears
q.feedback: A loss of productive resources reduces what the economy can produce, shifting the PPF inward.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: Moving along a PPF gives up 18 units of Good Y to gain 6 units of Good X. What is the opportunity cost per unit of Good X?
options: 6 units of Good Y
18 units of Good Y
3 units of Good Y
108 units of Good Y
q.feedback: Opportunity cost per Good X is what is given up divided by what is gained: 18 / 6 = 3.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A PPF move gains 5 units of Good X but gives up 20 units of Good Y. What is the opportunity cost per additional Good X?
options: 5 units of Good Y
20 units of Good Y
0.25 units of Good Y
4 units of Good Y
q.feedback: The economy gives up 20 units of Good Y to gain 5 units of Good X, so 20 / 5 = 4.

labels: LO2.2

q.q: A tax levied on sellers and an equal tax levied on buyers are generally:
options: Equivalent in their market effects
Completely unrelated
Opposite in their effect on quantity
Always paid only by sellers
q.feedback: A tax on buyers or sellers creates the same wedge and similar market effects.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the post-tax quantity of 60 thousand movies, what price do sellers receive?
options: $10.50 per movie
$13.50 per movie
$7.50 per movie
$6.00 per movie
q.feedback: At quantity 60 thousand, the shifted demand curve intersects supply at $7.50. That is the amount sellers receive before the buyer remits the tax.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers pay most of the burden. What explains this?
options: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden
Sellers always avoid all taxes
Buyers became legally responsible for the tax after prices adjusted.
The market must have a price ceiling
q.feedback: Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: Refer to the graph. What per-unit tax wedge is created by the buyer-side tax?
options: $3 per movie
$7.50 per movie
$21 per movie
$6 per movie
q.feedback: At the post-tax quantity, read the buyer price and seller receipt from the graph and take the difference: $13.50 − $7.50 = $6.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which side bears more of the buyer-side tax?
options: Neither; the burden is split equally.
Buyers bear more of the tax than sellers.
Sellers bear more of the tax than buyers.
Neither side bears any economic tax burden.
q.feedback: Buyers pay $3 more than the original $10.50 price, while sellers receive $3 less. The legal placement on buyers does not make buyers bear the entire tax.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers end up paying most of the burden. What does this show?
options: Economic incidence does not depend only on legal assignment
Sellers never pay taxes
Buyers must have become the statutory taxpayers when the market price changed.
The tax must be a price ceiling
q.feedback: Who legally pays the tax does not determine who bears the economic burden.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: A policy analyst says a tax legally placed on sellers will be paid entirely by sellers. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Legal assignment does not determine economic incidence
Sellers always pass the entire tax to buyers
Buyers always avoid taxes completely
A seller tax is the same as a price floor
q.feedback: Economic tax burden depends on market responses and elasticities, not only on who legally sends payment.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: A tax causes buyers to pay more, sellers to receive less, and quantity to fall. Which statement is false?
options: The side legally assigned the tax must bear the entire burden
The tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
The market quantity falls after the tax
Buyers and sellers can both be worse off per unit traded
q.feedback: The legal assignment does not determine the entire burden. Market elasticities matter.

labels: LO6.4

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. If the same per-unit tax is collected from buyers instead of sellers, with demand and supply unchanged, which outcome follows?
options: Buyers still pay $18 in total, sellers keep $12, and 80 units trade
Buyers pay $21 in total, sellers keep $15, and 80 units trade
Buyers pay $18 in total, sellers keep $18, and 100 units trade
