q.q: Refer to the graph. Which side bears more of the $8 tax, and what does that imply about relative elasticity?
options: Buyers bear 6 dollars; demand is less elastic
Sellers bear 2 dollars; supply is more elastic
Buyers bear all 8 dollars; demand is perfectly inelastic
Sellers bear $6; supply is less elastic.
q.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.
q.feedback: The seller price falls by $6 while the buyer price rises by $2. Sellers therefore bear more of the tax, consistent with supply being less elastic than demand.
q.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the graph. Why does a tax imposed on sellers not mean sellers bear the entire $8 burden?
options: Market prices adjust so buyers bear $2 of the tax and sellers bear $6.
Sellers bear no burden whenever the supply curve shifts
Buyers must bear all 8 dollars because demand slopes down
No tax wedge exists at the new equilibrium quantity
q.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.
q.feedback: Statutory placement does not prevent prices from splitting the burden.
q.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. A seller argues that its legal duty to remit the tax means it bears the entire revenue rectangle. What do the price changes and continuing quantity show?
options: Each side bears $3 per unit and $240 of the $480 rectangle
Sellers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle
Each side bears $3 per unit and $300 of the $600 rectangle
Buyers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle
q.feedback: Relative to $15, buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less. At 80 units, each incidence rectangle is $240, together equaling $480 of revenue. Remitting the money is different from bearing the price burden; these rectangles exclude gains lost on missing trades.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: A $4 tax is placed on concert tickets. Buyers pay $2.50 more than before, sellers receive $1.50 less than before, and fewer tickets are sold. Which statement is strongest?
options: The burden is shared, quantity falls, and the side less able to adjust bears more
The burden falls only on sellers because the legal tax is charged to sellers
The burden falls only on buyers because the buyer price increased
The burden disappears because tax revenue offsets the lower quantity sold
q.feedback: Legal responsibility for the tax does not determine economic burden. The wedge is shared and quantity falls.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: A market has an $8 tax, a total buyer price of $26 and a net seller receipt of $18. Buyers bear 75% of the per-unit burden. What was the untaxed price, and which side is less price responsive over this change?
options: $20; buyers
$24; sellers
$20; sellers
$24; buyers
q.feedback: Buyer burden is 0.75 × $8 = $6, so the old price was $26 − $6 = $20. Sellers bear the remaining $2, since $20 − $18 = $2. Under the standard tax-incidence comparison, the side bearing more of the wedge is less price responsive.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Supply is perfectly inelastic at 200 units and demand slopes downward. A $6 tax is imposed in a competitive market with no externalities or collection costs. Which combination follows?
options: Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
Buyers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is $1,200
Buyers and sellers each bear $3, revenue is $600, and quantity falls
q.feedback: The vertical supply curve holds quantity at 200. Buyers pay the same demand price at that quantity, so sellers absorb the full $6 wedge through lower net receipts. Revenue is $1,200. With no trades lost and no other distortions in the stated model, tax revenue is a transfer and there is no deadweight loss.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the graph. The tax is legally imposed on buyers. Which statement correctly describes who remits the tax, who bears the economic burden, and what the burden split implies about elasticity?
options: Buyers remit the tax, bear all $8, and are more elastic.
Sellers remit the tax, bear $6, and are less elastic.
Sellers bear $2, implying perfectly elastic supply.
Buyers remit the tax, bear $6, and are less elastic.
q.imageAlt: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.
q.feedback: The buyer-side tax is legally assigned to buyers, but prices split burden 6 to buyers and 2 to sellers.
q.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: A $5 tax causes buyers to pay $3 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. How is the burden split?
options: Buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $3
Sellers bear all $5
Buyers bear all $5
q.feedback: The buyer burden is the price increase paid by buyers. The seller burden is the price decrease received by sellers.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Before a tax, buyers pay $30 and sellers receive $30. After a tax, buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Who bears more of the burden?
options: Buyers
Sellers
They split it equally
No one bears any burden
q.feedback: Buyers pay $4 more, while sellers receive $3 less. Buyers bear more of the burden.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the buyers’ tax burden on the units still traded, excluding surplus lost on missing trades?
q.feedback: The per-unit buyer burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the seller-burden rectangle on the units still traded, excluding surplus lost on missing trades?
q.feedback: The per-unit seller burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the combined buyer- and seller-burden rectangle on units still traded, which becomes government revenue?
q.feedback: The $6 wedge applies to 80 continuing trades, so the rectangle is $480. This is the combined per-unit incidence times taxed quantity. Lost gains from the missing trades are additional welfare loss and are not government revenue.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. For the units still purchased after the tax, what is the total extra payment by buyers relative to paying the original price for those same units? This question excludes the welfare effect of purchases forgone.
options: $300: $3 extra on the original 100 units.
$480: the full $6 tax on the remaining 80 units.
$240: $3 extra on the remaining 80 units.
$540: the change in sellers’ total receipts.
q.feedback: The buyer price rises from $15 to $18 and 80 units are purchased after tax. For these continuing purchases, the extra payment is ($18 - $15) x 80 = $240. Using all 100 original units includes purchases no longer made; using $6 assigns the seller burden to buyers.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. A seller group divides the fall in total net-of-tax sales receipts by the 80 units still sold and calls the result its tax burden per continuing unit. Why is that calculation misleading?
options: The $540 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $3.
The $540 receipt decline is entirely a price effect; the burden on each continuing unit is $6.75.
The $240 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $6.
The $300 receipt decline is entirely a quantity effect; the price burden on each continuing unit is $0.
q.feedback: Receipts fall from $15 x 100 = $1,500 to $12 x 80 = $960, a $540 decline. This combines $300 from 20 fewer units valued at the old price and $240 from receiving $3 less on each of 80 continuing sales. The per-unit seller tax burden is $15 - $12 = $3; gross receipts are not a measure of producer surplus.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: A $6 tax causes buyers to pay $4 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. Who bears more of the tax burden?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Both sides bear zero burden
Only the government
q.feedback: Buyers bear $4 of the $6 tax, while sellers bear $2, so buyers bear more.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by buyers?
q.feedback: Buyers paid $15 before the tax and pay $18 after the tax, so their burden is $3.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by sellers?
q.feedback: Sellers received $15 before the tax and receive $12 after the tax, so their burden is $3.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: A $6 tax is imposed. Before the tax, buyers paid $20. After the tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. How much of the tax burden falls on buyers and sellers?
options: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
Buyers bear all $6 and sellers bear $0
Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18
q.feedback: Buyers now pay $4 more than before. Sellers receive $2 less than before. The $6 tax burden is split $4 on buyers and $2 on sellers.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Demand is much less elastic than supply. A tax is imposed on the good. Who bears more of the tax burden, and why?
options: Buyers bear more because they are less able to reduce quantity demanded
Sellers bear more because supply is more elastic
Buyers and sellers must split the burden equally
Sellers bear more because buyers pay the tax through the market price
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax because it is less able to change behavior in response to the tax.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Supply is much less elastic than demand. A tax is imposed. What is the likely result?
options: Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive
Buyers bear more of the burden because demand is more elastic
The burden must be equal because the tax wedge is fixed
The side required to remit the tax bears more because statutory payment determines the economic burden
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic than demand, sellers bear more of the burden.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: In a competitive market, demand elasticity is Ed=-0.25 and supply elasticity Es=1.20 near equilibrium. A small unit tax is introduced. Later, buyers gain substitutes and Ed becomes -1.50 while Es stays 1.20. Which comparison is best, holding the initial price, quantity and tax size comparable?
options: Buyers initially bear more; afterward sellers bear more, and the stronger demand response makes the tax-induced quantity reduction larger.
Sellers initially bear more; afterward buyers bear more, and stronger demand response makes the quantity reduction smaller.
Buyers bear more in both cases because the negative sign makes demand less elastic than every positive supply elasticity.
Burden shares reverse only if the law changes the tax remitter; elasticity changes affect quantity but not economic incidence.
q.feedback: Compare absolute elasticities. Initially 0.25<1.20, so buyers are less responsive and bear more. Later 1.50>1.20, so sellers are relatively less responsive. Greater demand responsiveness also increases the quantity response to a comparable small tax.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Demand elasticity is -1.80 and supply elasticity is 0.20 in a market. A small tax is imposed on sellers. Over time, sellers gain alternative uses for their resources and supply elasticity rises to 2.40, with demand elasticity unchanged. Compare equal small taxes from the same initial price and quantity. Which evaluation is correct?
options: Buyers initially bear more, but sellers bear more later; the legal seller tax becomes binding only in the long run.
Sellers initially bear more, but buyers bear more later; greater supply responsiveness also increases the quantity response to the tax.
Sellers bear more in both periods because the statute requires them to remit the tax, regardless of alternatives.
Burden becomes exactly equal later because both elasticity magnitudes exceed one, making relative sizes irrelevant.
q.feedback: Initially supply magnitude 0.20 is below demand magnitude 1.80, so sellers bear more. Later supply magnitude 2.40 exceeds demand, so buyers bear more. More responsive supply permits a greater quantity adjustment under a comparable small tax.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Before a tax, market price is $40. After a $12 unit tax, buyers pay $43 and sellers receive $31. A reform puts legal remittance on buyers without changing behavior or the tax size. Which combined inference is supported?
options: Buyers bear 75% and sellers 25%; demand is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone reverses the $43/$31 price pair.
Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; supply is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone leaves the $43/$31 price pair unchanged.
Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; demand is relatively less elastic, so buyer remittance makes buyers bear the entire $12.
Buyers bear 50% and sellers 50%; the $12 wedge must be split evenly once both sides participate in the market.
q.feedback: Buyer burden is 43-40=3 and seller burden 40-31=9, totaling 12. Shares are 3/12=25% and 9/12=75%. In the standard model the less elastic side bears more, indicating relatively less elastic supply. Legal remittance alone does not alter the wedge equilibrium.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: The less elastic side of the market usually bears:
options: More of the tax burden
Less of the tax burden
None of the tax burden
Only the portion of the tax named in the statute.
q.feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: When demand is less elastic than supply, which side is less able to avoid the tax?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Neither side
Only the government
q.feedback: If demand is less elastic, buyers bear more of the tax burden.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: A tax causes buyers to pay $5 more and sellers to receive $2 less. Which side likely has less elastic behavior?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Neither side
The government
q.feedback: The side bearing more of the tax is usually less elastic. Buyers bear $5, so demand is likely less elastic.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: Supply is less elastic than demand. Who is expected to bear more of a tax?
options: Sellers
Buyers
Both sides bear zero
Only the legal taxpayer
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic, sellers bear more.

labels: LO6.5

q.q: A tax on a good generally causes the quantity sold to:
options: Decrease
Increase
Stay exactly the same always
Become unlimited
q.feedback: A tax raises the effective cost of trade, so the quantity sold falls.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A tax creates a wedge between:
options: The price buyers pay and the price sellers receive
Demand and consumer income only
Two different PPFs
Positive and normative statements
q.feedback: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and what sellers receive.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: In the displayed movie market, how large is the vertical gap between S0 and the parallel “Supply with tax” curve at a given quantity?
options: $4 per movie
$2 per movie
$10 per movie
$14 per movie
q.feedback: At quantity 100 thousand, S0 is at $10 while Supply with tax is at $14. The parallel vertical gap is therefore $4 per movie.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A tax on sellers shifts the supply curve upward because:
options: The tax raises the cost of selling each unit
The tax increases buyers' income
The tax makes demand perfectly elastic
The tax eliminates opportunity cost
q.feedback: A tax on sellers raises the cost of selling each unit, shifting supply upward.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A tax reduces the quantity sold from 100 units to 75 units. What is the best interpretation?
options: The tax shrinks the size of the market
The tax eliminates scarcity
The tax increases both supply and demand
The tax causes quantity sold to rise
q.feedback: A tax raises the cost of exchange and reduces the quantity traded.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the original equilibrium price and quantity before the tax?
options: $15 and 100 units
$18 and 80 units
$12 and 80 units
$20 and 65 units
q.feedback: Before the tax, demand and the original supply curve intersect at $15 and 100 units.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. After the tax, what price do buyers pay?
q.feedback: After the tax, the price buyers pay is read from the demand curve at the new quantity, which is $18.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. After the tax, what price do sellers receive?
q.feedback: After the tax, sellers receive $12 per unit after the tax is accounted for.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What happens to the quantity sold after the tax?
options: It falls from 100 to 80 units
It rises from 80 to 100 units
It stays at 100 units
It rises from 100 to 120 units
q.feedback: The tax reduces the quantity sold from 100 units to 80 units.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. Which statement best describes the effect of the tax?
options: The tax creates a wedge and reduces the quantity traded
The tax increases both supply and demand
The tax raises quantity from 80 to 100
The tax removes scarcity from the market
q.feedback: The tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices and reduces the quantity traded.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: After the seller-side tax shown, quantity falls to 100 thousand movies. What prices do buyers pay and sellers receive?
options: Buyers pay $12 and sellers receive $12
Buyers pay $14 and sellers receive $10
Buyers pay $10 and sellers receive $14
Buyers pay $14 and sellers receive $12
q.feedback: At the post-tax quantity of 100 thousand, demand gives the buyer price of $14 while the original supply curve gives the seller receipt of $10.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the graph. After the tax is imposed, by how much does quantity traded fall?
options: 20 thousand movies
100 thousand movies
40 thousand movies
240 thousand movies
q.feedback: Read the pre-tax and post-tax quantities from the graph: 140 thousand − 100 thousand = 40 thousand movies.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the graph. What is the post-tax quantity?
options: 150 thousand tickets
50 thousand tickets
200 thousand tickets

q.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 16; original supply there gives seller price 8.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A $10 tax is imposed. Before the tax, price is $50. After the tax, buyers pay $56 and sellers receive $46. What happened to quantity sold?
options: It likely decreased because the tax created a wedge
It must have increased because buyers pay more
It stayed exactly the same because the tax is split
It became zero because all taxes eliminate trade
q.feedback: A tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices and usually reduces the quantity traded.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the tax wedge and what happens to quantity sold?
options: The wedge is $6 and quantity falls from 100 to 80
The wedge is $3 and quantity falls from 100 to 80
The wedge is $6 and quantity rises from 80 to 100
The wedge is $30 and quantity stays at 100
q.feedback: The wedge is $18 - $12 = $6, and quantity falls from 100 before the tax to 80 after the tax.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. What is the per-unit tax, and why is the rise in the buyer price alone insufficient?
options: $6; the buyer price rises $3 and the seller receipt falls $3
$3; only the buyer price change is part of the tax
$18; the entire buyer payment is remitted to government
$33; the original and new buyer prices must be added
q.feedback: The taxed quantity is 80. There, buyers pay $18 and sellers receive $12, so the wedge is $6. Relative to the original $15 price, each side bears $3. Using only the buyer increase omits the seller burden.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. If students use the original quantity of 100 to calculate tax revenue, what mistake are they making?
options: They are ignoring that the tax reduces quantity sold to 80
They are correctly using the pre-tax market size
They are measuring the buyer burden only
They are calculating a shortage
q.feedback: Tax revenue is based on the quantity actually sold after the tax, which is 80 units.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the graph. After the tax is imposed, how much tax revenue is collected?
q.feedback: Read the $4 per-movie wedge and the 100-thousand post-tax quantity from the graph. Revenue is $4 × 100,000 = $400,000.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: What revenue and quantity change are shown?
options: Revenue is 800,000 dollars; trips rise by 50 thousand
Revenue is 600,000 dollars; trips do not change
Revenue is 600,000 dollars; trips fall by 50 thousand
Revenue is 400,000 dollars; trips fall by 150 thousand
q.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 8.
q.feedback: Four dollars times 150 thousand is 600,000; quantity falls by 50 thousand.
q.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 8.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the graph. How much daily tax revenue is generated?
options: 400,000 dollars
1,000,000 dollars
1,200,000 dollars
800,000 dollars
q.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 250 and price 12 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 200 and buyer price 14; original supply there gives seller price 10.
q.feedback: The 4 dollar wedge applies to 200 thousand trips.
q.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 250 and price 12 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 200 and buyer price 14; original supply there gives seller price 10.

options: 400,000 dollars
800,000 dollars

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the graph. For the buyer-side tax, what are the wedge and revenue?
options: A 6 dollar wedge and 900,000
An 8 dollar wedge and 1.2 million dollars
An 8 dollar wedge and 1.6 million
A 2 dollar wedge and 300,000
q.imageAlt: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.
q.feedback: Buyers pay 16, sellers receive 8, and 150 thousand tickets are taxed.
q.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.

q.q: A tax on gasoline raises the price paid by drivers, lowers the price received by sellers, and reduces gallons sold. Which concept chain is correct?
options: Tax wedge → shared burden → lower quantity traded
Price ceiling → shortage → higher quantity traded
Demand increase → higher price → higher quantity
PPF shift → economic growth → lower price
q.feedback: A tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices, splits the burden, and reduces the quantity traded.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A market begins in equilibrium. A tax is imposed, and quantity falls from 1,000 to 850. Buyers pay $4 more and sellers receive $6 less. What is the tax revenue?
q.feedback: The tax is $4 + $6 = $10 per unit. Revenue is $10 × 850 = $8,500.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A market starts at price $40. After a tax, buyers pay $46 and sellers receive $34. Quantity sold falls from 500 to 420. What is total tax revenue?
q.feedback: The tax is $46 - $34 = $12. Tax revenue is $12 × 420 = $5,040.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A luxury tax causes quantity sold to fall sharply and tax revenue disappoints. What is the strongest explanation?
options: Elastic participants avoid much of the taxed exchange.
The tax must be too small to matter
The burden must fall entirely on buyers
A tax always increases total revenue
q.feedback: If market participants respond strongly, quantity falls sharply and tax revenue may be lower than expected.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the movie-tax graph. A report counts only the buyer price increase as the tax rate. Which correction correctly gives the two per-unit burdens and total government revenue?
options: Buyers bear $2 and sellers $2; revenue is $400,000
Buyers bear $2 and sellers $2; revenue is $560,000
Buyers bear $4 and sellers $0; revenue is $400,000
Buyers bear $2 and sellers $0; revenue is $200,000
q.feedback: The old price is $12, buyer price $14 and seller receipt $10. Thus the burdens are $2 each, summing to the $4 wedge. Apply that wedge to 100,000 taxed units: revenue is $400,000. The old quantity of 140,000 no longer trades.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which complete pre/post comparison is correct?
options: Buyer price +2, seller price -2, quantity -50 thousand
Buyer price +4, seller price unchanged, quantity +50 thousand
Buyer price +4, seller price -4, quantity unchanged
Buyer price -2, seller price +2, quantity -50 thousand
q.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 250 and price 12 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 200 and buyer price 14; original supply there gives seller price 10.
q.feedback: The market moves from price 12, quantity 250 to buyer 14, seller 10, quantity 200.
q.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 250 and price 12 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 200 and buyer price 14; original supply there gives seller price 10.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the rideshare graph with A at quantity 250 thousand. A proposal halves the displayed per-trip tax. Keeping the straight demand and supply curves fixed, what happens to daily tax revenue?
options: It falls from $800,000 to $400,000 because quantity stays fixed
It falls from $800,000 to $450,000 as quantity rises to 225,000
It rises from $800,000 to $900,000 as quantity rises to 225,000
It falls from $1,000,000 to $500,000 using the untaxed quantity
q.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 250 and price 12 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 200 and buyer price 14; original supply there gives seller price 10.
q.feedback: The displayed wedge is $14 − $10 = $4 at 200,000 trips. Halving it to $2 places quantity halfway between 200,000 and the untaxed 250,000: 225,000. Revenue changes from $4 × 200,000 = $800,000 to $2 × 225,000 = $450,000. The quantity response offsets part of the rate cut.
q.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 250 and price 12 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 200 and buyer price 14; original supply there gives seller price 10.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. A clerk uses only the buyer price increase as the tax rate and multiplies by the original quantity, reporting $300 of revenue. Which correction addresses both errors?
options: $6 per unit on 80 units gives $480; the report is $180 too low
$3 per unit on 80 units gives $240; the report is $60 too high
$6 per unit on 100 units gives $600; the report is $300 too low
$3 per unit on 100 units gives $300; the report is correct
q.feedback: The graph gives buyer price $18 and seller receipt $12, so the rate is $6, not the $3 buyer increase. Only 80 units trade after tax. Correct revenue is $480, which exceeds the reported $300 by $180. Fixing only one error still gives the wrong amount.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. What happens to market size after the tax is imposed?
options: Quantity falls from 100 to 80 because the tax creates a wedge
Quantity rises from 80 to 100 because the tax raises buyer price
Quantity stays at 100 because tax revenue replaces lost trades
Quantity rises to 150 because sellers receive the old price
q.feedback: A tax creates a wedge that reduces quantity traded.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. An analyst calls the government receipt the entire efficiency loss. With no externalities and using the straight curve segments around the two equilibria, which correction is right?
options: Revenue is $480; deadweight loss is $60
Revenue is $600; deadweight loss is $60
Revenue is $480; deadweight loss is $480
Revenue is $240; deadweight loss is $120
q.feedback: Buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12 and 80 units trade, so revenue is $6 × 80 = $480. Quantity falls from 100 to 80, giving a lost-gains triangle of 0.5 × 20 × $6 = $60. Revenue transfers surplus to government; the missing trades destroy surplus.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. Which statement correctly describes the supply + tax curve?
options: It shows sellers require a higher buyer price at each quantity because the tax raises cost per unit
It shows buyers demand more at each price because the tax raises value per unit
It shows the original supply curve shifting right because production is cheaper
It shows the demand curve shifting right because consumers pay the tax
q.feedback: A seller-side tax shifts supply upward/left by the amount of the tax.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A $7 tax reduces quantity from 500 to 420 units. What does this show beyond tax revenue?
options: The tax shrinks the market by discouraging mutually beneficial trades
The tax increases market size because government collects revenue
The tax leaves buyers and sellers unaffected if revenue is spent
The tax creates a surplus because quantity falls
q.feedback: A tax reduces quantity traded, meaning some mutually beneficial exchanges no longer happen.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Before tax, price is $20 and quantity is 1,000. After a $6 tax, buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18, and quantity is 850. What is tax revenue?
q.feedback: Tax revenue equals tax per unit times after-tax quantity: $6 × 850 = $5,100.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A linear market has demand P = 30 − Q and supply P = 6 + Q. Compare an $8 tax with a $14 ceiling. Under the ceiling, available units go to the highest-value buyers and lowest-cost sellers, with no search costs. With no externalities, which comparison is correct?
options: Both trade 8 units and retain $128 of total surplus; the ceiling gives consumers $64 more surplus
Both trade 8 units, but the tax destroys its $64 revenue and leaves only $64 of total surplus
The tax trades 8 units, but the ceiling trades all 16 units demanded at $14
Both retain $144 of total surplus because revenue and lower prices are transfers
q.feedback: Untaxed Q is 12 and TS is $144. With the tax, Q = 8, buyers pay $22 and sellers receive $14: CS = $32, PS = $32 and revenue = $64, totaling $128. The ceiling also supports 8 supplied units; efficient allocation gives CS = $96 and PS = $32. Each loses $16 of gains, but consumers receive $64 more under the ceiling. This equality depends on the stated allocation and cost assumptions.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A city taxes ride-share trips. Riders pay higher prices, drivers receive less per trip, and fewer trips occur. What is the best synthesis?
options: The tax wedge is shared and shrinks the number of exchanges
The tax affects only riders if they see the fee at checkout
The tax affects only drivers if the platform remits it
The tax increases quantity because government revenue rises
q.feedback: A tax creates a wedge shared by market participants and reduces the quantity traded.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the movie-tax graph. A review finds that CS plus PS falls by $480,000 after the displayed tax. With no externalities or collection costs, how should that change be reconciled with incidence and total surplus?
options: $480,000 is lost surplus, while the $400,000 revenue is an additional loss
$400,000 becomes revenue, $80,000 is lost surplus, and each side bears $2 per unit
$560,000 becomes revenue, total surplus rises $80,000, and each side bears $2
$400,000 becomes revenue, $80,000 is lost surplus, and buyers bear all $4 per unit
q.feedback: Read the old price $12, buyer price $14, seller receipt $10 and taxed quantity 100,000. The $4 wedge raises $400,000. Subtracting that transfer from the $480,000 private loss leaves $80,000 of lost surplus, also 0.5 × 40,000 × $4. Each side bears $2 on each remaining unit.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: After a tax, buyers pay $12 and sellers receive $9. What is the tax per unit?
q.feedback: The tax wedge is the difference between what buyers pay and sellers receive: $12 - $9 = $3.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: If buyers pay $15 after a tax and sellers receive $10, the wedge is:
q.feedback: The wedge is the difference between buyer price and seller price: $15 - $10 = $5.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Before a tax, buyers pay $30 and sellers receive $30. After a tax, buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. What is the tax per unit?
q.feedback: The tax wedge is the buyer price minus the seller price: $34 - $27 = $7.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A tax reduces quantity sold from 500 to 420 units. If the tax is $8 per unit, how much tax revenue is collected?
q.feedback: Tax revenue uses the quantity sold after the tax: $8 × 420 = $3,360.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. Before the tax, the equilibrium is $15 and 100 units. After the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and 80 units are sold. What is total tax revenue?
q.feedback: The tax is $18 - $12 = $6 per unit. Tax revenue is $6 × 80 = $480.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Before a tax, buyers pay $10 and sellers receive $10. After the tax, buyers pay $12 and sellers receive $8. What is the tax wedge?
q.feedback: The wedge is the price buyers pay minus the price sellers receive: $12 - $8 = $4.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the amount of the tax per unit?
q.feedback: The tax wedge is the difference between what buyers pay and what sellers receive: $18 - $12 = $6.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. By how many units does the tax reduce the quantity sold?
options: 20 units
80 units
100 units
180 units
q.feedback: Quantity falls from 100 to 80, so the tax reduces quantity sold by 20 units.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A $6 tax is placed on a good. Before the tax, equilibrium price is $20 and quantity is 1,000. After the tax, buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18, and quantity falls to 850. What is the tax wedge?
q.feedback: The tax wedge is the difference between what buyers pay and sellers receive. $24 - $18 = $6.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A tax causes buyers to pay $24, sellers to receive $18, and quantity sold to fall from 1,000 to 850. What happens to the market size and government tax revenue?
options: Market size shrinks to 850 units, and tax revenue is $5,100
Market size grows to 1,000 units, and tax revenue is $6,000
Market size stays at 1,000 units, and tax revenue is $5,100
Market size shrinks to 850 units, and tax revenue is $4,250
q.feedback: A tax shrinks the market. Revenue equals tax per unit times post-tax quantity: $6 x 850 = $5,100.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A policymaker compares two policies. Policy A is a binding price ceiling that creates a shortage. Policy B is a tax that creates a wedge between buyer price and seller price. What do both policies have in common?
options: Both can reduce the quantity traded below the unregulated market equilibrium
Both can raise the posted price buyers pay above the original equilibrium price
Both can create excess supply at the legal market price
Both can leave the market efficient if the legal price is clearly stated
q.feedback: Binding ceilings and taxes work differently, but both can reduce the quantity traded below the unregulated equilibrium.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Before a tax, buyers pay $30 and sellers receive $30. After a $7 tax, buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Which statement is correct?
options: The tax wedge is $4
The tax wedge is $7
Sellers bear the entire tax
Buyers bear the entire tax
q.feedback: The difference between the buyer price and seller receipt is $34 − $27 = $7.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A per-unit tax is imposed in a market with downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply. Which pair of effects is expected?
options: Buyer price falls and quantity rises
Seller receipt rises and quantity falls
Buyer price rises, seller receipt falls, and quantity falls
Buyer price and seller receipt both rise by the full tax
q.feedback: The tax creates a wedge: buyers pay more, sellers receive less, and fewer units are traded.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A $10 tax reduces equilibrium quantity only slightly in Market A but sharply in Market B. What is the strongest inference?
options: Market A likely has less elastic demand and/or supply around equilibrium
Market A must have more elastic demand and supply
Tax revenue must be zero in Market A
The statutory side paying the tax differs across markets
q.feedback: Less elastic curves produce a smaller quantity response to a given tax wedge.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A tax wedge is the difference between:
options: The price buyers pay and the price sellers receive
Quantity demanded and quantity supplied
Two points on a PPF
A price ceiling and a price floor
q.feedback: A tax wedge separates what buyers pay from what sellers receive.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Buyers pay $18 after a tax and sellers receive $12. What is the tax per unit?
q.feedback: The tax wedge is $18 - $12 = $6.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: Before a tax, buyers pay $20 and sellers receive $20. After the tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. What is the tax per unit?
q.feedback: The tax wedge is buyer price minus seller price: $24 - $18 = $6.

labels: LO6.3

q.q: A tax raises the price buyers pay and lowers the price sellers receive. What else usually happens?
options: Quantity traded falls
Quantity traded rises
Scarcity disappears
The PPF shifts outward
q.feedback: A tax creates a wedge and reduces the quantity traded.

labels: LO6.3
